The Tumblerock Cliffs rose ahead.
"You found it," said Pip.
"I always find things," said Flint.
"Eventually."

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Luna read out the race rules.
The course: from the Hollow Oak to the Crystal Stream to the Tumblerock Cliffs and back.
Everyone was at the starting line.
Everyone was ready.
Mostly.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon does not make its own light. It has no fire or glow inside. The light we see is sunlight bouncing off the Moon's surface.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: "What is this?" said Pip. He picked it up carefully. The glow made his fingers feel warm.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: That evening, Pip sat by the Crystal Stream. He looked at the stone. The gold glow had gone out.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
The mushroom's glow changed.
It pulsed once — pointing.
Another mushroom far away pulsed the same way.
And another.
A trail of glowing mushrooms lit up through the trees.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
The fire faded slowly.
Moonwood kept its glow.
Luna looked at Glimmer over her glasses.
"Quite controlled," said Luna.
"Thank you," said Glimmer.

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
The Deep Dark was very dark.
The trees had no glow.
The light went only a little way ahead.
They walked close together.
No one was last.
No one was alone.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Other volcanoes are very explosive. They blast ash, smoke and rocks high into the sky. The blast can be heard hundreds of kilometres away.

uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: Penguins live in large groups called colonies. Some colonies have hundreds of thousands of penguins! Each penguin recognises its partner and its chick by their call.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: Almost every plant starts as a tiny seed. Seeds come in hundreds of different shapes and sizes. Each one holds everything a plant needs to begin life.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Over time, tunnels and chambers form underground. Some cave systems stretch for hundreds of kilometres. The Mammoth Cave system in America has more than 650 kilometres of passages.

uses.title: Frogs
uses.pageText: A female frog lays hundreds of eggs in water. The eggs are called frogspawn. Each egg is surrounded by clear jelly that protects it and keeps it safe.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: They walked along the walls slowly. There were drawings of things no one had seen in hundreds of years. What is this place? asked Fern.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Sometimes, magma pushes up through a crack in the Earth. When it bursts out at the surface, we call it a volcano! The melted rock that flows out is called lava.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Lava can be as hot as 1,000 degrees. Some volcanoes are calm and slow. Their lava oozes out like very thick, very hot syrup.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Lava can be as hot as 1,000 degrees. Some volcanoes are calm and slow. Their lava oozes out like very thick, very hot syrup.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Volcanoes can be found on land and under the sea. When an underwater volcano keeps erupting, the lava builds up and can make a brand new island!

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: After a volcano, the cooled lava becomes new rock. Volcanic rock breaks down into rich, dark soil. Many plants and crops grow very well in volcanic soil.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Caves are hollow spaces underground or inside cliffs. They form in many different ways. Some are made by water, some by sea waves, and some by ancient flowing lava.

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: Stone stepped onto the bridge. It creaked under Stone's weight. Stone kept going.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Stone stood at the edge of the Crystal Stream.
The water sparkled.
Stone's feet stayed on the bank.
"I don't like getting wet," said Stone.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Stone's hand went into the stream.
It found the rock.
It gripped it.
Stone's face: very unhappy about this.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Stone's hand went into the stream.
It found the rock.
It gripped it.
Stone's face: very unhappy about this.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
The last star spirit sat in Stone's hand.
It blinked its large gold eyes at everyone.
"See you next year," it said.
Then it bounced once.
Then it went up.
Then it was gone.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
Everyone gasped.
Pip covered his mouth.
Stone's eyes went very wide.
Luna took off her glasses and put them back on.
It was real.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
On a mossy stone in the marsh sat a toadling.
It was very small.
Its mouth was very wide open.
All the noise was coming from it.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
The toadling stopped when it saw them.
Everything was suddenly very quiet.
"Oh," said Pip.
"Oh," said Stone.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
"Why were you shouting?" asked Pip.
The toadling blinked.
"I am lost," it said.
"I was calling for my family."
Its voice was very small now.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
Stone knelt down carefully.
"We will help," said Stone.
The toadling looked at Stone.
"You are very large," said the toadling.
"Yes," said Stone. "But I am gentle."

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
Stone knelt down carefully.
"We will help," said Stone.
The toadling looked at Stone.
"You are very large," said the toadling.
"Yes," said Stone. "But I am gentle."

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
Stone stood up and called out across the marsh.
It was the loudest sound Pip had ever heard.
Louder than the toadling.
Much louder.
Something answered from the far side of the marsh.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Fern looked around the room.
Then she looked at Twig.
The spectacles were on top of Twig's head.
They had been there all along.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
"I am Twig," said the tiny creature.
"I live here."
"I have always lived here."
She seemed perfectly happy about this.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Fern came back through the door.
"Her name is Twig," said Fern.
"She has lived here for many years."
Everyone looked at Luna.
"Of course," said Luna.
"Twig."

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Fern came back through the door.
"Her name is Twig," said Fern.
"She has lived here for many years."
Everyone looked at Luna.
"Of course," said Luna.
"Twig."

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
They made Twig a slightly larger door.
Twig came out for acorn biscuits.
She sat in the big room and looked around.
"I like it here," she said.
"But I like my room better."
"This is also very nice."

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
They made Twig a slightly larger door.
Twig came out for acorn biscuits.
She sat in the big room and looked around.
"I like it here," she said.
"But I like my room better."
"This is also very nice."

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
The room had carvings on every wall.
It had small glowing stones in the ceiling.
It smelled of old wood and old magic.
Burrow had never seen it before.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Luna walked slowly around the room.
She touched the carvings.
They lit up where she touched.
Blue and gold.
She had been here before.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
"This is the Memory Room," said Luna.
"This is where Moonwood keeps its oldest stories."
Burrow looked at the carvings.
"All of them?" he asked.
"All of them," said Luna.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Luna settled on a ledge.
She folded her wings.
She looked at the carvings for a moment.
"The first story of Moonwood," she began,
"is this."

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Burrow sat very still and listened.
The room grew warmer.
The carvings lit up one by one.
Luna's voice was quiet and certain.
She had always known these stories.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Caves are hollow spaces underground or inside cliffs. They form in many different ways. Some are made by water, some by sea waves, and some by ancient flowing lava.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Most caves form when rainwater seeps into limestone rock. The water is slightly acidic. It slowly dissolves the rock away. This takes thousands and thousands of years.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Caves are home to many animals. Bats sleep hanging upside down from cave ceilings by day. At dusk, thousands of bats fly out together to feed on insects in the night air.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Some creatures live only in caves and never come out. Over thousands of years, they have adapted. Cave fish are often pale or white — they have never needed colour. Many have no eyes at all.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Long ago, people lived in caves. They painted pictures on the cave walls. Cave paintings have been found that are more than 40,000 years old. The artists were humans just like us.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The top layer is full of life. Coral reefs grow in warm, shallow water. They are home to thousands of kinds of fish and animal. A coral reef is like an underwater city.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The top layer is full of life. Coral reefs grow in warm, shallow water. They are home to thousands of kinds of fish and animal. A coral reef is like an underwater city.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: Coral looks like rock or plant, but it is an animal. Each piece of coral is made of thousands of tiny creatures called polyps. Coral reefs take thousands of years to grow.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: Coral looks like rock or plant, but it is an animal. Each piece of coral is made of thousands of tiny creatures called polyps. Coral reefs take thousands of years to grow.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: Coral looks like rock or plant, but it is an animal. Each piece of coral is made of thousands of tiny creatures called polyps. Coral reefs take thousands of years to grow.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: Right, said Wren. She walked to the beginning of the spell. She read it again. This time, she read it forwards.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: "Fixing it," said tiny Wren. She raised her tiny hands. She said the spell again. Forwards, this time.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: Wren picked up her spell book. She turned to the next spell. "But I am going to find a better one," she said. She began to read very, very carefully. Forwards.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Wren found a cold remedy in her spell book. She read it very, very carefully. Forwards? said Spark. Forwards, said Wren.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Wren found a cold remedy in her spell book. She read it very, very carefully. Forwards? said Spark. Forwards, said Wren.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: "Maybe you need to try harder," said Spark. Spark's own magic crackled around his ears. Glimmer tried harder. More smoke came out. Still no fire.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Spark had a cold. Usually a cold was nothing much. But Spark's magic crackled around him all the time. A cold, for Spark, was a very big problem.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Spark tried to hold the sneeze in. His eyes went watery. His magic began to build and build. The sparkles around him grew very bright.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
The room had carvings on every wall.
It had small glowing stones in the ceiling.
It smelled of old wood and old magic.
Burrow had never seen it before.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
The magic seeds were gone.
The box that held them was open and empty.
Luna looked at the box for a long time.
"This is not good," she said.

uses.title: Space
uses.pageText:
Mars is red.
It is a planet.

uses.title: Water Everywhere
uses.pageText: Water is everywhere! Our Earth is a water planet.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Volcanoes can seem frightening. But they have helped shape our planet. They make new land, rich soil and even new islands. They have been doing this for billions of years.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon looks small from Earth, but it is very large. It is about a quarter the size of our whole planet. If Earth were a basketball, the Moon would be a tennis ball.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The ocean covers more than two thirds of our planet. It is the largest habitat on Earth. And most of it is still unexplored.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Most spiders can make silk. The silk comes out of tiny organs called spinnerets. Spider silk is incredibly strong — stronger than steel wire of the same thickness!

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Most spiders can make silk. The silk comes out of tiny organs called spinnerets. Spider silk is incredibly strong — stronger than steel wire of the same thickness!

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Most spiders can make silk. The silk comes out of tiny organs called spinnerets. Spider silk is incredibly strong — stronger than steel wire of the same thickness!

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: When an insect is caught, the spider wraps it in silk. This keeps it still. Then the spider injects venom to begin digesting its meal.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Female spiders lay eggs in a silk sac. The sac protects the eggs. When they hatch, tiny spiderlings emerge. Some mothers carry the sac everywhere.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon does not make its own light. It has no fire or glow inside. The light we see is sunlight bouncing off the Moon's surface.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: Plants use sunlight, water, and air to make food. This is called photosynthesis. It also makes the oxygen we breathe. Plants feed us and give us air!

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The ocean has different layers. Near the surface, there is plenty of sunlight and warmth. Further down, it grows colder and darker. Below 200 metres, no sunlight reaches at all.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The ocean has different layers. Near the surface, there is plenty of sunlight and warmth. Further down, it grows colder and darker. Below 200 metres, no sunlight reaches at all.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The ocean makes more than half the oxygen we breathe. Tiny plants called phytoplankton float near the surface. They use sunlight to make oxygen. Every other breath you take came from the ocean.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: "Try something scary," said Burrow. So Pip walked to the Tumblerock Cliffs. He found the high ledge and began to climb.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: He drew as he walked. He mapped the Crystal Stream path. He mapped the way to Tumblerock Cliffs. He drew everything carefully.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
Pip searched the Fog Marsh.
He found no seeds.
He found mud.
Flint searched the Tumblerock Cliffs.
He found no seeds.
He found three new things to map.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
"This way," said Flint.
He was right.
The Tumblerock Cliffs rose ahead.
"You found it," said Pip.
"I always find things," said Flint.
"Eventually."

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Luna read out the race rules.
The course: from the Hollow Oak to the Crystal Stream to the Tumblerock Cliffs and back.
Everyone was at the starting line.
Everyone was ready.
Mostly.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Many spiders spin webs to catch food. Orb webs are circular with spokes like a wheel. The spider starts with the spokes, then spins a sticky spiral between them.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Many spiders spin webs to catch food. Orb webs are circular with spokes like a wheel. The spider starts with the spokes, then spins a sticky spiral between them.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Not all webs look the same. Sheet webs are flat like a hammock. Cobwebs are messy tangles. Every type of spider makes its own kind of web.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Not all webs look the same. Sheet webs are flat like a hammock. Cobwebs are messy tangles. Every type of spider makes its own kind of web.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Some spiders do not use webs at all. Jumping spiders leap onto their food. They have big eyes that face forward to judge distance. A jumping spider can leap 20 times its own body length!

uses.title: Fern Grows Too Much
uses.pageText: By evening, it was a large, beautiful plant beside the Hollow Oak. Not too small. Not too large. Luna came out through the door.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: Flint sat down on a mossy rock. He looked at the map for a long time. It was very beautiful. It was also completely wrong.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: Flint pinned the first map up inside the Hollow Oak. It was very beautiful. Everyone agreed it was the best wrong map they had ever seen.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
Moonwood blazed with gold.
Every mushroom.
Every lamp.
Every glowing stone.
The forest was more beautiful than anyone had ever seen it.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: As the plant grows bigger, it makes flowers. Flowers attract bees and butterflies. These visitors carry pollen from flower to flower. This is called pollination.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Butterflies are insects. Like all insects, they have six legs, four wings, and a body in three parts. They also have two long antennae.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Butterflies drink nectar from flowers. They find flowers using their eyes and sense of smell. But they taste with their feet! Standing on a flower tells them if it is good to eat.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Some butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres. The monarch butterfly flies from Canada to Mexico every year — a journey of 4,000 kilometres. They always find the same trees.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon's surface is covered in craters. Craters are bowl-shaped holes made by space rocks crashing into the Moon long ago. Some craters are bigger than cities.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon's surface is covered in craters. Craters are bowl-shaped holes made by space rocks crashing into the Moon long ago. Some craters are bigger than cities.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon's surface is covered in craters. Craters are bowl-shaped holes made by space rocks crashing into the Moon long ago. Some craters are bigger than cities.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: You can see the Moon most nights. On a clear night with a telescope, you can see the craters clearly. Look up tonight — the Moon is always there.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: I have found something, Burrow told everyone. They gathered at the Hollow Oak. A door, said Burrow, underground. Very old. I don't know what is inside.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: They gathered around the door. Luna looked at it for a long time. I know this door, she said slowly. I think. A very long time ago.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
They gathered the star spirits.
There were many of them.
Stone held several.
Wren had two in her hat.
They kept bouncing.

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
The creature ran to its family.
The family gathered around it.
They looked at the Moonwood creatures.
Not afraid.
Just looking.
Then one of them blinked.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
That afternoon, it was Glimmer's turn to teach.
Glimmer spread both wings.
Glimmer hovered for a moment.
Then landed.
"Like that," said Glimmer.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
It was very late.
The clearing was empty.
Glimmer's eyes kept closing.
"Don't fall asleep," whispered Pip.
"I am not asleep," said Glimmer.
Glimmer was almost asleep.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
There was a sign on the Hollow Oak door.
GLIMMER'S FIRE PERFORMANCE — TODAY.
Everyone came.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
Glimmer did it again.
Longer.
The fire was steady.
It was warm.
Glimmer's scales caught the light.
Glimmer had never looked so much like a dragon.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
Wren tried her direction spell.
The arrow spun three times.
Then it pointed at Flint.
"That's you," said Wren.
"I know I'm here," said Flint.

uses.title: Fern and Wren and the Wrong Potion
uses.pageText:
Everything was back.
"I'm sorry," said Wren.
"Did you learn something?" asked Fern.
"Yes," said Wren. "I need more books."
"Fewer," said Fern.
"Fewer books."

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
The fish made a very large splash.
Stone was completely wet.
All of Stone.
Dewdrop was not wet.
"I'm sorry," said Dewdrop.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
That night, Moonwood glowed more than ever.
The seedlings lit the ground.
Everyone sat outside the Hollow Oak.
"I'm sorry I forgot," said Fern.
"Don't be," said Luna.
"They like it better here."

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Stage three: the caterpillar makes a hard shell around itself. This is called a chrysalis. Inside, an extraordinary change is about to happen.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar breaks down completely. Its body rebuilds itself as a butterfly. This amazing process is called metamorphosis. It takes one to two weeks.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
They sat on the bank and listened.
The stream sang around them.
"We did it," said Fern.
Dewdrop smiled.
"It sang itself. We just moved the stone."

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
When the edge was clear, the spirit stood.
Its shape was clearer now.
"Thank you," said the spirit.
It was not mist anymore.
It was something more solid.
Something more itself.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: He walked for three days. He did not stop. His map grew longer and longer. It was full of detail.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: He walked for three days. He did not stop. His map grew longer and longer. It was full of detail.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: I have been here longer than the Hollow Oak, said the fish. Dewdrop looked carefully. The fish was, if anything, quite new-looking. I know all the secrets of the Deep Dark, the fish added.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
Glimmer did it again.
Longer.
The fire was steady.
It was warm.
Glimmer's scales caught the light.
Glimmer had never looked so much like a dragon.

uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: The female emperor penguin lays one egg. The father balances it on his feet and covers it with a warm flap of skin. He keeps it safe from the freezing cold.

uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: Penguins live in large groups called colonies. Some colonies have hundreds of thousands of penguins! Each penguin recognises its partner and its chick by their call.

uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: There are 18 species of penguin. Not all live in cold places. Little blue penguins live in Australia. African penguins live on warm, sunny beaches. Every kind of penguin is remarkable.

uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: There are 18 species of penguin. Not all live in cold places. Little blue penguins live in Australia. African penguins live on warm, sunny beaches. Every kind of penguin is remarkable.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
Dewdrop tried to push it with water.
She pushed as hard as she could.
The boulder did not move.
"I am not strong enough," said Dewdrop.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
They pushed and pulled together.
The boulder shifted.
The mud let go.
The boulder rolled aside.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Stone pushed.
The rock moved.
The mud let go.
The fish was free.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
Luna pushed forward.
She looked at the star spirit over her glasses.
"I know what these are," said Luna.
"They lose their grip once a year."
"They need to go back before dawn."

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Sometimes, magma pushes up through a crack in the Earth. When it bursts out at the surface, we call it a volcano! The melted rock that flows out is called lava.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: First, a tiny root pushes down into the soil. Roots drink up water from the ground. Then a small shoot pushes up toward the light above.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: First, a tiny root pushes down into the soil. Roots drink up water from the ground. Then a small shoot pushes up toward the light above.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Stage four: the butterfly pushes out of the chrysalis. Its wings are wet and crumpled. The butterfly hangs still and waits. Slowly, its wings unfurl and dry.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
The Crystal Stream was not singing.
Fern heard it first.
Or rather — she heard nothing.
She went to find Dewdrop.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
At the source, they found it.
A great boulder had fallen.
It lay across the singing stones.
The stones could not sing.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
The water rushed over the singing stones.
And the Crystal Stream began to sing.
First very quietly.
Then louder.
Then loud enough to hear all the way to the Hollow Oak.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
At the Hollow Oak, everyone heard it.
"The stream is singing again!" said Pip.
"We just moved a stone," said Fern.
"And asked the water nicely," said Dewdrop.
"It did the rest."

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
They gathered the star spirits.
There were many of them.
Stone held several.
Wren had two in her hat.
They kept bouncing.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
They climbed to the top.
Moonwood spread below them in the dark.
The sky was full of stars above.
The star spirits reached upward with their tiny arms.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
Stone raised their hands high.
Pip and Spark added a little push.
The star spirits lifted.
Up.
And up.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
The star spirits went up.
Slowly at first.
Then faster.
One by one they found their places.
The sky filled back up with stars.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
At the source, they found it.
A great boulder had fallen.
It lay across the singing stones.
The stones could not sing.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
At the source, they found it.
A great boulder had fallen.
It lay across the singing stones.
The stones could not sing.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
The water rushed over the singing stones.
And the Crystal Stream began to sing.
First very quietly.
Then louder.
Then loud enough to hear all the way to the Hollow Oak.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
The room had carvings on every wall.
It had small glowing stones in the ceiling.
It smelled of old wood and old magic.
Burrow had never seen it before.

uses.pageText: One morning, a new fish appeared. It was silver with a bright blue stripe. Dewdrop had never seen a fish like it.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: Can fish lie? Dewdrop asked Burrow. Some of them can, said Burrow. Which fish? The new one with the blue stripe, said Dewdrop. Burrow had not seen a new fish.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: You are interesting, said Dewdrop. You are the only fish in this stream with a blue stripe. The fish looked at its own stripe. That is true, it said.

uses.pageText: Luna smiled. "That is quite nice, actually," said Luna. Fern smiled. She was very tired.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: Moonwood seeds, said Luna. From the first trees. For the day the old trees grow tired and need new ones beside them.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
They sat down under a large mushroom.
They were tired.
They were lost.
The mushroom glowed cheerfully.
Wren looked at it.

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Luna counted everyone.
Everyone was back.
Then there was a rumbling.
Burrow came up through the ground.
Right beside the finish line.
He did not look tired.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
The mushroom's glow changed.
It pulsed once — pointing.
Another mushroom far away pulsed the same way.
And another.
A trail of glowing mushrooms lit up through the trees.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
Wren and Flint followed the mushroom trail.
The forest opened up.
The golden light of the Whispering Meadow was ahead.
"Oh," said Flint.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
They arrived at the Whispering Meadow.
It was exactly where they had been going.
Flint wrote something on his map.
"Mushroom trail," he said.
"I should have had that already."

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
"Why didn't we try that first?" asked Flint.
"I don't know," said Wren.
She looked back at the mushroom trail.
"They seemed happy about it though."
The last mushroom blinked once and went out.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
He found the acorn biscuits.
He put some in his pocket.
He was still asleep.
Glimmer covered their mouth.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
They made Twig a slightly larger door.
Twig came out for acorn biscuits.
She sat in the big room and looked around.
"I like it here," she said.
"But I like my room better."
"This is also very nice."

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
Pip brought it inside.
Everyone woke up.
Stone brought a piece of acorn biscuit.
The creature ate it very carefully.
It watched everyone with its large silver eyes.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: After a volcano, the cooled lava becomes new rock. Volcanic rock breaks down into rich, dark soil. Many plants and crops grow very well in volcanic soil.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: The shoot breaks through the soil. It opens its first leaves toward the sun. Now the plant can begin to make its own food.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar breaks down completely. Its body rebuilds itself as a butterfly. This amazing process is called metamorphosis. It takes one to two weeks.

uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: Penguins are extraordinary swimmers. They can swim at 25 kilometres per hour. They leap in and out of the water and can dive very deep to catch fish.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Many spiders spin webs to catch food. Orb webs are circular with spokes like a wheel. The spider starts with the spokes, then spins a sticky spiral between them.

uses.title: Frogs
uses.pageText: Frogs are expert hunters. They have long, sticky tongues. A frog can flip its tongue out and back in less time than a blink to catch an insect.

uses.pageText: Stage four: the butterfly pushes out of the chrysalis. Its wings are wet and crumpled. The butterfly hangs still and waits. Slowly, its wings unfurl and dry.

It is fast!

A crab can crawl.
Snip, snip!

The reeds shook.
The water rippled.
They crept closer.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:

A shuffling.
A round shape moving through the clearing.
Pip and Glimmer looked at each other.
They crept closer.

The mushrooms at the edge were going out.
One by one.
The fog was not stopping.

The family gathered around it.
They looked at the Moonwood creatures.
Not afraid.
Just looking.
Then one of them blinked.

Glimmer spread both wings.
Glimmer jumped.

They were off.
Pip ran.
Fern flew.
Stone trotted.
Dewdrop glided.
Wren ran and read her spell book.
Flint took a very confident turn left.

She had glided the whole way.
She was not wet.
She was not ruffled.
"Finished," said Dewdrop.

uses.pageText: Sometimes, magma pushes up through a crack in the Earth. When it bursts out at the surface, we call it a volcano! The melted rock that flows out is called lava.

uses.pageText: The memory room, said Luna. That is what it was called. She touched the wall very gently. I remember now.

uses.pageText:
"This is the Memory Room," said Luna.
"This is where Moonwood keeps its oldest stories."
Burrow looked at the carvings.
"All of them?" he asked.
"All of them," said Luna.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon does not make its own light. It has no fire or glow inside. The light we see is sunlight bouncing off the Moon's surface.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon's surface is covered in craters. Craters are bowl-shaped holes made by space rocks crashing into the Moon long ago. Some craters are bigger than cities.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans. This causes the tides. When the tide comes in, the sea rises up the beach. When it goes out, it pulls back.

The mushrooms began to come back on.
One by one.
Pip watched them light up.
The marsh was where it should be.
The forest was where it should be.

uses.pageText: Worker bees fly from flower to flower. They collect a sweet liquid from inside flowers. This liquid is called nectar.

uses.title: Bees
uses.pageText: Bees carry nectar back to the hive. They pass it from bee to bee. Slowly, it turns into honey.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Butterflies drink nectar from flowers. They find flowers using their eyes and sense of smell. But they taste with their feet! Standing on a flower tells them if it is good to eat.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: Plants use sunlight, water, and air to make food. This is called photosynthesis. It also makes the oxygen we breathe. Plants feed us and give us air!

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The ocean makes more than half the oxygen we breathe. Tiny plants called phytoplankton float near the surface. They use sunlight to make oxygen. Every other breath you take came from the ocean.

It was even louder.
Pip's hair stood on end.
Stone appeared behind him.
"I came anyway," said Stone.

uses.pageText:
One morning, things had moved in the night.
Pip's boots were not where he had left them.
A bench was tipped over.
Someone had been in the clearing.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
Burrow bumped the bench.
It fell over.
Burrow kept walking.
He found Pip's door.
He moved the boots with his paws.
He did not wake up.

uses.title: Fern Grows Too Much
uses.pageText: Fern had one small seed. She planted it in the soft ground near the Hollow Oak.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: They planted the seeds in a ring around the Hollow Oak. One from each of them. In the golden afternoon light.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
"Oh," said Fern.
She remembered.
Two nights ago she had been in the clearing.
She had planted the seeds.
She had not meant to forget.

uses.title: Bees
uses.pageText: This is called pollination. Without bees, many plants could not make seeds. No seeds means no fruits or vegetables. We need bees very much.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: As the plant grows bigger, it makes flowers. Flowers attract bees and butterflies. These visitors carry pollen from flower to flower. This is called pollination.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: After pollination, the flower makes seeds. The seeds grow inside the plant protected by a pod, a fruit, or a shell.

uses.title: Fern and Wren and the Wrong Potion
uses.pageText:
Fern's garden was her favourite place.
One morning, Wren arrived with a cauldron.
"I have a potion," said Wren.
"It will help your plants."

uses.title: Fern and Wren and the Wrong Potion
uses.pageText:
Wren stirred the potion.
It was meant to be green.
It was more purple.
Wren did not notice this.

uses.title: Fern and Wren and the Wrong Potion
uses.pageText:
Wren poured the potion on the plants.
The plants stood very straight.
Then they leaned.
Then one of them took a step.

uses.pageText: I think, said Dewdrop slowly, we should find you a cold remedy before anything else changes.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Wren found a cold remedy in her spell book. She read it very, very carefully. Forwards? said Spark. Forwards, said Wren.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: The remedy worked. Spark's cold was gone. The flowers slowly turned back to their usual colours. The fish returned to normal.

uses.pageText: A root grows down in the soil.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: First, a tiny root pushes down into the soil. Roots drink up water from the ground. Then a small shoot pushes up toward the light above.

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Stone hit a root.
Stone began to fall.
This took a while.
Stone was very large.
Stone fell slowly.
Magnificently.
Like a small cliff sitting down.

uses.pageText: By the time Flint found his way home, he was, as usual, slightly lost. The new map was already three pages long. He had taken a very interesting route.

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Flint went left.
Then left again.
Then the Fog Marsh was ahead of him.
"I am taking a scenic route," said Flint.
There was no one to hear him.

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Dewdrop won a gold leaf for finishing.
Burrow won a gold leaf for best route.
"I did not win," said Flint.
"You went to the Fog Marsh," said Pip.
"I saw many things," said Flint.
He was already drawing them.

uses.pageText:
Everyone came back with nothing.
Then they saw Fern.
She was sitting in the middle of the clearing.
Small glowing seedlings were growing all around her.
"Oh," said everyone.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
Luna bent down to look.
The seedlings were strong.
They were growing along the paths.
Around the Hollow Oak.
All through the clearing.
"Better than a box," said Luna.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
That night, Moonwood glowed more than ever.
The seedlings lit the ground.
Everyone sat outside the Hollow Oak.
"I'm sorry I forgot," said Fern.
"Don't be," said Luna.
"They like it better here."

uses.pageText: He sneezed at breakfast. The porridge turned into a bird. The bird flew out of the window. Spark stared at his empty bowl.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: He sneezed in the Whispering Meadow. Every flower changed colour at the same moment. The meadow turned entirely blue. It was very quiet.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Spark sneezed near the Crystal Stream.

uses.pageText: She did not use a spell. She sang to it, very softly. She sang the song her mother had taught her about seeds.

uses.pageText:
"The song comes from the source," said Dewdrop.
"We must follow the stream up."
Fern looked at the deep forest ahead.
"Then we go," said Fern.

uses.pageText:
Fern went to the middle of the clearing.
She closed her eyes.
She sang.
Very softly.
The same song from long ago.

uses.pageText:
"It flows," said Fern.
"But it does not sing," said Dewdrop.
"Something is wrong at the source."

"Then we go," said Fern.

uses.pageText:
At the source, they found it.
A great boulder had fallen.
It lay across the singing stones.
The stones could not sing.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: "Maybe you need to try harder," said Spark. Spark's own magic crackled around his ears. Glimmer tried harder. More smoke came out. Still no fire.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Spark had a cold. Usually a cold was nothing much. But Spark's magic crackled around him all the time. A cold, for Spark, was a very big problem.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: The remedy worked. Spark's cold was gone. The flowers slowly turned back to their usual colours. The fish returned to normal.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Spark tried to hold the sneeze in. His eyes went watery. His magic began to build and build. The sparkles around him grew very bright.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
Spark tried.
Sparkles shot everywhere.
His hat fell off.
His feet stayed on the ground.
"I think I need more practice," said Spark.

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Glimmer could not stop.
Glimmer hit Spark.
Sparkles went everywhere.
They both kept moving.
Very fast.
In new directions.

Glimmer thought.
"Like falling upward," said Glimmer.
Spark nodded slowly.

She remembered.
Two nights ago she had been in the clearing.
She had planted the seeds.
She had not meant to forget.

It can bloom!

uses.pageText:
Everyone gasped.
Pip covered his mouth.
Stone's eyes went very wide.
Luna took off her glasses and put them back on.
It was real.

uses.pageText:
The small things landed and bounced.
They bounced along the ground.
They made a sound like giggling.
They left gold trails where they bounced.
"What ARE they?" said Pip.

It glows.

uses.pageText:

The fog was thick and grey-green.
The noise bounced off the twisted trees.
"Together," said Stone.
Pip nodded.

uses.pageText:

She looked at the star spirit over her glasses.
"I know what these are," said Luna.
"They lose their grip once a year."
"They need to go back before dawn."

uses.pageText:

It found the rock.
It gripped it.
Stone's face: very unhappy about this.

Everyone looked at Flint.
"I know exactly where it is," said Flint.
Everyone kept looking at him.

Glimmer spread both wings.
Glimmer hovered for a moment.
Then landed.
"Like that," said Glimmer.

Some walked toward the Crystal Stream.

They were not in a hurry.
They were just walking.

uses.pageText:

"You did," said Pip.
"I'd like to do it again," said Glimmer.
Everyone who heard this took a small step back.
"We know," said everyone.

uses.pageText: Dewdrop went back to the Crystal Stream. Why do you say things that are not true? she asked. She said it kindly. She just wanted to know.

uses.pageText: Rain fills rivers and lakes. Animals drink the water.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
They made Twig a slightly larger door.
Twig came out for acorn biscuits.
She sat in the big room and looked around.
"I like it here," she said.
"But I like my room better."
"This is also very nice."

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Pip reached the Crystal Stream.
He leaped from stone to stone.
One stone was slippery.
Pip went in.
He came out the other side.
Still running.
Very wet.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: Can fish lie? Dewdrop asked Burrow. Some of them can, said Burrow. Which fish? The new one with the blue stripe, said Dewdrop. Burrow had not seen a new fish.

uses.pageText: A butterfly's life has four stages. This is called a lifecycle. Each stage looks completely different from the one before.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
Stone raised their hands high.
Pip and Spark added a little push.
The star spirits lifted.
Up.
And up.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
The light spread.
Mushroom to mushroom.
Lamp to lamp.
Through every path.
Through every dark corner of Moonwood.
All of it lighting up.

uses.pageText:
Wren and Spark tried search spells.
The spells pointed at each other.
Stone looked under every log.
Gently.
There were no seeds under the logs.

uses.pageText:
Fern grew a strong vine around the boulder.
Dewdrop sent water under it to loosen the mud.
"Ready?" said Fern.
"Ready," said Dewdrop.

uses.pageText:
Burrow sat very still and listened.
The room grew warmer.
The carvings lit up one by one.
Luna's voice was quiet and certain.
She had always known these stories.

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Stone hit a root.
Stone began to fall.
This took a while.
Stone was very large.
Stone fell slowly.
Magnificently.
Like a small cliff sitting down.

uses.pageText: "How was the mapping?" asked Pip. "Perfect," said Flint. "I know exactly where everything was."

Seven maps fell out.
One was of the coast.
One was upside down.
None of them were quite right.

It is a planet.

GLIMMER'S FIRE PERFORMANCE — TODAY.
Everyone came.

They were very polite about it.
They walked around Fern.
They walked around Wren.
They went for a stroll.

She was not wet.
She was not ruffled.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Most caves form when rainwater seeps into limestone rock. The water is slightly acidic. It slowly dissolves the rock away. This takes thousands and thousands of years.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Over time, tunnels and chambers form underground. Some cave systems stretch for hundreds of kilometres. The Mammoth Cave system in America has more than 650 kilometres of passages.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Water drips from cave ceilings for thousands of years. The minerals in the water build up slowly. These hanging stone shapes are called stalactites. They form one tiny drip at a time.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: When drips hit the cave floor, minerals build up there too. These rising stone shapes are called stalagmites. They grow just a few centimetres every hundred years.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Caves are home to many animals. Bats sleep hanging upside down from cave ceilings by day. At dusk, thousands of bats fly out together to feed on insects in the night air.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Long ago, people lived in caves. They painted pictures on the cave walls. Cave paintings have been found that are more than 40,000 years old. The artists were humans just like us.

uses.title: Frogs
uses.pageText: A female frog lays hundreds of eggs in water. The eggs are called frogspawn. Each egg is surrounded by clear jelly that protects it and keeps it safe.

uses.title: Frogs
uses.pageText: After a few weeks, tadpoles wriggle out of the eggs. Tadpoles have tails and no legs. They breathe underwater using gills, like fish.

uses.title: Frogs
uses.pageText: Slowly, the tadpole changes. Back legs appear first. Then front legs. The tail shrinks away. After about twelve weeks, it is a frog!

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: The summer holidays were over at last. Aiden sat on his bed and stared at his new school bag. Grade 1. The words sounded bigger than they looked.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Their new classroom was bright and busy, with bookshelves along every wall and a large window that looked out onto the playing field. Their teacher was called Miss Okafor. She had bright yellow glasses and smiled like she really meant it.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: "In Grade 1," said Miss Okafor, "we will read chapter books, solve number puzzles and begin to understand how the world around us works." Aiden thought that sounded like an awful lot — but he found he was leaning forward slightly without meaning to.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: The first lesson was handwriting — joined-up letters, which were completely new and seemed designed to be tricky. Aiden's pen slipped and he made a large blot right across the middle of the page. He went very red.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: After lunch came Maths. Miss Okafor wrote sums on the board, each one slightly harder than the last. Some of them made Aiden's brain feel stretched in an unfamiliar way. He was discovering that this was not entirely a bad feeling.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Betty answered three questions out loud and got them all right. Aiden raised his hand once, very carefully, and he got his right too. Miss Okafor stuck a gold star beside both their names on the board. Aiden looked at his star for quite a long time.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Then there was Science — real Science, with a magnifying glass and a tray of soil and seeds. Aiden forgot to be nervous. He was too busy looking at a woodlouse through the magnifying glass and writing down exactly what he saw.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: At home time, Mum was waiting at the gate. She crouched down with an expectant look. "Well?" she said. They both started talking at exactly the same moment and didn't stop for ten minutes.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: "Grade 1 is brilliant," announced Betty, just before bed. "It's actually not that bad," said Aiden, which from Aiden meant exactly the same thing. He turned his light off, closed his eyes, and was asleep before he could think of anything to worry about.

uses.pageText: Their first customer was Mr Perkins from next door, who was very old and took a very long time about everything. He picked up every single item on the table, turned it over carefully, and put it back. After twenty minutes, he held up one small rubber duck. It cost twenty cents.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: Then things got busy. Children came from further up the street with their parents. A woman bought a whole crate of craft supplies without looking at any of them. A small boy bought four plastic dinosaurs and a jigsaw puzzle and carried them away in a tight proud bundle. Things were selling faster than Betty could write them down.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: By midday, more than half the table was clear. Betty sat down on the front step and counted the money tin carefully, then counted it again. "Forty-eight dollars and thirty cents," she announced. Aiden let out a long, astonished breath, which was all he could manage.

They flipped a coin — Aiden got the bigger room, but Betty got the one with the sea view, which meant it was perfectly even.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: The beach was a five-minute walk down a steep sandy path through tall marram grass. When they came over the last dune and the sea appeared — wide and green and going all the way to the horizon — Aiden stopped walking entirely and just looked for a long moment.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: It was an ordinary Saturday in late August when Uncle Eddie arrived at the door with a travelling bag, a very wide smile, and something small and determined making a noise from inside his coat.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie was Dad's younger brother, and he was a wildlife researcher who had spent the last two years living near a tropical rainforest, studying primates. He had, apparently, brought one with him.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Carefully, Uncle Eddie unzipped the carry-case. Inside, curled up like a small comma, was the most compact monkey Aiden had ever seen. He had cream-white fur on his face and chest, darker brown on his back, and small black hands and feet that looked, unmistakably, like he was wearing a pair of extremely neat little socks.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie explained that he was returning to the rainforest for six months and couldn't bring Socks along this time. He looked at Dad with a hopeful expression. Dad said yes before Mum could say anything at all, which was exactly what Mum had expected him to do.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks explored the house in eleven minutes. He opened every drawer he could reach, rearranged the fruit bowl into a different order, sat briefly on each windowsill and posted three letters from the hall table into the back of the television. He seemed very pleased with his work.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "He loves shiny objects," Uncle Eddie explained at dinner. "He adores warm spots — the airing cupboard is a particular risk. And if he gets bored, he will find a way to become interesting." Everyone filed this information away carefully.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks sat at the table in a tiny red waistcoat that Uncle Eddie had stitched for him. He watched everyone use their fork with great attention. Then he picked up his own fork and used it correctly. Then he threw the fork across the room. "He does that every evening," said Uncle Eddie. "We've never understood why."

He hoped, quietly, that he had the time.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: It started with the waistcoat hook being empty.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Every morning, Socks sat on the kitchen counter and waited while Betty did up the buttons on his little red waistcoat, which always lived on its own peg beside the back door. But on a Tuesday in October, the peg was empty. And when Aiden went to check, Socks's sleeping box in the corner of his room was empty too.

Dad searched the garden again, more systematically, with a torch — even though it was daytime. Socks was not anywhere.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "He couldn't have got out," said Dad. "All the windows were shut last night." Then Mum remembered the bathroom window — the small one above the bath, left open just a crack for steam. She looked at Aiden and Aiden looked at Betty. A crack that was, they all realised at the same moment, almost exactly the width of a small monkey.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Betty designed a MISSING MONKEY poster on her tablet in under five minutes. It had a photograph of Socks in his waistcoat, a written description, and their phone number in large digits. She printed fourteen copies. They posted them through letter boxes up and down both sides of the street without stopping.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: By three o'clock, the sky had gone grey and the wind had picked up. Aiden was sitting on the front step, not saying much. He kept thinking about what Uncle Eddie had said once: that animals raised by hand always know where home is. He held onto that thought very carefully.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Then the phone rang. It was their neighbour Mrs Obi, from number thirty-seven, three houses down. Her voice was very precise. "I believe," she said carefully, "that there may be a small monkey in my kitchen. He appears to be eating my shortbread."

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: They ran. All four of them, in their socks, without stopping to find shoes, down the pavement to number thirty-seven. They could hear, even from the gate, a small and very determined crunching sound coming from inside.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: There was Socks, sitting on Mrs Obi's kitchen counter beside an open shortbread tin. He was wearing his waistcoat — which they had also assumed was missing — and had crumbs on his face and the expression of someone who sees absolutely no problem with any of this whatsoever.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "How on earth did he get in?" asked Dad. Mrs Obi pointed to the cat flap in her back door. Of course. Socks had worked out the cat flap. He had also — from the state of the shortbread tin — clearly been in before, which nobody had known and which explained certain things about Mrs Obi's biscuit situation.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Aiden picked him up and held him. Socks was warm and solid and smelled faintly of shortbread. He patted Aiden's cheek twice with one small black hand, the way he sometimes did when he felt like being kind, and then tucked his head under Aiden's chin. Aiden breathed out slowly.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: On the way home, Betty said they needed a tracker collar. Aiden said they needed to block every cat flap on the street. Mum said they needed a more interesting biscuit tin. Dad said they should call Uncle Eddie and tell him what his monkey had been up to. They all laughed, and kept laughing, all the way home — and Socks rode on Aiden's shoulder the whole way, looking, as always, entirely pleased with himself.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie came back for a long weekend in June — browner from the sun, with a new bag of unusual gifts and more stories than they had time to hear. Socks heard the doorbell and ran in circles for forty-five seconds without stopping.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie told them about the nature reserve two miles from town — woodland, a river, meadows, a hide for watching birds. "Socks would understand it completely," he said. Mum said she wasn't certain that made it a good idea. They went anyway.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: The reserve was layered with sounds — insects, birds, the river — all at once and all different. Socks sat on Aiden's shoulder and went completely still, his head turning slowly to track each sound. Aiden had never seen him so quiet.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Betty found the bird hide first — a long wooden structure with narrow slot windows over the reed bed. Inside: a log book, borrowed binoculars, and a board listing twelve species to find. She was immediately in her element.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Through the binoculars, Betty saw a kingfisher — a bright impossible dart of blue-orange above the water, there and then gone. She had to put the binoculars down and close her eyes for a moment. She had seen it. She wrote it in the log book.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: "Do you think he misses the rainforest?" Aiden asked one evening. Betty thought for a long time. "I think he's decided this is his rainforest," she said. Aiden looked at Socks on his shoulder. "Yeah," he said. "I think so too."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Aiden didn't say anything. He went home and sat on his bed and stared at the ceiling. He wasn't crying, but he wasn't fine either. He didn't really want to talk about it — which Betty noticed immediately.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "What happened?" said Betty. Aiden told her in pieces, looking at the floor. Betty listened to all of it without saying anything. Then she said: "He's wrong. And being wrong loudly is still just being wrong." Aiden thought about that.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: That night, Aiden wrote in his notebook: When something is unfair, you have two choices — pretend it isn't happening, or decide what to do. He starred the second option. He didn't quite know yet what doing something looked like.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: On Friday, Marcus said it again in the lunch queue. Betty was right there. She looked at Marcus with exactly one raised eyebrow and said, clearly: "His name is Aiden. Which you know." Marcus looked surprised. He didn't say anything else.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Miss Okafor had noticed, in the way that good teachers always notice. She started a class discussion about what it means to be fair, and what you do when things aren't. Several children looked at the floor. Marcus looked at the window.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "The point," said Miss Okafor, "is not that everyone will always be kind. The point is that you always have a choice about how to respond — and that choice is completely yours." Aiden wrote it down. It felt like something worth keeping.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: It started with a slight wobble. Aiden was eating an apple when he felt, for the first time in his life, that one of his front teeth was moving in a way that front teeth were definitely not supposed to move.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: He told Betty. Betty got the torch and studied it with great interest. "It's definitely loose," she said. "It'll fall out and a permanent one will grow. That's much better, actually." Aiden was not entirely sure that it was.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: That night, Aiden worried about the tooth. It felt wrong — like something was breaking. He wrote in his notebook: Things that are strange: losing a tooth. Also, why teeth? Socks sat on the desk and watched him with great curiosity.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: That night, Aiden worried about the tooth. It felt wrong — like something was breaking. He wrote in his notebook: Things that are strange: losing a tooth. Also, why teeth? Socks sat on the desk and watched him with great curiosity.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Betty lost her first tooth the very next day, which nobody had seen coming. It came out at lunch, and she held it up and examined it with great interest before putting it in her pocket, as if this were a routine scientific procedure.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: "Does it hurt?" said Aiden. "Not really," said Betty. "It felt strange for a second. Then it was over." She looked at the gap in her mouth in a small mirror. "It's just a tooth," she said. "A very old, very small tooth."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: He held it up for a long time. It was tiny. It was the smallest thing that had ever felt significant. He put it in the small envelope Mum left for him, and when he placed it under his pillow it felt ceremonial.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: In the morning, the tooth was gone and there was a coin in its place. Aiden knew, in the way children who read a lot know things, that it was Mum or Dad who had swapped it. He said nothing, because some things are better left as stories.

uses.pageText: Three weeks later, the new tooth began to come through. It was enormous relative to the gap — a proper square adult tooth in a mouth that had been full of small rounded baby ones. Aiden looked at himself in the mirror and felt extremely strange.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Socks was fascinated by both of them through this whole period. He kept trying to look in their mouths. He seemed to find it deeply interesting, which Aiden added to the field notebook under: Primate-specific dental curiosity — possible.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: "I think he'll be disappointed when we stop changing," said Aiden. "He already has all the teeth he'll get," said Betty. Socks demonstrated this by grinning at them both from very close range, showing every single tooth.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: Dad had been talking about the castle trip since January. A proper medieval castle, forty minutes away — with a tower you could actually climb, a dungeon that was a real dungeon, and a great hall whose stone floor had been there for six hundred years. Betty had already read a book about it.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: They drove there on a bright Saturday in April. Aiden pressed his face to the car window when the castle appeared over the hill — grey stone towers above the treeline, impossibly old and very much still there. He felt something he didn't yet have a word for.

uses.pageText: The entrance was a proper drawbridge — working, over a real water-filled moat. It was smaller than he'd imagined and more real than he'd imagined. Aiden crossed it one step at a time, listening to the echo of his footsteps on old wood, thinking about every person who had crossed it before him.

uses.title: Chompy's Big Lunch
uses.pageText: Oh, Chompy! laughed all the Dino Pals. Chompy laughed too.

uses.title: Chompy's Big Lunch
uses.pageText: That night, Chompy looked at the stars. I wonder what breakfast will be, said Chompy.

uses.title: Sunny's Rainy Day
uses.pageText: Sunny jumped in the puddles. SPLASH! SPLASH! SPLASH!

uses.title: Sunny's Rainy Day
uses.pageText: One by one, the Dino Pals joined in.

uses.title: Sunny's Rainy Day
uses.pageText: The sun came back out. See? said Sunny. Every day is a good day!

uses.title: Dozy Won't Wake Up
uses.pageText: We have a problem, said Bossy. We need Dozy for the picnic!

uses.title: Dozy Won't Wake Up
uses.pageText: Chompy had an idea. Chompy found the biggest, yummiest lunch in Sunny Hollow.

uses.title: Grumpy Needs Help
uses.pageText: Can WE help? said all the Dino Pals. NO! said Grumpy.

uses.title: Grumpy Needs Help
uses.pageText: Oh, fine, said Grumpy quietly. All the Dino Pals helped together. POP!

uses.title: Bossy Makes a Plan
uses.pageText: Everyone got to work. Chompy ate the berries. Chompy! said Bossy.

uses.title: Bossy Makes a Plan
uses.pageText: The plan was a mess. Nobody is doing it right! said Bossy.

uses.title: Bossy Makes a Plan
uses.pageText: Hmm, said Bossy. Bossy wrote on the clipboard: New plan: ask nicely.

uses.title: Bouncy Bumps Into Everything
uses.pageText: Bouncy woke up. Bouncy bounced straight into the cave wall. BONK!

uses.title: Bouncy Bumps Into Everything
uses.pageText: Bouncy bounced to the waterfall. Bouncy bumped into Fancy. BOING!

uses.title: Bouncy Bumps Into Everything
uses.pageText: All the Dino Pals looked at Bouncy. Sorry, said Bouncy, smiling.

uses.title: Bouncy Bumps Into Everything
uses.pageText: Maybe I should bounce in the meadow, said Bouncy. BOING! BOING! BOING!

uses.title: Wiggly's Messy Day
uses.pageText: Wiggly walked SO carefully. Wiggly's tail knocked Fancy into the mud puddle. Oh no.

uses.title: Wiggly's Messy Day
uses.pageText: Wiggly sat very, very still. The tail still knocked over three berries and a leaf.

uses.title: Wiggly's Messy Day
uses.pageText: I like your tail, said Dozy sleepily. It fans me while I nap. The Dino Pals all agreed.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down
uses.pageText: Zippy ran to the waterfall. Zippy ran back. Zippy ran to the meadow. Zippy ran back.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down
uses.pageText: Zippy ran to the waterfall. Zippy ran back. Zippy ran to the meadow. Zippy ran back.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down
uses.pageText: Zippy ran so fast that Zippy ran right past the picnic. And the waterfall. And Sunny Hollow.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down

uses.title: Honky's Inside Voice
uses.pageText: Then a thunderstorm came. Dozy woke up frightened. All the Dino Pals hid.

uses.title: Honky's Inside Voice
uses.pageText: IT IS OKAY! called Honky. Honky's voice was louder than the thunder. Dozy stopped shaking.

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Cheeky hid in the ferns. Cheeky tied Wiggly's tail to a tree. Hee hee, said Cheeky.

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Cheeky laughed and laughed. But then Cheeky slipped on the same mud. SPLAT!

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Now Cheeky was muddy. The Dino Pals looked at Cheeky. Cheeky looked at the Dino Pals.

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Now Cheeky was muddy. The Dino Pals looked at Cheeky. Cheeky looked at the Dino Pals.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: Every morning, the Dino Pals found a small gift on the Big Flat Rock. Nobody knew who left them.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: Every morning, the Dino Pals found a small gift on the Big Flat Rock. Nobody knew who left them.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: Sunny saw two small eyes behind a rock. And two small pink paws placing a tiny woven grass bracelet on the rock.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: Shy! said Sunny, softly. The gifts are from you, aren't they? Shy nodded, going very pink.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: They were the best gifts we ever had, said Sunny. Will you come and sit with us? Shy came out. Just a little way. But it was something.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: The next morning, eleven gifts were on the Big Flat Rock. One from each Dino Pal. A small pink paw reached out and took them, one by one.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: I cannot leave the cave, said Fancy. Not like this. Fancy sat very still and stared at the cave wall.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: I cannot leave the cave, said Fancy. Not like this. Fancy sat very still and stared at the cave wall.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Chompy offered to sit on the sail to flatten it. ABSOLUTELY NOT, said Fancy.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Wiggly fetched water from the waterfall very carefully. The tail only knocked over two things. Sorry, said Wiggly.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Wiggly fetched water from the waterfall very carefully. The tail only knocked over two things. Sorry, said Wiggly.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Wiggly dampened the sail gently and pressed it very softly. Slowly, slowly, it began to straighten.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Fancy looked in the pool. Oh, said Fancy. Oh, that is much better. Fancy looked at Wiggly. Thank you. A real thank you.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: The next morning, Fancy left a beautifully woven bracelet outside Wiggly's cave. Wiggly's tail knocked it away at once. Sorry! said Wiggly. It is fine, said Fancy. And meant it.

uses.pageText: Everyone searched. Bouncy bounced into every corner. Zippy ran everywhere twice. Cheeky looked in all the hiding spots. Nothing.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: It could be anywhere, said Bossy, looking at the clipboard. Sunny Hollow is very big.

uses.pageText: Clumsy could see over all the ferns, past the waterfall, all the way to the Long Meadow and beyond.

uses.pageText: Flappy woke up and tried to fly. Flappy got three wing-flaps up. Then landed in the mud.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy tried roaring like the other dinosaurs. A small squawk came out. Some feathers drifted down.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy went back to the tree. Got three wing-flaps up. Landed neatly on a branch. Sat very high up and looked at all of Sunny Hollow below. Oh, said Flappy quietly. That is quite good actually.

uses.pageText: One morning, Rainbow Waterfall was not making rainbows. It was not making anything at all. The waterfall had stopped.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: The Dino Pals went to look. A huge pile of rocks had fallen in the night and blocked the stream above.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: We need to move those rocks, said Bossy. Everyone tried pushing. The rocks did not move at all.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: Grumpy has a strong tail, said Sunny. Grumpy swung the club tail at the rocks. CLONK. One small rock moved. There were fifty more.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: Sneezy took a breath in. The biggest breath anyone in Sunny Hollow had ever taken. The ferns bent backwards.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: AAAAAAACHOOOOOO! The sneeze hit the rocks like a wave. Rocks scattered in every direction. The stream burst free. The waterfall roared back. A rainbow appeared.

uses.pageText: Sorry, said Sneezy, dabbing with the handkerchief. Every leaf had fallen off every tree. Do not apologise, said Grumpy. For once, Grumpy was actually smiling.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: I am going to the Long Meadow, said Grumpy. There is a good flat rock there. Peaceful. No one around. Chompy appeared. Can I come? said Chompy. Grumpy closed their eyes. Fine.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: This is a pebble, said Grumpy. I am not eating the pebble, said Chompy. Glad to hear it, said Grumpy.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: They reached the meadow. Grumpy found the flat rock and sat on it. Chompy found a berry patch immediately.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: Grumpy's club tail lowered into the ditch. Chompy grabbed on. Grumpy pulled. Chompy came out covered in mud.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: Thank you, said Chompy. Hmph, said Grumpy. They sat on the rock together. Less peaceful with Chompy. But not actually terrible.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: This is a good rock, said Chompy. Yes, said Grumpy. Is there anything to eat near it? said Chompy. Grumpy pointed at the berry patch. Chompy went happily.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: Grumpy sat on the rock alone. It was peaceful. But after a while, Grumpy called: There is a good-looking bush to your left. Thanks, Grumpy! said Chompy. Grumpy said nothing. But the corner of the mouth went up. Just slightly.

uses.pageText: There would be a running race, a jumping contest, a loudness competition, and a prize for the tidiest corner of the Hollow. More events to be decided, said Bossy. I have a clipboard.

Everyone was asleep.

Scratch.
Shuffle.

They listened together.
Scratch.
Shuffle.
"...they were right here..."

They stood outside the Hollow Oak.
"It makes those sounds," said Luna.
"It always has."
"It HAS?" said everyone.

He found a small door near the roots.
It was very small.
Too small for most of them.
"I can go," said Fern.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Fern went through the small door.
She was inside for a moment.
Then she called back:
"There is someone here."
Everyone pressed their ears to the door.

"Have you seen my spectacles?" she said.
"I've been looking for three days."

uses.title: Water Everywhere
uses.pageText: Water is everywhere! Our Earth is a water planet.

uses.title: Bees
uses.pageText: Bees live together in a hive. One hive can hold up to 60,000 bees. The queen bee lays all the eggs.

uses.title: Bees
uses.pageText: Worker bees fly from flower to flower. They collect a sweet liquid from inside flowers. This liquid is called nectar.

uses.title: Bees
uses.pageText: We can help bees by planting flowers. Bees love lavender, sunflowers, and daisies. Even a small garden or a pot of flowers can help.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Sometimes, magma pushes up through a crack in the Earth. When it bursts out at the surface, we call it a volcano! The melted rock that flows out is called lava.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Sometimes, magma pushes up through a crack in the Earth. When it bursts out at the surface, we call it a volcano! The melted rock that flows out is called lava.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Volcanoes can be found on land and under the sea. When an underwater volcano keeps erupting, the lava builds up and can make a brand new island!

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: After a volcano, the cooled lava becomes new rock. Volcanic rock breaks down into rich, dark soil. Many plants and crops grow very well in volcanic soil.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Most volcanoes are quiet for a very long time. Scientists called volcanologists watch them carefully. They use special equipment to spot the signs of an eruption.

uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: The female emperor penguin lays one egg. The father balances it on his feet and covers it with a warm flap of skin. He keeps it safe from the freezing cold.

uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: When the egg hatches, a tiny chick comes out. The chick has thick grey fluffy feathers. It cuddles close to its parent to stay warm.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon is a huge ball of rock. It travels around the Earth. It takes about one month to go all the way around. The Moon is our nearest neighbour in space.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon looks different every night. Sometimes it is a full, bright circle. Sometimes it is a thin crescent. These different shapes are called the phases of the Moon.

uses.title: The Moon

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The Moon looks small from Earth, but it is very large. It is about a quarter the size of our whole planet. If Earth were a basketball, the Moon would be a tennis ball.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: You can see the Moon most nights. On a clear night with a telescope, you can see the craters clearly. Look up tonight — the Moon is always there.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: Almost every plant starts as a tiny seed. Seeds come in hundreds of different shapes and sizes. Each one holds everything a plant needs to begin life.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: A seed needs three things to start growing: water, warmth, and air. When it gets all three, it wakes up and begins to grow.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: First, a tiny root pushes down into the soil. Roots drink up water from the ground. Then a small shoot pushes up toward the light above.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: After pollination, the flower makes seeds. The seeds grow inside the plant protected by a pod, a fruit, or a shell.

uses.pageText: You can grow your own plant. Put a seed in some soil. Add water. Put it in a sunny spot. Then watch the cycle begin.
