uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: Penguins live in large groups called colonies. Some colonies have hundreds of thousands of penguins! Each penguin recognises its partner and its chick by their call.

uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: Penguins are black on top and white underneath. This is called countershading. From above, their dark back blends with the deep water. From below, their white front looks like the bright surface.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: Almost every plant starts as a tiny seed. Seeds come in hundreds of different shapes and sizes. Each one holds everything a plant needs to begin life.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: A seed needs three things to start growing: water, warmth, and air. When it gets all three, it wakes up and begins to grow.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: A seed needs three things to start growing: water, warmth, and air. When it gets all three, it wakes up and begins to grow.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: Plants use sunlight, water, and air to make food. This is called photosynthesis. It also makes the oxygen we breathe. Plants feed us and give us air!

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: Plants use sunlight, water, and air to make food. This is called photosynthesis. It also makes the oxygen we breathe. Plants feed us and give us air!

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: As the plant grows bigger, it makes flowers. Flowers attract bees and butterflies. These visitors carry pollen from flower to flower. This is called pollination.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: Seeds travel away from the parent plant. Some fly on the wind. Some stick to animals' fur. Some are eaten by birds and fall far away. Some float on water.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Most spiders are harmless to people. They eat insects that damage our plants. Without spiders, our gardens and crops would be full of pests. Spiders are very helpful friends.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The ocean covers more than two thirds of our planet. It is the largest habitat on Earth. And most of it is still unexplored.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The ocean has different layers. Near the surface, there is plenty of sunlight and warmth. Further down, it grows colder and darker. Below 200 metres, no sunlight reaches at all.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The ocean has different layers. Near the surface, there is plenty of sunlight and warmth. Further down, it grows colder and darker. Below 200 metres, no sunlight reaches at all.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The top layer is full of life. Coral reefs grow in warm, shallow water. They are home to thousands of kinds of fish and animal. A coral reef is like an underwater city.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: Further down, in the deep and dark, strange creatures live. Many have enormous eyes to see in the dim light. Some are found nowhere else on Earth.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Butterflies are insects. Like all insects, they have six legs, four wings, and a body in three parts. They also have two long antennae.

uses.title: Butterflies

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Butterflies drink nectar from flowers. They find flowers using their eyes and sense of smell. But they taste with their feet! Standing on a flower tells them if it is good to eat.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Caves are hollow spaces underground or inside cliffs. They form in many different ways. Some are made by water, some by sea waves, and some by ancient flowing lava.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Most caves form when rainwater seeps into limestone rock. The water is slightly acidic. It slowly dissolves the rock away. This takes thousands and thousands of years.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Over time, tunnels and chambers form underground. Some cave systems stretch for hundreds of kilometres. The Mammoth Cave system in America has more than 650 kilometres of passages.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: When a stalactite and a stalagmite meet, they form a column. A cave column can take tens of thousands of years to grow. Each one is unique.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Some creatures live only in caves and never come out. Over thousands of years, they have adapted. Cave fish are often pale or white — they have never needed colour. Many have no eyes at all.

uses.title: Frogs
uses.pageText: Frogs are amphibians. Amphibians can live in water and on land. Frogs begin their life in water and later move onto land.

uses.title: Frogs
uses.pageText: A female frog lays hundreds of eggs in water. The eggs are called frogspawn. Each egg is surrounded by clear jelly that protects it and keeps it safe.

uses.title: Frogs
uses.pageText: After a few weeks, tadpoles wriggle out of the eggs. Tadpoles have tails and no legs. They breathe underwater using gills, like fish.

uses.title: Frogs
uses.pageText: Frogs are expert hunters. They have long, sticky tongues. A frog can flip its tongue out and back in less time than a blink to catch an insect.

uses.title: James and Anna build a Tree House
uses.pageText: That night, they got their sleeping bags and climbed up to sleep. Stars shone above them. "Best. Night. Ever," said James. Anna smiled. She agreed.

uses.pageText: Anna found the duck pond. Three white ducks swam in slow circles. One waddled right up and ate seeds from Anna's hand.

uses.title: James and Anna visit Grandma's Farm
uses.pageText: Grandma had a big brown horse called Bess. She was huge and gentle. Her nose was the softest thing James had ever felt.

uses.title: James and Anna visit Grandma's Farm

uses.pageText: That evening, Grandma made soup from the garden and fried the eggs James had found. It was the best meal they had ever tasted.

uses.title: James and Anna and the School Play
uses.pageText: Anna painted for three whole days. She made mountains, a red sunset sky and a tall castle with a flag. Everyone said it was brilliant.

uses.title: James and Anna and the School Play
uses.pageText: On the night of the play, James wore a green scale costume and a red dragon mask. He looked completely brilliant.

uses.title: James and Anna and the School Play
uses.pageText: Then the lights went up and James walked on stage. He could see the WHOLE school in the dark. His legs went very wobbly.

uses.title: James and Anna and the School Play
uses.pageText: He forgot his first line. The hall went silent. Anna was watching from the side. She caught his eye and gave him a thumbs up.

uses.title: James and Anna and the School Play
uses.pageText: The play went brilliantly after that. James roared and stomped and the little ones in the front row screamed and giggled.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: "Yes!" said James and Anna. They were absolutely sure it would be fine. They were wrong.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: Bella ran in circles round and round Chips. Chips watched her. Then Chips decided to chase Bella.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: Bella chased Chips. Chips chased Bella. They ran round and round the garden at an absolutely ridiculous speed.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: Bella crashed into the paddling pool. Water exploded in every direction. James and Anna were completely soaked.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: Chips jumped over the flower bed. Bella jumped after him. Daisies and petals flew in all directions.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: Mrs. Chen stood at the garden gate and laughed so hard that she had to sit down on the grass.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: At last, both Chips and Bella lay down on the lawn side by side, panting. Chips licked Bella's ear. Bella licked Chips's nose.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: "CHIPS!" said James and Anna. Chips blinked. Bella wagged her tail. It had been the very best play date.

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: For their birthdays, James and Anna each got a new bike. James's was red. Anna's was purple.

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: They put on their helmets and walked the bikes outside. James could not wait. Anna checked the brakes first.

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: Anna set off nice and slowly. She did not wobble. She did not crash. She rode all the way to the end of the path and back.

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: By lunchtime, they could both ride all the way down the long lane and back without stopping once.

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: Dad got his old bike out and the three of them went for a long ride down to the duck pond.

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: They ate their sandwiches by the duck pond. Chips waited at home. Chips and bikes were definitely not a good idea.

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: On the way home, James and Anna raced. They crossed the gate post at exactly the same time. A perfect tie.

uses.title: James, Anna and Chips go Camping
uses.pageText: James and Anna helped bang in the tent pegs and thread the poles through. Chips ate one peg. Then he tried to eat a second.

uses.title: James, Anna and Chips go Camping
uses.pageText: They packed their sleeping bags, a torch, a pack of cards, two books and lots of snacks.

uses.title: James, Anna and Chips go Camping
uses.pageText: Chips was coming too. He had his own little blanket and his bell, which jingled every single time he moved.

uses.title: James, Anna and Chips go Camping
uses.pageText: The marshmallow on Chips's stick got too close to the fire. It caught light. Chips ate the whole thing — stick and all.

uses.title: James, Anna and Chips go Camping
uses.pageText: In the morning, dew was on the grass and the birds sang. Chips had eaten a corner of the tent in the night.

uses.title: James, Anna and Chips go Camping
uses.pageText: "CHIPS!" they said. But the sun was warm and breakfast was good and it had been a perfect camp.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: The summer holidays were over at last. Aiden sat on his bed and stared at his new school bag. Grade 1. The words sounded bigger than they looked.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Betty was not worried at all. She had already packed her bag twice. "We're going to have proper lessons and proper homework," she said, bouncing on her toes. "Isn't that brilliant?" Aiden wasn't absolutely sure that it was.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Their new classroom was bright and busy, with bookshelves along every wall and a large window that looked out onto the playing field. Their teacher was called Miss Okafor. She had bright yellow glasses and smiled like she really meant it.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: "In Grade 1," said Miss Okafor, "we will read chapter books, solve number puzzles and begin to understand how the world around us works." Aiden thought that sounded like an awful lot — but he found he was leaning forward slightly without meaning to.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Everyone had their own desk with a name label. Aiden's said AIDEN in neat blue letters. He ran his finger over it slowly and felt, just slightly, like it might turn out to be all right.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: The first lesson was handwriting — joined-up letters, which were completely new and seemed designed to be tricky. Aiden's pen slipped and he made a large blot right across the middle of the page. He went very red.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Betty leaned over and showed him her page quietly. Her joined-up writing was also not her best work. "Mine looks like a wonky caterpillar," she whispered. Aiden laughed before he could stop himself, and his face stopped being red.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: At lunch, they sat together by the window. Aiden opened his lunchbox and found a small folded note from Mum tucked under his sandwich. It said: You've got this, star. He smiled all the way through his apple.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Betty answered three questions out loud and got them all right. Aiden raised his hand once, very carefully, and he got his right too. Miss Okafor stuck a gold star beside both their names on the board. Aiden looked at his star for quite a long time.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Then there was Science — real Science, with a magnifying glass and a tray of soil and seeds. Aiden forgot to be nervous. He was too busy looking at a woodlouse through the magnifying glass and writing down exactly what he saw.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: At home time, Mum was waiting at the gate. She crouched down with an expectant look. "Well?" she said. They both started talking at exactly the same moment and didn't stop for ten minutes.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: "Grade 1 is brilliant," announced Betty, just before bed. "It's actually not that bad," said Aiden, which from Aiden meant exactly the same thing. He turned his light off, closed his eyes, and was asleep before he could think of anything to worry about.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: It was the first warm Saturday of spring, and Aiden and Betty stood in the middle of the playroom staring at something that had got entirely out of control. Toys, books, games and puzzles were piled up to the shelves. There was even a foam sword that neither of them remembered buying.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: "We should have a yard sale," said Betty. She said it the way she said all her best ideas — quickly and firmly, as though the idea had already made up its mind. "We could make actual money." Aiden wasn't certain at first, but when she said the word money, he started to listen.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: They spent Friday evening sorting everything into three piles: SELL, KEEP and MAYBE. The MAYBE pile kept losing things to SELL, because, as Betty pointed out, they hadn't touched any of them in over a year. By nine o'clock, the MAYBE pile had completely disappeared.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: On Saturday morning, they dragged two folding tables out to the front path and arranged everything carefully. The old teddies sat in a row at the back and looked slightly sorry for themselves. "They'll go to good homes," said Aiden, mostly to himself, as a form of reassurance.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: Their first customer was Mr Perkins from next door, who was very old and took a very long time about everything. He picked up every single item on the table, turned it over carefully, and put it back. After twenty minutes, he held up one small rubber duck. It cost twenty cents.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: Then things got busy. Children came from further up the street with their parents. A woman bought a whole crate of craft supplies without looking at any of them. A small boy bought four plastic dinosaurs and a jigsaw puzzle and carried them away in a tight proud bundle. Things were selling faster than Betty could write them down.

uses.pageText: By midday, more than half the table was clear. Betty sat down on the front step and counted the money tin carefully, then counted it again. "Forty-eight dollars and thirty cents," she announced. Aiden let out a long, astonished breath, which was all he could manage.

uses.pageText: As Aiden folded up the last table, he found something wedged at the very back — his old stuffed elephant, Nelly, who he had completely forgotten was there. He held her for a long moment. Then he carried her inside and put her on the shelf above his desk. Some things, he decided, were not for selling.

uses.pageText: The last day of the summer term was also the loudest day of the school year. Aiden and Betty burst through the front door and both shouted "HOLIDAY!" at exactly the same moment, which echoed all the way up the stairs and made the dog next door bark.

uses.pageText: The drive took three hours. Betty counted every red car they passed. Aiden read two chapters of his book, fell asleep on his own shoulder, woke up, read another chapter, and then asked "Are we nearly there?" for the fourth time. They were, finally, nearly there.

uses.pageText: The cottage smelled of sea salt and old wood and something warm that Aiden couldn't name. They raced upstairs to choose rooms. There was a small room and a slightly bigger room. They flipped a coin — Aiden got the bigger room, but Betty got the one with the sea view, which meant it was perfectly even.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: It was an ordinary Saturday in late August when Uncle Eddie arrived at the door with a travelling bag, a very wide smile, and something small and determined making a noise from inside his coat.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: It was an ordinary Saturday in late August when Uncle Eddie arrived at the door with a travelling bag, a very wide smile, and something small and determined making a noise from inside his coat.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie was Dad's younger brother, and he was a wildlife researcher who had spent the last two years living near a tropical rainforest, studying primates. He had, apparently, brought one with him.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Carefully, Uncle Eddie unzipped the carry-case. Inside, curled up like a small comma, was the most compact monkey Aiden had ever seen. He had cream-white fur on his face and chest, darker brown on his back, and small black hands and feet that looked, unmistakably, like he was wearing a pair of extremely neat little socks.

He had cream-white fur on his face and chest, darker brown on his back, and small black hands and feet that looked, unmistakably, like he was wearing a pair of extremely neat little socks.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "His name is Socks," said Uncle Eddie. "He was orphaned when he was very small, and I've raised him from a baby. He understands a lot of what you say, he copies behaviour, and he is completely tame." He paused just a moment. "He is also, just occasionally, a little bit naughty."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "His name is Socks," said Uncle Eddie. "He was orphaned when he was very small, and I've raised him from a baby. He understands a lot of what you say, he copies behaviour, and he is completely tame." He paused just a moment. "He is also, just occasionally, a little bit naughty."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks looked at Aiden. Then he looked at Betty. Then he reached out one small black hand, calmly removed Aiden's watch from Aiden's wrist, and put it on his own. He looked at it with great satisfaction. "Charming," said Mum. "Yes," said Uncle Eddie, completely unsurprised.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie explained that he was returning to the rainforest for six months and couldn't bring Socks along this time. He looked at Dad with a hopeful expression. Dad said yes before Mum could say anything at all, which was exactly what Mum had expected him to do.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks explored the house in eleven minutes. He opened every drawer he could reach, rearranged the fruit bowl into a different order, sat briefly on each windowsill and posted three letters from the hall table into the back of the television. He seemed very pleased with his work.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "He loves shiny objects," Uncle Eddie explained at dinner. "He adores warm spots — the airing cupboard is a particular risk. And if he gets bored, he will find a way to become interesting." Everyone filed this information away carefully.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks sat at the table in a tiny red waistcoat that Uncle Eddie had stitched for him. He watched everyone use their fork with great attention. Then he picked up his own fork and used it correctly. Then he threw the fork across the room. "He does that every evening," said Uncle Eddie. "We've never understood why."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: That night, Dad built Socks a cosy sleeping box — a wooden crate lined with a soft fleece blanket — and settled it in the warm corner of the kitchen. In the morning, Socks was not in it. He was curled up fast asleep at the foot of Aiden's bed, his small black hand curled around Aiden's pencil torch.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Over the following weeks, Socks wove himself into the house. He had his own peg for his waistcoat. He met them at the door when they came home from school. He sat on Dad's shoulder while Dad read the newspaper and turned the pages for him, very seriously.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: He was also, as promised, occasionally naughty. He dropped a teaspoon into the toaster. He unravelled the entire roll of cling film in the kitchen drawer. He stole every single one of Betty's hair bobbles and lined them up on the windowsill in a precise order that nobody could explain.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "He is completely impossible," said Mum, as she did most evenings. But she had also started setting a small dish of whatever she was cooking on the corner of the counter every night, because Socks knew exactly where it appeared and waited there very patiently, and she had not been able to bring herself to stop.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "He is completely impossible," said Mum, as she did most evenings. But she had also started setting a small dish of whatever she was cooking on the corner of the counter every night, because Socks knew exactly where it appeared and waited there very patiently, and she had not been able to bring herself to stop.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Every morning, Socks sat on the kitchen counter and waited while Betty did up the buttons on his little red waistcoat, which always lived on its own peg beside the back door. But on a Tuesday in October, the peg was empty. And when Aiden went to check, Socks's sleeping box in the corner of his room was empty too.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Every morning, Socks sat on the kitchen counter and waited while Betty did up the buttons on his little red waistcoat, which always lived on its own peg beside the back door. But on a Tuesday in October, the peg was empty. And when Aiden went to check, Socks's sleeping box in the corner of his room was empty too.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: They searched everywhere. Aiden checked under every sofa cushion and behind every bookshelf. Betty methodically looked in every high cupboard. Mum turned the garden upside down. Dad searched the garden again, more systematically, with a torch — even though it was daytime. Socks was not anywhere.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "He couldn't have got out," said Dad. "All the windows were shut last night." Then Mum remembered the bathroom window — the small one above the bath, left open just a crack for steam. She looked at Aiden and Aiden looked at Betty. A crack that was, they all realised at the same moment, almost exactly the width of a small monkey.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: They went out onto the pavement and called his name. "Socks! Socks!" The October wind moved through the trees and sent leaves skittering across the path. No small monkey appeared. Aiden put his hands in his pockets and tried not to feel too worried. It didn't work very well.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Betty designed a MISSING MONKEY poster on her tablet in under five minutes. It had a photograph of Socks in his waistcoat, a written description, and their phone number in large digits. She printed fourteen copies. They posted them through letter boxes up and down both sides of the street without stopping.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: By three o'clock, the sky had gone grey and the wind had picked up. Aiden was sitting on the front step, not saying much. He kept thinking about what Uncle Eddie had said once: that animals raised by hand always know where home is. He held onto that thought very carefully.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: They ran. All four of them, in their socks, without stopping to find shoes, down the pavement to number thirty-seven. They could hear, even from the gate, a small and very determined crunching sound coming from inside.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: There was Socks, sitting on Mrs Obi's kitchen counter beside an open shortbread tin. He was wearing his waistcoat — which they had also assumed was missing — and had crumbs on his face and the expression of someone who sees absolutely no problem with any of this whatsoever.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: There was Socks, sitting on Mrs Obi's kitchen counter beside an open shortbread tin. He was wearing his waistcoat — which they had also assumed was missing — and had crumbs on his face and the expression of someone who sees absolutely no problem with any of this whatsoever.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "How on earth did he get in?" asked Dad. Mrs Obi pointed to the cat flap in her back door. Of course. Socks had worked out the cat flap. He had also — from the state of the shortbread tin — clearly been in before, which nobody had known and which explained certain things about Mrs Obi's biscuit situation.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Aiden picked him up and held him. Socks was warm and solid and smelled faintly of shortbread. He patted Aiden's cheek twice with one small black hand, the way he sometimes did when he felt like being kind, and then tucked his head under Aiden's chin. Aiden breathed out slowly.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: On the way home, Betty said they needed a tracker collar. Aiden said they needed to block every cat flap on the street. Mum said they needed a more interesting biscuit tin. Dad said they should call Uncle Eddie and tell him what his monkey had been up to. They all laughed, and kept laughing, all the way home — and Socks rode on Aiden's shoulder the whole way, looking, as always, entirely pleased with himself.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: "What shall we study?" said Betty. They sat with the notebook between them and listed every idea they had. Aiden had eleven. Betty had nine. Three of them were exactly the same, which Betty said proved they had good scientific minds.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: They decided to grow crystals. It was Betty's original idea and Aiden's second choice, which Betty said made it the obvious answer. They ordered the kit and spent four days watching for the post.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: They decided to grow crystals. It was Betty's original idea and Aiden's second choice, which Betty said made it the obvious answer. They ordered the kit and spent four days watching for the post.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: The crystal-growing worked perfectly. Blue copper sulphate crystals grew on a thread in a jam jar, getting bigger and more geometric every day. Aiden photographed them every morning. Betty kept a careful growth chart.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: "Socks!" said Aiden and Betty. Socks examined the jar from every angle, turning it slowly. He handed it back eventually — and the crystals were, miraculously, completely intact.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: "Socks!" said Aiden and Betty. Socks examined the jar from every angle, turning it slowly. He handed it back eventually — and the crystals were, miraculously, completely intact.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: They made their display board on a rainy Saturday — a bright blue background, a photograph of each day's crystal growth, Betty's data chart, and a title in Aiden's best six-colour lettering: HOW DO CRYSTALS GROW?

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: The school hall was full of projects — a volcano that erupted three times, a model solar system, a survey about favourite foods with real graphs. Betty looked at all of them carefully and said nothing. Aiden chewed the inside of his cheek.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: The judges spent a very long time with Aiden and Betty's crystals — because Betty could explain not just what had happened but why, which turned out to be the whole point of the exercise.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: That evening, Aiden added a new page to his field notebook: WHAT MAKES A GOOD EXPERIMENT. He had six points. Socks sat on the desk and watched him write, which Aiden had never seen him do before.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie came back for a long weekend in June — browner from the sun, with a new bag of unusual gifts and more stories than they had time to hear. Socks heard the doorbell and ran in circles for forty-five seconds without stopping.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie came back for a long weekend in June — browner from the sun, with a new bag of unusual gifts and more stories than they had time to hear. Socks heard the doorbell and ran in circles for forty-five seconds without stopping.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: The reserve was layered with sounds — insects, birds, the river — all at once and all different. Socks sat on Aiden's shoulder and went completely still, his head turning slowly to track each sound. Aiden had never seen him so quiet.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: The reserve was layered with sounds — insects, birds, the river — all at once and all different. Socks sat on Aiden's shoulder and went completely still, his head turning slowly to track each sound. Aiden had never seen him so quiet.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Betty found the bird hide first — a long wooden structure with narrow slot windows over the reed bed. Inside: a log book, borrowed binoculars, and a board listing twelve species to find. She was immediately in her element.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Through the binoculars, Betty saw a kingfisher — a bright impossible dart of blue-orange above the water, there and then gone. She had to put the binoculars down and close her eyes for a moment. She had seen it. She wrote it in the log book.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Through the binoculars, Betty saw a kingfisher — a bright impossible dart of blue-orange above the water, there and then gone. She had to put the binoculars down and close her eyes for a moment. She had seen it. She wrote it in the log book.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: He led them to a shallow pool in a mossy clearing — fed by a spring, perfectly clear and still. Two dragonflies skimmed the surface, electric blue. Aiden crouched at the edge and looked in. Small things moved in the shallows. He forgot to breathe.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: He led them to a shallow pool in a mossy clearing — fed by a spring, perfectly clear and still. Two dragonflies skimmed the surface, electric blue. Aiden crouched at the edge and looked in. Small things moved in the shallows. He forgot to breathe.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: On the way back, the sun was low and the meadow was full of seed heads catching the light. Socks rode on Uncle Eddie's shoulder, which he had always done but which now looked, here, like a kind of homecoming.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie left on Sunday evening. He stayed on the doorstep a long time, saying goodbye properly. When the car was gone, Socks sat on the hall windowsill and watched the empty road. Then he came inside and sat on Aiden's lap, which he had never done before. Aiden stayed very still.

Then he came inside and sat on Aiden's lap, which he had never done before. Aiden stayed very still.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Aiden didn't say anything. He went home and sat on his bed and stared at the ceiling. He wasn't crying, but he wasn't fine either. He didn't really want to talk about it — which Betty noticed immediately.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Aiden didn't say anything. He went home and sat on his bed and stared at the ceiling. He wasn't crying, but he wasn't fine either. He didn't really want to talk about it — which Betty noticed immediately.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "What happened?" said Betty. Aiden told her in pieces, looking at the floor. Betty listened to all of it without saying anything. Then she said: "He's wrong. And being wrong loudly is still just being wrong." Aiden thought about that.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: On Friday, Marcus said it again in the lunch queue. Betty was right there. She looked at Marcus with exactly one raised eyebrow and said, clearly: "His name is Aiden. Which you know." Marcus looked surprised. He didn't say anything else.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Aiden felt two things: grateful for Betty, and also frustrated, because he wanted to have done it himself. Betty, who had been watching him think, said: "Next time you'll do it. I was just practising with you."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: It was quiet. Nobody laughed. Marcus said something low, but nobody around him responded. Aiden walked on. His legs were slightly shaky — but he hadn't shown it, and he was extremely proud of himself.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: He wrote in his notebook that evening: Saying a true thing clearly is harder than it looks and better than it sounds. He underlined it twice.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Betty read it over his shoulder. She didn't comment on it. She put her hand on his shoulder for a moment and went back to her own desk. That was enough.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Miss Okafor had noticed, in the way that good teachers always notice. She started a class discussion about what it means to be fair, and what you do when things aren't. Several children looked at the floor. Marcus looked at the window.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "The point," said Miss Okafor, "is not that everyone will always be kind. The point is that you always have a choice about how to respond — and that choice is completely yours." Aiden wrote it down. It felt like something worth keeping.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: He told Betty. Betty got the torch and studied it with great interest. "It's definitely loose," she said. "It'll fall out and a permanent one will grow. That's much better, actually." Aiden was not entirely sure that it was.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: He told Betty. Betty got the torch and studied it with great interest. "It's definitely loose," she said. "It'll fall out and a permanent one will grow. That's much better, actually." Aiden was not entirely sure that it was.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: That night, Aiden worried about the tooth. It felt wrong — like something was breaking. He wrote in his notebook: Things that are strange: losing a tooth. Also, why teeth? Socks sat on the desk and watched him with great curiosity.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Mum said it was completely normal and that they had both lost teeth before when they were smaller — Aiden had even eaten one inside a peanut butter sandwich and not noticed for an hour. Aiden was not certain this was reassuring.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Mum said it was completely normal and that they had both lost teeth before when they were smaller — Aiden had even eaten one inside a peanut butter sandwich and not noticed for an hour. Aiden was not certain this was reassuring.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Betty lost her first tooth the very next day, which nobody had seen coming. It came out at lunch, and she held it up and examined it with great interest before putting it in her pocket, as if this were a routine scientific procedure.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Aiden's tooth came out on a Thursday. Not dramatically — he was reading his book and he touched it and then it was just there in his fingers, which was very quick and very strange and did not hurt at all.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: He held it up for a long time. It was tiny. It was the smallest thing that had ever felt significant. He put it in the small envelope Mum left for him, and when he placed it under his pillow it felt ceremonial.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: In the morning, the tooth was gone and there was a coin in its place. Aiden knew, in the way children who read a lot know things, that it was Mum or Dad who had swapped it. He said nothing, because some things are better left as stories.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Three weeks later, the new tooth began to come through. It was enormous relative to the gap — a proper square adult tooth in a mouth that had been full of small rounded baby ones. Aiden looked at himself in the mirror and felt extremely strange.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: Dad had been talking about the castle trip since January. A proper medieval castle, forty minutes away — with a tower you could actually climb, a dungeon that was a real dungeon, and a great hall whose stone floor had been there for six hundred years. Betty had already read a book about it.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: They drove there on a bright Saturday in April. Aiden pressed his face to the car window when the castle appeared over the hill — grey stone towers above the treeline, impossibly old and very much still there. He felt something he didn't yet have a word for.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The entrance was a proper drawbridge — working, over a real water-filled moat. It was smaller than he'd imagined and more real than he'd imagined. Aiden crossed it one step at a time, listening to the echo of his footsteps on old wood, thinking about every person who had crossed it before him.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The great hall was vast and grey and cool. The stone floor was uneven and worn in paths where feet had walked for centuries. Aiden crouched and pressed his hand flat to the floor. Six hundred years of footsteps had passed here. He could not quite hold that thought all at once.

uses.pageText: The dungeon was underground and smelled of cold stone and old air. Betty read every board by torchlight. Aiden stood still in the near-dark for a moment and thought about how this exact place had been here through everything — and felt briefly, appropriately small.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The North Tower had one hundred and twelve steps. They counted every one, out loud, all together. The staircase was so narrow they had to go single file. At the top: the whole landscape, the river, the town, a motorway miles away. The same view and entirely different.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The North Tower had one hundred and twelve steps. They counted every one, out loud, all together. The staircase was so narrow they had to go single file. At the top: the whole landscape, the river, the town, a motorway miles away. The same view and entirely different.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: "Imagine standing here," said Betty quietly, "and not knowing what was coming." Aiden thought about that for a long time, looking out. There was something important in it he couldn't quite hold yet. He wrote it in his notebook anyway, to think about later.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The drive home was quiet in the way that follows something large. "What are you thinking about?" said Mum. Aiden and Betty both answered at the same time, with completely different answers. "That," said Mum, "is exactly right."

uses.title: Chompy's Big Lunch
uses.pageText: Chompy ate and ate. More, please! said Chompy.

uses.title: Grumpy Needs Help
uses.pageText: Grumpy pulled and pulled. Grumpy was still stuck.

uses.title: Bossy Makes a Plan
uses.pageText: Bossy, said Sunny, can we try YOUR way AND our way? They worked together. It worked!

uses.title: Bouncy Bumps Into Everything
uses.pageText: AAAACHOOOO! Leaves, berries, and Bossy's clipboard all blew away.

uses.title: Wiggly's Messy Day
uses.pageText: Wiggly sat very, very still. The tail still knocked over three berries and a leaf.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down
uses.pageText: Zippy ran so fast that Zippy ran right past the picnic. And the waterfall. And Sunny Hollow.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down
uses.pageText: Zippy ran so fast that Zippy ran right past the picnic. And the waterfall. And Sunny Hollow.

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Cheeky laughed and laughed. But then Cheeky slipped on the same mud. SPLAT!

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Cheeky helped clean Fancy's rock. Will you do any more pranks? asked Fancy. Maybe just one more, said Cheeky. And winked.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: One morning, Sunny stayed very still and very quiet behind a fern. Sunny waited.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: Sunny saw two small eyes behind a rock. And two small pink paws placing a tiny woven grass bracelet on the rock.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: They were the best gifts we ever had, said Sunny. Will you come and sit with us? Shy came out. Just a little way. But it was something.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: The next morning, eleven gifts were on the Big Flat Rock. One from each Dino Pal. A small pink paw reached out and took them, one by one.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Fancy woke up and found something terrible. Fancy's sail was bent. Not a little bent. Very bent.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: I cannot leave the cave, said Fancy. Not like this. Fancy sat very still and stared at the cave wall.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Wiggly dampened the sail gently and pressed it very softly. Slowly, slowly, it began to straighten.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: The next morning, Fancy left a beautifully woven bracelet outside Wiggly's cave. Wiggly's tail knocked it away at once. Sorry! said Wiggly. It is fine, said Fancy. And meant it.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: Clumsy could see over all the ferns, past the waterfall, all the way to the Long Meadow and beyond.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: I can reach it, said Wiggly. Wiggly stretched the long neck down, down, down. The tail swept three rocks and a berry bush. Sorry. But Wiggly had the pillow.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: We make a good team, said Clumsy. You see the problem. I reach the problem. Exactly, said Clumsy, and accidentally knocked off Wiggly's hat. Sorry.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy woke up and tried to fly. Flappy got three wing-flaps up. Then landed in the mud.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: But dinosaurs do not nest in trees, said Flappy. You do, said Grumpy. And birds do not live in Sunny Hollow with everyone else. You do, said Grumpy.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy went back to the tree. Got three wing-flaps up. Landed neatly on a branch. Sat very high up and looked at all of Sunny Hollow below. Oh, said Flappy quietly. That is quite good actually.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: The Dino Pals went to look. A huge pile of rocks had fallen in the night and blocked the stream above.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: They reached the meadow. Grumpy found the flat rock and sat on it. Chompy found a berry patch immediately.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: There would be a running race, a jumping contest, a loudness competition, and a prize for the tidiest corner of the Hollow. More events to be decided, said Bossy. I have a clipboard.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Dozy slept through most of the events and woke up in time for the picnic. Did I win anything? said Dozy. Most restful competitor, said Bossy. Deserved, said Dozy, and fell asleep again.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Dozy slept through most of the events and woke up in time for the picnic. Did I win anything? said Dozy. Most restful competitor, said Bossy. Deserved, said Dozy, and fell asleep again.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: Inside the dream, Dozy was wide awake. Dozy had never been so awake. Everything was golden and warm and soft.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: Inside the dream, Dozy was wide awake. Dozy had never been so awake. Everything was golden and warm and soft.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: In the dream, Sunny Hollow was made of clouds. Dozy was walking on clouds. The clouds were warm and soft, which was very agreeable.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: Dream Bouncy bounced so high that Bouncy went above the clouds and kept going. Everyone watched. Nobody was surprised.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: At the top of Mount Rumble, all the Dino Pals were there. Sitting on the warm peak. Watching all of Sunny Hollow spread out below, tiny and green and perfect.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: At the top of Mount Rumble, all the Dino Pals were there. Sitting on the warm peak. Watching all of Sunny Hollow spread out below, tiny and green and perfect.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: Zippy held the small winner's pebble and looked at it. Zippy, said Sunny, are you all right? I nearly lost, said Zippy.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: The morning felt strange. The air was heavy and still. Mount Rumble was not puffing its usual heart-shaped rings.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Clumsy stood tall and looked out over the whole Hollow. The storm is coming from the east, said Clumsy. The tall ferns are already bending. That gives us time.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Honky called all the Dino Pals from across the Hollow. One enormous blast. Every leaf fell off. But everyone heard and came running.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Zippy ran back and forth collecting everything needed before anyone could finish asking. Twelve trips in four minutes. Done, said Zippy.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Bouncy bounced up to reach the high branches and secure anything at risk. Only bumped into three things. A new record, said Bouncy.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: The storm arrived. It was loud and wild. But inside Cozy Cave it was warm. Fifteen Dino Pals, very close together. Even Grumpy did not mind.

uses.title: Shy Comes Out to Play
uses.pageText:
Bouncy went past.
"Come and play!"
Shy hid.

uses.title: Shy Comes Out to Play
uses.pageText:
Tiny went past.
"Come and play!"
Shy hid.

uses.title: Splashy Finds a Puddle
uses.pageText: Splashy jumps and jumps.

uses.title: Muddy and Splashy Make a Mess
uses.pageText: Mud and water make... mud!

uses.title: Bouncy and Speedy Have a Race
uses.pageText: They ran and ran.

uses.title: Shy and Cuddly Find Each Other
uses.pageText: Cuddly wants a hug. Cuddly looks and looks.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: "Try something scary," said Burrow. So Pip walked to the Tumblerock Cliffs. He found the high ledge and began to climb.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: The fog was thick and grey. Something rustled in the reeds nearby. Pip kept walking. He came out the other side.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: Burrow smiled. "The stone doesn't do anything," he said. "I wanted to see what you would do. And you were brave."

uses.title: Fern Grows Too Much
uses.pageText: By afternoon, the plant had grown through the roof. It was still growing. Everyone stood back and watched.

uses.title: Fern Grows Too Much
uses.pageText: Fern sat down and thought. Spells had made it grow. But a growing thing needed something different.

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: Stone reached the other side. Stone reached down and picked up Burrow very carefully. "Oh, thank you," said Burrow. "I was going in circles."

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: Every morning, Glimmer practised. Fire breathing was the most important thing a dragon could do. And Glimmer could not do it yet.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: On the tenth day, Glimmer went to the Crystal Stream alone. Again and again. Smoke. Sparks. Warm cinnamon breath. Still no fire.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: Glimmer sat down. "I will never breathe fire," said Glimmer. "I have tried every day and it is never fire."

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: That evening, a Fog Marsh fox came creeping into Moonwood. It had found Fern's seed collection. The seeds were small and precious. Glimmer saw the fox.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: And a jet of brilliant orange fire came out. The fox ran. The seeds were safe.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: Wren found her spell book. It was enormous now. She climbed up onto it and looked at the spell. She had read it backwards.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: Flint had decided to map every single path in Moonwood. He had a new roll of parchment and a good quill. He started at the Hollow Oak and walked north.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: Flint had decided to map every single path in Moonwood. He had a new roll of parchment and a good quill. He started at the Hollow Oak and walked north.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: He walked for three days. He did not stop. His map grew longer and longer. It was full of detail.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: The fish was quiet for a while. It swam a small, slow circle. Then it came back. Because I am new here, said the fish. And I wanted to sound interesting.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: Burrow was digging a new tunnel. He dug down, and he dug sideways, and he dug carefully around the roots. Then his spade hit something hard and wooden.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: Burrow was digging a new tunnel. He dug down, and he dug sideways, and he dug carefully around the roots. Then his spade hit something hard and wooden.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: Burrow was digging a new tunnel. He dug down, and he dug sideways, and he dug carefully around the roots. Then his spade hit something hard and wooden.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: He polished his glasses and looked more closely. On the door was a small carving. A tree with roots going in every direction. It was very old.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: Inside was a small round room. The walls were covered in tiny glowing drawings. Trees and streams. Creatures and old paths. Every living thing that had ever been in Moonwood.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: Inside was a small round room. The walls were covered in tiny glowing drawings. Trees and streams. Creatures and old paths. Every living thing that had ever been in Moonwood.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: They stayed for a long time. No one wanted to leave. The room was very quiet and very warm.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Spark tried to hold the sneeze in. His eyes went watery. His magic began to build and build. The sparkles around him grew very bright.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Every fish in the stream turned purple. The water sang in a different key. One fish turned into a frog for a moment, and then turned back.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: What do you remember about it? asked Pip. I remember it was today, said Luna. And it was important. And... she paused. I think it was outside.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: What do you remember about it? asked Pip. I remember it was today, said Luna. And it was important. And... she paused. I think it was outside.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: Moonwood seeds, said Luna. From the first trees. For the day the old trees grow tired and need new ones beside them.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
Pip and Stone were sitting outside the Hollow Oak.
Then a noise came from the Fog Marsh.
It was very, very loud.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
They stood at the edge together.
The fog was thick and grey-green.
The noise bounced off the twisted trees.
"Together," said Stone.
Pip nodded.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
Stone stood up and called out across the marsh.
It was the loudest sound Pip had ever heard.
Louder than the toadling.
Much louder.
Something answered from the far side of the marsh.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
Fern tried to push with her hands.
The boulder did not move.
Fern stepped back and thought.
"We need each other," said Fern.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
They pushed and pulled together.
The boulder shifted.
The mud let go.
The boulder rolled aside.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
The water rushed over the singing stones.
And the Crystal Stream began to sing.
First very quietly.
Then louder.
Then loud enough to hear all the way to the Hollow Oak.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
They sat on the bank and listened.
The stream sang around them.
"We did it," said Fern.
Dewdrop smiled.
"It sang itself. We just moved the stone."

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
At the Hollow Oak, everyone heard it.
"The stream is singing again!" said Pip.
"We just moved a stone," said Fern.
"And asked the water nicely," said Dewdrop.
"It did the rest."

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
Glimmer and Spark made a deal.
Spark would teach Glimmer to breathe fire properly.
Glimmer would teach Spark to fly.
They shook on it.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
Glimmer tried.
Smoke came out.
Just smoke.
"Interesting," said Spark, and wrote things down.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
Wren and Flint were going to the Whispering Meadow.
Flint had a map.
Wren had a direction spell.
"We will be perfectly fine," said Flint.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
The mushroom's glow changed.
It pulsed once — pointing.
Another mushroom far away pulsed the same way.
And another.
A trail of glowing mushrooms lit up through the trees.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
Wren and Flint followed the mushroom trail.
The forest opened up.
The golden light of the Whispering Meadow was ahead.
"Oh," said Flint.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
"Why didn't we try that first?" asked Flint.
"I don't know," said Wren.
She looked back at the mushroom trail.
"They seemed happy about it though."
The last mushroom blinked once and went out.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
The room had carvings on every wall.
It had small glowing stones in the ceiling.
It smelled of old wood and old magic.
Burrow had never seen it before.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Luna walked slowly around the room.
She touched the carvings.
They lit up where she touched.
Blue and gold.
She had been here before.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Burrow sat very still and listened.
The room grew warmer.
The carvings lit up one by one.
Luna's voice was quiet and certain.
She had always known these stories.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Burrow sat very still and listened.
The room grew warmer.
The carvings lit up one by one.
Luna's voice was quiet and certain.
She had always known these stories.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
Night fell.
Moonwood glowed softly.
Pip and Glimmer hid behind the big mushroom.
They watched.
Nothing happened.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
Then — a sound.
A shuffling.
A round shape moving through the clearing.
Pip and Glimmer looked at each other.
They crept closer.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
Then Burrow sat down.
Against the big mushroom.
Pip and Glimmer were still behind it.
Burrow began to snore.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
In the morning, Burrow woke up.
He looked around.
Pip and Glimmer were standing in front of him.
"Good morning," said Burrow.
There was a long pause.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Dewdrop found Stone at the Hollow Oak.
"I need your hands," she said.
"Just to reach in and move a rock."
Stone understood immediately.
Then Stone understood all of it.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Stone sat and dripped.
Stone looked at the arm.
Stone looked at the rest of Stone.
"The fish is free," said Stone.
"Yes," said Dewdrop.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
They sat by the stream together.
Stone dripped for a long time.
The fish surfaced once.
It seemed happy.
"Good," said Stone.
And meant it.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
The magic seeds were gone.
The box that held them was open and empty.
Luna looked at the box for a long time.
"This is not good," she said.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
Wren and Spark tried search spells.
The spells pointed at each other.
Stone looked under every log.
Gently.
There were no seeds under the logs.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
The small things landed and bounced.
They bounced along the ground.
They made a sound like giggling.
They left gold trails where they bounced.
"What ARE they?" said Pip.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
Pip caught one.
It was warm.
It had very large golden eyes.
It looked up at Pip and giggled.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
Stone raised their hands high.
Pip and Spark added a little push.
The star spirits lifted.
Up.
And up.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
Stone raised their hands high.
Pip and Spark added a little push.
The star spirits lifted.
Up.
And up.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Pip, Wren, Burrow, and Fern went inside to search.
They searched every room.
They found nothing.
Then Burrow's nose twitched.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Inside was a room.
It was small and warm.
It was full of collected things.
A tiny creature was searching through them.
She did not look up.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
They made Twig a slightly larger door.
Twig came out for acorn biscuits.
She sat in the big room and looked around.
"I like it here," she said.
"But I like my room better."
"This is also very nice."

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Luna read out the race rules.
The course: from the Hollow Oak to the Crystal Stream to the Tumblerock Cliffs and back.
Everyone was at the starting line.
Everyone was ready.
Mostly.

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
They were off.
Pip ran.
Fern flew.
Stone trotted.
Dewdrop glided.
Wren ran and read her spell book.
Flint took a very confident turn left.

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
Pip told Luna.
Luna listened carefully.
"Something is wrong at the marsh," she said.
"We must go in."
Pip, Fern, and Dewdrop came too.

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
They marked the boundary at the Hollow Oak.
Everyone placed a stone.
"The marsh is the marsh," said Luna.
"Moonwood is Moonwood."
"And we leave space for both."

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
Everyone gasped.
Pip covered his mouth.
Stone's eyes went very wide.
Luna took off her glasses and put them back on.
It was real.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: A butterfly's life has four stages. This is called a lifecycle. Each stage looks completely different from the one before.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Stage one: the butterfly lays tiny eggs on a leaf. The eggs are very small — some are no bigger than a pinhead. The leaf is food for the caterpillar inside.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Stage two: the egg hatches into a caterpillar. The caterpillar's only job is to eat. It eats and eats and grows and grows. Some caterpillars eat their own eggshell first!

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Stage three: the caterpillar makes a hard shell around itself. This is called a chrysalis. Inside, an extraordinary change is about to happen.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Stage three: the caterpillar makes a hard shell around itself. This is called a chrysalis. Inside, an extraordinary change is about to happen.

uses.title: Butterflies
uses.pageText: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar breaks down completely. Its body rebuilds itself as a butterfly. This amazing process is called metamorphosis. It takes one to two weeks.

uses.title: Butterflies

uses.title: Frogs

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "His name is Socks," said Uncle Eddie. "He was orphaned when he was very small, and I've raised him from a baby. He understands a lot of what you say, he copies behaviour, and he is completely tame." He paused just a moment. "He is also, just occasionally, a little bit naughty."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "He loves shiny objects," Uncle Eddie explained at dinner. "He adores warm spots — the airing cupboard is a particular risk. And if he gets bored, he will find a way to become interesting." Everyone filed this information away carefully.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "He is completely impossible," said Mum, as she did most evenings. But she had also started setting a small dish of whatever she was cooking on the corner of the counter every night, because Socks knew exactly where it appeared and waited there very patiently, and she had not been able to bring herself to stop.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: By three o'clock, the sky had gone grey and the wind had picked up. Aiden was sitting on the front step, not saying much. He kept thinking about what Uncle Eddie had said once: that animals raised by hand always know where home is. He held onto that thought very carefully.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: "Do you think he misses the rainforest?" Aiden asked one evening. Betty thought for a long time. "I think he's decided this is his rainforest," she said. Aiden looked at Socks on his shoulder. "Yeah," he said. "I think so too."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "What happened?" said Betty. Aiden told her in pieces, looking at the floor. Betty listened to all of it without saying anything. Then she said: "He's wrong. And being wrong loudly is still just being wrong." Aiden thought about that.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: That night, Aiden wrote in his notebook: When something is unfair, you have two choices — pretend it isn't happening, or decide what to do. He starred the second option. He didn't quite know yet what doing something looked like.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: On Friday, Marcus said it again in the lunch queue. Betty was right there. She looked at Marcus with exactly one raised eyebrow and said, clearly: "His name is Aiden. Which you know." Marcus looked surprised. He didn't say anything else.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: On Monday, Marcus said it one more time, in front of a small group. Aiden turned around. He looked at Marcus directly for a moment. Then he said, clearly: "My name is Aiden." That was all. He turned back.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: He wrote in his notebook that evening: Saying a true thing clearly is harder than it looks and better than it sounds. He underlined it twice.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "The point," said Miss Okafor, "is not that everyone will always be kind. The point is that you always have a choice about how to respond — and that choice is completely yours." Aiden wrote it down. It felt like something worth keeping.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The drive home was quiet in the way that follows something large. "What are you thinking about?" said Mum. Aiden and Betty both answered at the same time, with completely different answers. "That," said Mum, "is exactly right."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: That evening, Aiden wrote in his field notebook for a long time — the drawbridge, the worn floor, the arrow loop, the view. At the bottom of the last page he wrote: Things were happening before we got here. They'll keep happening after. That's not sad. That's just how big it is. He underlined it.

uses.title: Sunny's Rainy Day
uses.pageText: Come in! called Sunny. It is lovely!

uses.title: Sunny's Rainy Day
uses.pageText: Hmph, said Grumpy. This is... not terrible.

uses.title: Sunny's Rainy Day
uses.pageText: The sun came back out. See? said Sunny. Every day is a good day!

uses.title: Dozy Won't Wake Up
uses.pageText: Dozy sniffed. Dozy opened one eye. Is that... lunch? said Dozy.

uses.title: Bossy Makes a Plan
uses.pageText: The plan was a mess. Nobody is doing it right! said Bossy.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down
uses.pageText: Oh, said Zippy. This is... nice. Zippy sat down. Zippy had never sat down before.

uses.title: Honky's Inside Voice
uses.pageText: Honky, said Bossy, you need an inside voice. What is an inside voice? A quiet one. I do not have one of those.

uses.title: Honky's Inside Voice
uses.pageText: IT IS OKAY! called Honky. Honky's voice was louder than the thunder. Dozy stopped shaking.

uses.title: Honky's Inside Voice
uses.pageText: Maybe Honky's voice is very useful after all, said Bossy. THANK YOU! said Honky. Every leaf fell off again.

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Wiggly walked off. BOING! Wiggly bounced back. My tail is stuck! HEE HEE HEE! said Cheeky.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: One day it was a leafy fan for Dozy. This is perfect, said Dozy, already asleep with it.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: Who is leaving these gifts? said Bossy. I need to know. It is not on my clipboard.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: Who is leaving these gifts? said Bossy. I need to know. It is not on my clipboard.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Bouncy offered to bounce on it gently. That is not what gently means, said Fancy.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Fancy looked in the pool. Oh, said Fancy. Oh, that is much better. Fancy looked at Wiggly. Thank you. A real thank you.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: The next morning, Fancy left a beautifully woven bracelet outside Wiggly's cave. Wiggly's tail knocked it away at once. Sorry! said Wiggly. It is fine, said Fancy. And meant it.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: It could be anywhere, said Bossy, looking at the clipboard. Sunny Hollow is very big.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: I can see the mud puddle, said Clumsy. I can see the berry bushes. I can see Chompy at the berry bushes, which is not a surprise.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: Can you see the pillow? said Dozy. There was a long pause. Oh, said Clumsy. Yes. It is in the waterfall.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Bossy flies, said Flappy. Bossy is a Pterodactyl. You are an Archaeopteryx. That is different. How is it different? said Flappy. Grumpy did not actually know.

uses.title: What is Flappy?

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Grumpy, said Flappy. Am I a dinosaur or a bird? Grumpy thought for a very long time. You are Flappy, said Grumpy. That is enough.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: So I am something new? said Flappy. You are something Flappy, said Grumpy. Which nobody else is.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy went back to the tree. Got three wing-flaps up. Landed neatly on a branch. Sat very high up and looked at all of Sunny Hollow below. Oh, said Flappy quietly. That is quite good actually.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: Chompy is strong, said Sunny. Chompy tried. Chompy ate a nearby berry bush instead. Sorry, said Chompy.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: I am going to the Long Meadow, said Grumpy. There is a good flat rock there. Peaceful. No one around. Chompy appeared. Can I come? said Chompy. Grumpy closed their eyes. Fine.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: This is a leaf, said Grumpy. I know, said Chompy. It is a good leaf.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: This is a leaf, said Grumpy. I know, said Chompy. It is a good leaf.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: This is a pebble, said Grumpy. I am not eating the pebble, said Chompy. Glad to hear it, said Grumpy.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: This is a good rock, said Chompy. Yes, said Grumpy. Is there anything to eat near it? said Chompy. Grumpy pointed at the berry patch. Chompy went happily.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: This is a good rock, said Chompy. Yes, said Grumpy. Is there anything to eat near it? said Chompy. Grumpy pointed at the berry patch. Chompy went happily.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: Grumpy sat on the rock alone. It was peaceful. But after a while, Grumpy called: There is a good-looking bush to your left. Thanks, Grumpy! said Chompy. Grumpy said nothing. But the corner of the mouth went up. Just slightly.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Grumpy won the grumpiest face competition that Cheeky invented. Grumpy won immediately. I am not sure that is a compliment, said Grumpy. It absolutely is, said Cheeky.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: Chompy was there, but all the food was made of more clouds. This is disappointing, said Dream Chompy.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: Dozy floated on a cloud past the Rainbow Waterfall. But in the dream, the waterfall was made of warm golden light. Oh, said Dozy. This is very nice.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Clumsy stood tall and looked out over the whole Hollow. The storm is coming from the east, said Clumsy. The tall ferns are already bending. That gives us time.

uses.pageText: Muddy is in the mud.

uses.pageText: Muddy is very muddy.

uses.pageText: Muddy is muddy again.

uses.title: Muddy Has a Bath
uses.pageText: Muddy is happy.

uses.pageText: It is Grumpy's birthday.

uses.pageText: Noisy is not good at quiet.

uses.pageText: But Shy is behind the barn.

uses.pageText: The hay bale is big.

uses.pageText: It is a small puddle.

uses.pageText: "My hat is wet!" said Clucky.

uses.title: Splashy Finds a Puddle
uses.pageText: "My bed is wet!" said Sleepy.

uses.title: Splashy Finds a Puddle
uses.pageText: Splashy is very happy.

uses.pageText: It is still dark.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: "What is this?" said Pip. He picked it up carefully. The glow made his fingers feel warm.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: Burrow appeared from a nearby tunnel. "That is a Bravery Stone," said Burrow. "Whoever holds it will feel brave."

uses.title: Fern Grows Too Much
uses.pageText: Luna smiled. "That is quite nice, actually," said Luna. Fern smiled. She was very tired.

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: Stone would not cross the bridge. "There is a troll under the bridge," said Stone. "I do not want to meet it."

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: "That is not fire," said Glimmer. "No," agreed Pip. "But it smells nice." Glimmer did not look convinced.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: Glimmer sat down. "I will never breathe fire," said Glimmer. "I have tried every day and it is never fire."

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: You are interesting, said Dewdrop. You are the only fish in this stream with a blue stripe. The fish looked at its own stripe. That is true, it said.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: Is being the only blue-stripe fish enough? asked the fish. Yes, said Dewdrop. It is very enough.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: Is being the only blue-stripe fish enough? asked the fish. Yes, said Dewdrop. It is very enough.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: What is the fish called? asked Pip. I... said Dewdrop. She stopped. She had forgotten to ask. She turned back toward the water.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: I have found something, Burrow told everyone. They gathered at the Hollow Oak. A door, said Burrow, underground. Very old. I don't know what is inside.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: What is inside? said Pip. Luna was quiet. Good things, I think, she said finally. I cannot quite remember what kind.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: They walked along the walls slowly. There were drawings of things no one had seen in hundreds of years. What is this place? asked Fern.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: The memory room, said Luna. That is what it was called. She touched the wall very gently. I remember now.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: What would have happened if you hadn't remembered? asked Wren. I did remember, said Luna. With help. She looked at all of them. That is the point.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
"I want to find out what it is," said Pip.
"I do not," said Stone.
"It is very loud."

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
"I want to find out what it is," said Pip.

"It is very loud."

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
"It flows," said Fern.
"But it does not sing," said Dewdrop.
"Something is wrong at the source."

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
At the Hollow Oak, everyone heard it.
"The stream is singing again!" said Pip.
"We just moved a stone," said Fern.
"And asked the water nicely," said Dewdrop.
"It did the rest."

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
"Spark," said Glimmer.
"You are trying too hard."
"Fire is not thinking."
"It is feeling."
Spark looked at Glimmer for a long time.

uses.pageText:
"Spark," said Glimmer.
