uses.pageText: The drive took three hours. Betty counted every red car they passed. Aiden read two chapters of his book, fell asleep on his own shoulder, woke up, read another chapter, and then asked "Are we nearly there?" for the fourth time. They were, finally, nearly there.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: The cottage smelled of sea salt and old wood and something warm that Aiden couldn't name. They raced upstairs to choose rooms. There was a small room and a slightly bigger room. They flipped a coin — Aiden got the bigger room, but Betty got the one with the sea view, which meant it was perfectly even.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: Aiden spent the whole first morning at a rock pool near the headland. He found three kinds of crab, a sea anemone that closed when you touched it, and a tiny fish he thought might be a blenny. He wrote everything down in his field notebook in careful columns.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: On Wednesday it rained all morning. They played three rounds of Cluedo, drank hot chocolate in large mugs and listened to the rain hammer against the cottage windows. It was, Aiden thought, pressing his mug to his chin, one of the cosiest mornings he could remember.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: On Wednesday it rained all morning. They played three rounds of Cluedo, drank hot chocolate in large mugs and listened to the rain hammer against the cottage windows. It was, Aiden thought, pressing his mug to his chin, one of the cosiest mornings he could remember.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: The lighthouse was Dad's idea. It was tall and white and stood on a headland two miles along the coastal path. There were one hundred and forty-seven steps to the top — they counted every single one, out loud, all together, and arrived slightly out of breath but very proud.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: Betty found a small smooth white pebble at the shoreline and turned it over and over in her fingers all the way back to the cottage. She was going to put it on her windowsill at home, so she'd always have a piece of the coast — something real from a real day.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Carefully, Uncle Eddie unzipped the carry-case. Inside, curled up like a small comma, was the most compact monkey Aiden had ever seen. He had cream-white fur on his face and chest, darker brown on his back, and small black hands and feet that looked, unmistakably, like he was wearing a pair of extremely neat little socks.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "His name is Socks," said Uncle Eddie. "He was orphaned when he was very small, and I've raised him from a baby. He understands a lot of what you say, he copies behaviour, and he is completely tame." He paused just a moment. "He is also, just occasionally, a little bit naughty."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks explored the house in eleven minutes. He opened every drawer he could reach, rearranged the fruit bowl into a different order, sat briefly on each windowsill and posted three letters from the hall table into the back of the television. He seemed very pleased with his work.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: That night, Dad built Socks a cosy sleeping box — a wooden crate lined with a soft fleece blanket — and settled it in the warm corner of the kitchen. In the morning, Socks was not in it. He was curled up fast asleep at the foot of Aiden's bed, his small black hand curled around Aiden's pencil torch.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: That night, Dad built Socks a cosy sleeping box — a wooden crate lined with a soft fleece blanket — and settled it in the warm corner of the kitchen. In the morning, Socks was not in it. He was curled up fast asleep at the foot of Aiden's bed, his small black hand curled around Aiden's pencil torch.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: He was also, as promised, occasionally naughty. He dropped a teaspoon into the toaster. He unravelled the entire roll of cling film in the kitchen drawer. He stole every single one of Betty's hair bobbles and lined them up on the windowsill in a precise order that nobody could explain.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: He was also, as promised, occasionally naughty. He dropped a teaspoon into the toaster. He unravelled the entire roll of cling film in the kitchen drawer. He stole every single one of Betty's hair bobbles and lined them up on the windowsill in a precise order that nobody could explain.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "He is completely impossible," said Mum, as she did most evenings. But she had also started setting a small dish of whatever she was cooking on the corner of the counter every night, because Socks knew exactly where it appeared and waited there very patiently, and she had not been able to bring herself to stop.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "He is completely impossible," said Mum, as she did most evenings. But she had also started setting a small dish of whatever she was cooking on the corner of the counter every night, because Socks knew exactly where it appeared and waited there very patiently, and she had not been able to bring herself to stop.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Aiden had been keeping a field notebook — just as Uncle Eddie had shown him. He had titled it: Socks: A Field Study. He had written things like: Prefers grapes to apple. Expresses disapproval by sitting with back turned. Unusually precise about the order of objects. He turned to a fresh page. It was going to take a very long time to fully understand Socks. He hoped, quietly, that he had the time.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Every morning, Socks sat on the kitchen counter and waited while Betty did up the buttons on his little red waistcoat, which always lived on its own peg beside the back door. But on a Tuesday in October, the peg was empty. And when Aiden went to check, Socks's sleeping box in the corner of his room was empty too.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "He couldn't have got out," said Dad. "All the windows were shut last night." Then Mum remembered the bathroom window — the small one above the bath, left open just a crack for steam. She looked at Aiden and Aiden looked at Betty. A crack that was, they all realised at the same moment, almost exactly the width of a small monkey.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Betty designed a MISSING MONKEY poster on her tablet in under five minutes. It had a photograph of Socks in his waistcoat, a written description, and their phone number in large digits. She printed fourteen copies. They posted them through letter boxes up and down both sides of the street without stopping.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Betty designed a MISSING MONKEY poster on her tablet in under five minutes. It had a photograph of Socks in his waistcoat, a written description, and their phone number in large digits. She printed fourteen copies. They posted them through letter boxes up and down both sides of the street without stopping.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: They ran. All four of them, in their socks, without stopping to find shoes, down the pavement to number thirty-seven. They could hear, even from the gate, a small and very determined crunching sound coming from inside.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: There was Socks, sitting on Mrs Obi's kitchen counter beside an open shortbread tin. He was wearing his waistcoat — which they had also assumed was missing — and had crumbs on his face and the expression of someone who sees absolutely no problem with any of this whatsoever.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: There was Socks, sitting on Mrs Obi's kitchen counter beside an open shortbread tin. He was wearing his waistcoat — which they had also assumed was missing — and had crumbs on his face and the expression of someone who sees absolutely no problem with any of this whatsoever.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "How on earth did he get in?" asked Dad. Mrs Obi pointed to the cat flap in her back door. Of course. Socks had worked out the cat flap. He had also — from the state of the shortbread tin — clearly been in before, which nobody had known and which explained certain things about Mrs Obi's biscuit situation.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "How on earth did he get in?" asked Dad. Mrs Obi pointed to the cat flap in her back door. Of course. Socks had worked out the cat flap. He had also — from the state of the shortbread tin — clearly been in before, which nobody had known and which explained certain things about Mrs Obi's biscuit situation.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Aiden picked him up and held him. Socks was warm and solid and smelled faintly of shortbread. He patted Aiden's cheek twice with one small black hand, the way he sometimes did when he felt like being kind, and then tucked his head under Aiden's chin. Aiden breathed out slowly.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: "What shall we study?" said Betty. They sat with the notebook between them and listed every idea they had. Aiden had eleven. Betty had nine. Three of them were exactly the same, which Betty said proved they had good scientific minds.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: Then Socks found the crystal jar. He did not eat it. He simply moved it from the windowsill to a high shelf, where he sat beside it with the expression of someone who had just acquired something important.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: They made their display board on a rainy Saturday — a bright blue background, a photograph of each day's crystal growth, Betty's data chart, and a title in Aiden's best six-colour lettering: HOW DO CRYSTALS GROW?

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: On the morning of the Science Fair, Betty packed the display board in a folder while Aiden carried the crystal jar carefully in both hands. Socks watched from the hallway with what Aiden's notebook called 'intense strategic interest.'

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: The school hall was full of projects — a volcano that erupted three times, a model solar system, a survey about favourite foods with real graphs. Betty looked at all of them carefully and said nothing. Aiden chewed the inside of his cheek.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: The school hall was full of projects — a volcano that erupted three times, a model solar system, a survey about favourite foods with real graphs. Betty looked at all of them carefully and said nothing. Aiden chewed the inside of his cheek.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: The school hall was full of projects — a volcano that erupted three times, a model solar system, a survey about favourite foods with real graphs. Betty looked at all of them carefully and said nothing. Aiden chewed the inside of his cheek.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: The judges spent a very long time with Aiden and Betty's crystals — because Betty could explain not just what had happened but why, which turned out to be the whole point of the exercise.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: Third place, with a commendation for experimental method, went to HOW DO CRYSTALS GROW? The commendation was on a proper certificate with a gold border. Betty read every word of it, twice.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie came back for a long weekend in June — browner from the sun, with a new bag of unusual gifts and more stories than they had time to hear. Socks heard the doorbell and ran in circles for forty-five seconds without stopping.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Through the binoculars, Betty saw a kingfisher — a bright impossible dart of blue-orange above the water, there and then gone. She had to put the binoculars down and close her eyes for a moment. She had seen it. She wrote it in the log book.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: The far bank was different — thicker trees, softer ground, a field of tall meadow grass beyond the treeline. Socks bounded ahead, turning back every few steps to make sure they were following.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: On the way back, the sun was low and the meadow was full of seed heads catching the light. Socks rode on Uncle Eddie's shoulder, which he had always done but which now looked, here, like a kind of homecoming.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: On the way back, the sun was low and the meadow was full of seed heads catching the light. Socks rode on Uncle Eddie's shoulder, which he had always done but which now looked, here, like a kind of homecoming.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "What happened?" said Betty. Aiden told her in pieces, looking at the floor. Betty listened to all of it without saying anything. Then she said: "He's wrong. And being wrong loudly is still just being wrong." Aiden thought about that.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: On Monday, Marcus said it one more time, in front of a small group. Aiden turned around. He looked at Marcus directly for a moment. Then he said, clearly: "My name is Aiden." That was all. He turned back.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: It was quiet. Nobody laughed. Marcus said something low, but nobody around him responded. Aiden walked on. His legs were slightly shaky — but he hadn't shown it, and he was extremely proud of himself.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: A week later, Marcus bumped into Aiden's tray at lunch — accidentally this time, genuinely. He said sorry, just once, with his eyes down. Aiden nodded. He didn't make a big thing of it. Some things, he thought, didn't need to become a story.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: It started with a slight wobble. Aiden was eating an apple when he felt, for the first time in his life, that one of his front teeth was moving in a way that front teeth were definitely not supposed to move.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Three weeks later, the new tooth began to come through. It was enormous relative to the gap — a proper square adult tooth in a mouth that had been full of small rounded baby ones. Aiden looked at himself in the mirror and felt extremely strange.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Socks was fascinated by both of them through this whole period. He kept trying to look in their mouths. He seemed to find it deeply interesting, which Aiden added to the field notebook under: Primate-specific dental curiosity — possible.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The entrance was a proper drawbridge — working, over a real water-filled moat. It was smaller than he'd imagined and more real than he'd imagined. Aiden crossed it one step at a time, listening to the echo of his footsteps on old wood, thinking about every person who had crossed it before him.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The great hall was vast and grey and cool. The stone floor was uneven and worn in paths where feet had walked for centuries. Aiden crouched and pressed his hand flat to the floor. Six hundred years of footsteps had passed here. He could not quite hold that thought all at once.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: Betty had the guide map. She navigated with precise efficiency — Great Hall, Armoury, North Tower, King's Chamber, Dungeon — the best order for minimum backtracking. Aiden followed behind her, reading every information board they passed, completely at home in a world of facts.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: In the armoury, there was a full suit of plate armour. It was smaller than Aiden expected. The guide told them that real knights were roughly the same size as Dad, which was very hard to imagine. Aiden tried on a gauntlet under supervision. His hand barely fit inside.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The dungeon was underground and smelled of cold stone and old air. Betty read every board by torchlight. Aiden stood still in the near-dark for a moment and thought about how this exact place had been here through everything — and felt briefly, appropriately small.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: On the way down, Aiden stopped at a narrow slit window in the tower wall — an arrow loop. He looked through it. The angle was exact — a perfect line of sight across the approach. Everything in this building was designed for a specific purpose.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: In the castle shop, Betty bought a small accurate model of the castle as it looked in 1350, before a section of wall fell. Aiden bought a book on medieval building techniques. Dad bought a novelty ceramic goblet that Mum said, quietly but firmly, would not be coming into the kitchen.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: In the castle shop, Betty bought a small accurate model of the castle as it looked in 1350, before a section of wall fell. Aiden bought a book on medieval building techniques. Dad bought a novelty ceramic goblet that Mum said, quietly but firmly, would not be coming into the kitchen.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: That evening, Aiden wrote in his field notebook for a long time — the drawbridge, the worn floor, the arrow loop, the view. At the bottom of the last page he wrote: Things were happening before we got here. They'll keep happening after. That's not sad. That's just how big it is. He underlined it.

uses.title: Wiggly's Messy Day
uses.pageText: Wiggly felt sad. My tail has a mind of its own, said Wiggly.

uses.title: Honky's Inside Voice
uses.pageText: Honky, said Bossy, you need an inside voice. What is an inside voice? A quiet one. I do not have one of those.

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Cheeky had an idea. Cheeky always had ideas. Most of them were pranks.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: One day it was a pile of extra berries for Chompy. Someone knows me very well, said Chompy, already eating them.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: Dozy hugged the pillow. Thank you, said Dozy. Both of you. Then Dozy fell asleep, right there, on the spot.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy went back to the tree. Got three wing-flaps up. Landed neatly on a branch. Sat very high up and looked at all of Sunny Hollow below. Oh, said Flappy quietly. That is quite good actually.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: The Dino Pals went to look. A huge pile of rocks had fallen in the night and blocked the stream above.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: Grumpy sat on the rock alone. It was peaceful. But after a while, Grumpy called: There is a good-looking bush to your left. Thanks, Grumpy! said Chompy. Grumpy said nothing. But the corner of the mouth went up. Just slightly.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: There would be a running race, a jumping contest, a loudness competition, and a prize for the tidiest corner of the Hollow. More events to be decided, said Bossy. I have a clipboard.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Dozy slept through most of the events and woke up in time for the picnic. Did I win anything? said Dozy. Most restful competitor, said Bossy. Deserved, said Dozy, and fell asleep again.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Who won the Games overall? said Chompy, having eaten most of the prize berries. Everyone won something, said Bossy. That is the point. Even me? said Chompy. Chompy wins: Most Enthusiastic Participant. That is because I ate all the prizes, said Chompy. Yes, said Bossy.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: In the dream, Sunny Hollow was made of clouds. Dozy was walking on clouds. The clouds were warm and soft, which was very agreeable.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: Chompy was there, but all the food was made of more clouds. This is disappointing, said Dream Chompy.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: Dozy floated on a cloud past the Rainbow Waterfall. But in the dream, the waterfall was made of warm golden light. Oh, said Dozy. This is very nice.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: At the top of Mount Rumble, all the Dino Pals were there. Sitting on the warm peak. Watching all of Sunny Hollow spread out below, tiny and green and perfect.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: At the top of Mount Rumble, all the Dino Pals were there. Sitting on the warm peak. Watching all of Sunny Hollow spread out below, tiny and green and perfect.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: It was exactly like this, said Dozy, looking at all of them, but cloudier. Dozy's eyes closed again. Wake me for supper.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: Zippy ran three circuits of Sunny Hollow. Then four. Then five. Then kept going.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: BANG. They were off. Zippy was first. Of course. But the very fast runner was close. Very close.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: But you didn't, said Sunny. Zippy ran four more circuits of Sunny Hollow. I know, said Zippy, on the third lap. I just like to make sure.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Shy, who knew every hidden corner of the Fernwood, led everyone to the deepest part of Cozy Cave. Shy knew exactly where it was warmest.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Shy, who knew every hidden corner of the Fernwood, led everyone to the deepest part of Cozy Cave. Shy knew exactly where it was warmest.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: When it passed, Sunny Hollow sparkled. We did that, said Sunny. All of us. Not bad, said Grumpy. From Grumpy, that meant wonderful.

uses.title: Grumpy Gets a Surprise
uses.pageText: Grumpy had a lot of cake.

uses.title: Hungry Eats Everything
uses.pageText: Hungry ate one more bit of grass.

uses.title: Shy and Cuddly Find Each Other
uses.pageText: Both of them are happy.

uses.title: The Big Farm Party
uses.pageText: Grumpy had a lot of cake.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: "Did it run out of brave?" asked Pip.

uses.title: Fern Grows Too Much
uses.pageText: The next morning, the plant had grown so much it filled the Hollow Oak doorway. Leaves were coming out of every window. "Oh," said Fern.

uses.title: Fern Grows Too Much
uses.pageText: Luna was inside. "Fern," said Luna, through a curtain of leaves, "do something, please."

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: One day, Burrow got stuck on the other side of the stream. "Help!" called Burrow. "I cannot find the tunnel. Everything looks the same to me!"

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: They crossed back together. Stone did not look at the water. Stone looked at the far end of the bridge. One step, then another.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: On the first day: a small puff of smoke. Just smoke. No fire at all.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: On the fifth day, Glimmer breathed in as deeply as possible. A warm puff came out. It smelled of cinnamon. "That's something," said Pip.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: And a jet of brilliant orange fire came out. The fox ran. The seeds were safe.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: She said the spell. There was a flash of bright blue light. Then it was quiet.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: Right, said Wren. She walked to the beginning of the spell. She read it again. This time, she read it forwards.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: There was another flash of blue. Wren was back to her normal size. She brushed off her robe. She straightened her hat.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: Flint had decided to map every single path in Moonwood. He had a new roll of parchment and a good quill. He started at the Hollow Oak and walked north.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: He walked for three days. He did not stop. His map grew longer and longer. It was full of detail.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: On the fourth day, Flint held up his finished map. "There," he said. "Every path in Moonwood. All of it."

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: Flint took out a new piece of parchment. "I'll make another one," he said. He was not upset about this. He had always known the paths would move.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: I have been here longer than the Hollow Oak, said the fish. Dewdrop looked carefully. The fish was, if anything, quite new-looking. I know all the secrets of the Deep Dark, the fish added.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: Dewdrop was not sure any of this was true. She knew the Deep Dark secrets. They were kept by a very old badger, not a fish.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: Can fish lie? Dewdrop asked Burrow. Some of them can, said Burrow. Which fish? The new one with the blue stripe, said Dewdrop. Burrow had not seen a new fish.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: They walked along the walls slowly. There were drawings of things no one had seen in hundreds of years. What is this place? asked Fern.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: They walked along the walls slowly. There were drawings of things no one had seen in hundreds of years. What is this place? asked Fern.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: Burrow found a blank patch of wall. He picked up a small flat stone. Very carefully, he drew the Hollow Oak. Now we are in it too, he said.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: He sneezed at breakfast. The porridge turned into a bird. The bird flew out of the window. Spark stared at his empty bowl.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Sorry, said Spark. This was his third sorry. He meant all three of them very much.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: Luna gave one to each creature. One for each of them. The seeds glowed gently in their hands. Plant them this afternoon, said Luna.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: They planted the seeds in a ring around the Hollow Oak. One from each of them. In the golden afternoon light.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: What would have happened if you hadn't remembered? asked Wren. I did remember, said Luna. With help. She looked at all of them. That is the point.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
At the edge of the marsh, the noise came again.
It was even louder.
Pip's hair stood on end.
Stone appeared behind him.
"I came anyway," said Stone.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
Stone stood up and called out across the marsh.
It was the loudest sound Pip had ever heard.
Louder than the toadling.
Much louder.
Something answered from the far side of the marsh.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
On the first day, Spark explained fire.
He drew many diagrams.
The diagrams were very complicated.
Glimmer did not understand any of them.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
At the end of the day, they sat down.
Spark could not fly.
Glimmer had not breathed fire properly yet.
But something was different.
Neither of them could say exactly what.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
At the end of the day, they sat down.
Spark could not fly.
Glimmer had not breathed fire properly yet.
But something was different.
Neither of them could say exactly what.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
Flint opened his satchel.
Seven maps fell out.
One was of the coast.
One was upside down.
None of them were quite right.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
Flint opened his satchel.
Seven maps fell out.
One was of the coast.
One was upside down.
None of them were quite right.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
The mushroom's glow changed.
It pulsed once — pointing.
Another mushroom far away pulsed the same way.
And another.
A trail of glowing mushrooms lit up through the trees.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
Wren and Flint followed the mushroom trail.
The forest opened up.
The golden light of the Whispering Meadow was ahead.
"Oh," said Flint.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Burrow was digging a new tunnel.
He dug every morning.
He liked the quiet of it.
He liked the dark of it.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Burrow was digging a new tunnel.
He dug every morning.
He liked the quiet of it.
He liked the dark of it.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
The room had carvings on every wall.
It had small glowing stones in the ceiling.
It smelled of old wood and old magic.
Burrow had never seen it before.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
"This is the Memory Room," said Luna.
"This is where Moonwood keeps its oldest stories."
Burrow looked at the carvings.
"All of them?" he asked.
"All of them," said Luna.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
"This is the Memory Room," said Luna.
"This is where Moonwood keeps its oldest stories."
Burrow looked at the carvings.
"All of them?" he asked.
"All of them," said Luna.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Luna settled on a ledge.
She folded her wings.
She looked at the carvings for a moment.
"The first story of Moonwood," she began,
"is this."

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
In the morning, Burrow woke up.
He looked around.
Pip and Glimmer were standing in front of him.
"Good morning," said Burrow.
There was a long pause.

uses.title: Fern and Wren and the Wrong Potion
uses.pageText:
Wren poured the potion on the plants.
The plants stood very straight.
Then they leaned.
Then one of them took a step.

uses.title: Fern and Wren and the Wrong Potion
uses.pageText:
Fern went to the middle of the clearing.
She closed her eyes.
She sang.
Very softly.
The same song from long ago.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Dewdrop found Stone at the Hollow Oak.
"I need your hands," she said.
"Just to reach in and move a rock."
Stone understood immediately.
Then Stone understood all of it.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Stone stood at the edge of the Crystal Stream.
The water sparkled.
Stone's feet stayed on the bank.
"I don't like getting wet," said Stone.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
The fish made a very large splash.
Stone was completely wet.
All of Stone.
Dewdrop was not wet.
"I'm sorry," said Dewdrop.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Stone sat and dripped.
Stone looked at the arm.
Stone looked at the rest of Stone.
"The fish is free," said Stone.
"Yes," said Dewdrop.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
Everyone came back with nothing.
Then they saw Fern.
She was sitting in the middle of the clearing.
Small glowing seedlings were growing all around her.
"Oh," said everyone.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
It was the middle of the night.
Everyone was nearly asleep.
Then a light flashed.
Then another.
Then small glowing things began to fall from the sky.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
They gathered the star spirits.
There were many of them.
Stone held several.
Wren had two in her hat.
They kept bouncing.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
They climbed to the top.
Moonwood spread below them in the dark.
The sky was full of stars above.
The star spirits reached upward with their tiny arms.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
"There is a room here," said Burrow.
He found a small door near the roots.
It was very small.
Too small for most of them.
"I can go," said Fern.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Inside was a room.
It was small and warm.
It was full of collected things.
A tiny creature was searching through them.
She did not look up.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Fern looked around the room.
Then she looked at Twig.
The spectacles were on top of Twig's head.
They had been there all along.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Fern came back through the door.
"Her name is Twig," said Fern.
"She has lived here for many years."
Everyone looked at Luna.
"Of course," said Luna.
"Twig."

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Flint went left.
Then left again.
Then the Fog Marsh was ahead of him.
"I am taking a scenic route," said Flint.
There was no one to hear him.

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
Pip noticed it on a Tuesday.
The grey fog of the Fog Marsh was closer.
It had never come this near before.
He marked the edge with a stick.

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
By the end of the week, the fog had crept closer.
The mushrooms at the edge were going out.
One by one.
The fog was not stopping.

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
At the centre of the marsh, they found it.
A figure made of grey mist.
It sat against a dead tree.
It was very still.
It looked very sad.

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
At the centre of the marsh, they found it.
A figure made of grey mist.
It sat against a dead tree.
It was very still.
It looked very sad.

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
The spirit pointed to the edges.
They looked.
There were things left behind.
A rope.
An old lamp.
A pile of mushroom caps.
Left by Moonwood creatures.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
Glimmer breathed in.
Deeply.
Glimmer breathed out.
A jet of orange fire came out.
Small.
Perfect.
Real.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
The light spread.
Mushroom to mushroom.
Lamp to lamp.
Through every path.
Through every dark corner of Moonwood.
All of it lighting up.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
The light spread.
Mushroom to mushroom.
Lamp to lamp.
Through every path.
Through every dark corner of Moonwood.
All of it lighting up.

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
It was the deepest part of the night.
Moonwood was very quiet.
Then there was a sound at the edge of the clearing.
Something small was there.

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
It was the deepest part of the night.
Moonwood was very quiet.
Then there was a sound at the edge of the clearing.
Something small was there.

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
Pip opened the door.
A small creature was at the edge of the clearing.
It had very large silver eyes.
It was frightened.
It did not run.

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
Pip brought it inside.
Everyone woke up.
Stone brought a piece of acorn biscuit.
The creature ate it very carefully.
It watched everyone with its large silver eyes.

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
The creature ran to its family.
The family gathered around it.
They looked at the Moonwood creatures.
Not afraid.
Just looking.
Then one of them blinked.

uses.title: Day and Night
uses.pageText: We sleep at night.

uses.title: Animals at Night
uses.pageText: Some animals sleep in the day. They wake up at night. They are nocturnal.

uses.title: Animals at Night
uses.pageText: An owl can see in the dark. It hunts at night. Twit-twoo!

uses.title: Animals at Night
uses.pageText: A bat flies at night. It finds food in the dark. Bats eat insects.

uses.title: Animals at Night
uses.pageText: A fox hunts at night. It has big ears. It moves quietly.

uses.title: Animals at Night
uses.pageText: These animals come out at night. We are asleep when they are busy!

uses.title: Hello, Sun!
uses.pageText: At midday, the sun is high. It is the hottest part of the day.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: Look up at night. You can see the moon! The moon is big and round.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: The moon shines at night. It gives us light in the dark.

uses.title: Day and Night
uses.pageText: At night, the sun goes away. The sky turns dark.

uses.title: Day and Night
uses.pageText: At night, we sleep. Our bodies rest.

uses.title: Rocks and Pebbles
uses.pageText: Go outside and find a rock! Look at it carefully.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Sometimes, magma pushes up through a crack in the Earth. When it bursts out at the surface, we call it a volcano! The melted rock that flows out is called lava.

uses.title: Penguins
uses.pageText: Penguins are extraordinary swimmers. They can swim at 25 kilometres per hour. They leap in and out of the water and can dive very deep to catch fish.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Some spiders do not use webs at all. Jumping spiders leap onto their food. They have big eyes that face forward to judge distance. A jumping spider can leap 20 times its own body length!

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The ocean has different layers. Near the surface, there is plenty of sunlight and warmth. Further down, it grows colder and darker. Below 200 metres, no sunlight reaches at all.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Water drips from cave ceilings for thousands of years. The minerals in the water build up slowly. These hanging stone shapes are called stalactites. They form one tiny drip at a time.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Caves are home to many animals. Bats sleep hanging upside down from cave ceilings by day. At dusk, thousands of bats fly out together to feed on insects in the night air.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Some creatures live only in caves and never come out. Over thousands of years, they have adapted. Cave fish are often pale or white — they have never needed colour. Many have no eyes at all.

uses.title: Bob and Nan go to the Beach
uses.pageText: Bob and Nan had fun at the beach!

uses.title: Bob and Nan's First Day at School
uses.pageText: Bob and Nan sit at a desk.

uses.title: Bob and Nan's First Day at School
uses.pageText: Bob and Nan had fun at school!

uses.title: James and Anna go to Space
uses.pageText: Anna grabbed her pen and drew the plan. "It needs big wings," she said, "and a pointed nose cone at the top."

uses.title: James and Anna and Chips
uses.pageText: They set off down the lane. Chips trotted along and stopped to munch the long grass at the sides.

uses.title: James and Anna and Chips
uses.pageText: Then Chips saw a big rose bush. He ran at it. CRUNCH! MUNCH! SNAP! The rose bush was gone.

uses.title: James and Anna and Chips
uses.pageText: Chips ate it all in a flash. He looked at the bowl. Then he looked at James. Then he looked at James's jumper.

uses.title: James and Anna and Chips
uses.pageText: Chips ate it all in a flash. He looked at the bowl. Then he looked at James. Then he looked at James's jumper.

uses.title: James and Anna and Chips
uses.pageText: Chips ate it all in a flash. He looked at the bowl. Then he looked at James. Then he looked at James's jumper.

uses.title: James and Anna go Shopping
uses.pageText: It was a bright autumn day. Mum had a long list. "I need help at the shop," she said. "Can you both come?"

uses.title: James and Anna go Shopping
uses.pageText: At the till, Mum let James put the shopping on the belt. He was VERY careful with the eggs.

uses.title: James and Anna go Shopping
uses.pageText: At home, Mum made lunch. After, they had their cakes. Chips ate the paper bag. "CHIPS!" they said. But they were laughing too hard to be cross.

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: At the dentist, there was a big fish tank in the waiting room! Bright fish darted in and out of rocks and weeds.

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: James came out. "It did not hurt at all!" he said. "And the chair goes UP and DOWN!" Anna laughed.

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: That night, they brushed their teeth for a very long time. Chips sat at the bathroom door and watched. "Good night, Chips," said Anna. Chips blinked.

uses.title: James and Anna build a Tree House
uses.pageText: At the end of the garden stood a big old oak tree. James and Anna had been staring at it for days.

uses.title: James and Anna build a Tree House
uses.pageText: At the end of the garden stood a big old oak tree. James and Anna had been staring at it for days.

uses.title: James and Anna build a Tree House
uses.pageText: James and Anna climbed up and sat at the little window. "This is the best thing we have ever made," said Anna.

uses.title: James and Anna build a Tree House
uses.pageText: Mum sent up a tray of juice and biscuits on a rope. Dad waved from below. Chips jangled at the base of the tree, trying to reach the biscuits.

uses.title: James and Anna visit Grandma's Farm
uses.pageText: James and Anna were going to stay at Grandma's farm for the week. They packed their bags — and Chips got in the car too.

uses.title: James and Anna visit Grandma's Farm
uses.pageText: Then Percy the pig got out. He ran in and out of the hen house and round and round the yard at top speed.

uses.title: James and Anna and the School Play
uses.pageText: At the very end, everyone stood and clapped. James and Anna walked to the front of the stage and bowed together.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: Bella chased Chips. Chips chased Bella. They ran round and round the garden at an absolutely ridiculous speed.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: Mrs. Chen stood at the garden gate and laughed so hard that she had to sit down on the grass.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: At last, both Chips and Bella lay down on the lawn side by side, panting. Chips licked Bella's ear. Bella licked Chips's nose.

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: "How did you DO that?" said James. "I kept my eyes on where I wanted to go," said Anna. "Don't look at the ground."

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: They ate their sandwiches by the duck pond. Chips waited at home. Chips and bikes were definitely not a good idea.

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: On the way home, James and Anna raced. They crossed the gate post at exactly the same time. A perfect tie.

uses.title: James, Anna and Chips go Camping
uses.pageText: At midnight, a fox barked in the lane. Chips went very still. James shone the torch outside. Nothing was there.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: The summer holidays were over at last. Aiden sat on his bed and stared at his new school bag. Grade 1. The words sounded bigger than they looked.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: The summer holidays were over at last. Aiden sat on his bed and stared at his new school bag. Grade 1. The words sounded bigger than they looked.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Betty was not worried at all. She had already packed her bag twice. "We're going to have proper lessons and proper homework," she said, bouncing on her toes. "Isn't that brilliant?" Aiden wasn't absolutely sure that it was.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: At lunch, they sat together by the window. Aiden opened his lunchbox and found a small folded note from Mum tucked under his sandwich. It said: You've got this, star. He smiled all the way through his apple.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Betty answered three questions out loud and got them all right. Aiden raised his hand once, very carefully, and he got his right too. Miss Okafor stuck a gold star beside both their names on the board. Aiden looked at his star for quite a long time.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Then there was Science — real Science, with a magnifying glass and a tray of soil and seeds. Aiden forgot to be nervous. He was too busy looking at a woodlouse through the magnifying glass and writing down exactly what he saw.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: At home time, Mum was waiting at the gate. She crouched down with an expectant look. "Well?" she said. They both started talking at exactly the same moment and didn't stop for ten minutes.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: At home time, Mum was waiting at the gate. She crouched down with an expectant look. "Well?" she said. They both started talking at exactly the same moment and didn't stop for ten minutes.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: At home time, Mum was waiting at the gate. She crouched down with an expectant look. "Well?" she said. They both started talking at exactly the same moment and didn't stop for ten minutes.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: It was the first warm Saturday of spring, and Aiden and Betty stood in the middle of the playroom staring at something that had got entirely out of control. Toys, books, games and puzzles were piled up to the shelves. There was even a foam sword that neither of them remembered buying.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: "We should have a yard sale," said Betty. She said it the way she said all her best ideas — quickly and firmly, as though the idea had already made up its mind. "We could make actual money." Aiden wasn't certain at first, but when she said the word money, he started to listen.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: On Saturday morning, they dragged two folding tables out to the front path and arranged everything carefully. The old teddies sat in a row at the back and looked slightly sorry for themselves. "They'll go to good homes," said Aiden, mostly to himself, as a form of reassurance.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: Then things got busy. Children came from further up the street with their parents. A woman bought a whole crate of craft supplies without looking at any of them. A small boy bought four plastic dinosaurs and a jigsaw puzzle and carried them away in a tight proud bundle. Things were selling faster than Betty could write them down.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: A girl called Rosa arrived late with her grandmother and spent a thoughtful amount of time choosing. She ended up with three books, a snow globe and the foam sword, which she tucked under her arm like a very satisfied general. Aiden watched the sword go and found he didn't mind at all.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: As Aiden folded up the last table, he found something wedged at the very back — his old stuffed elephant, Nelly, who he had completely forgotten was there. He held her for a long moment. Then he carried her inside and put her on the shelf above his desk. Some things, he decided, were not for selling.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: The last day of the summer term was also the loudest day of the school year. Aiden and Betty burst through the front door and both shouted "HOLIDAY!" at exactly the same moment, which echoed all the way up the stairs and made the dog next door bark.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: Aiden spent the whole first morning at a rock pool near the headland. He found three kinds of crab, a sea anemone that closed when you touched it, and a tiny fish he thought might be a blenny. He wrote everything down in his field notebook in careful columns.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: Betty was brilliant at boogie boarding from the very first wave. She rode it all the way to shore, fell off, laughed, and waded back in immediately. By the afternoon she was steering around in the foam. Dad tried it once and fell off at once, which everyone found funny, including Dad.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: Betty was brilliant at boogie boarding from the very first wave. She rode it all the way to shore, fell off, laughed, and waded back in immediately. By the afternoon she was steering around in the foam. Dad tried it once and fell off at once, which everyone found funny, including Dad.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: Betty found a small smooth white pebble at the shoreline and turned it over and over in her fingers all the way back to the cottage. She was going to put it on her windowsill at home, so she'd always have a piece of the coast — something real from a real day.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: Betty found a small smooth white pebble at the shoreline and turned it over and over in her fingers all the way back to the cottage. She was going to put it on her windowsill at home, so she'd always have a piece of the coast — something real from a real day.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: It was an ordinary Saturday in late August when Uncle Eddie arrived at the door with a travelling bag, a very wide smile, and something small and determined making a noise from inside his coat.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks looked at Aiden. Then he looked at Betty. Then he reached out one small black hand, calmly removed Aiden's watch from Aiden's wrist, and put it on his own. He looked at it with great satisfaction. "Charming," said Mum. "Yes," said Uncle Eddie, completely unsurprised.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks looked at Aiden. Then he looked at Betty. Then he reached out one small black hand, calmly removed Aiden's watch from Aiden's wrist, and put it on his own. He looked at it with great satisfaction. "Charming," said Mum. "Yes," said Uncle Eddie, completely unsurprised.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks looked at Aiden. Then he looked at Betty. Then he reached out one small black hand, calmly removed Aiden's watch from Aiden's wrist, and put it on his own. He looked at it with great satisfaction. "Charming," said Mum. "Yes," said Uncle Eddie, completely unsurprised.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie explained that he was returning to the rainforest for six months and couldn't bring Socks along this time. He looked at Dad with a hopeful expression. Dad said yes before Mum could say anything at all, which was exactly what Mum had expected him to do.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie explained that he was returning to the rainforest for six months and couldn't bring Socks along this time. He looked at Dad with a hopeful expression. Dad said yes before Mum could say anything at all, which was exactly what Mum had expected him to do.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "He loves shiny objects," Uncle Eddie explained at dinner. "He adores warm spots — the airing cupboard is a particular risk. And if he gets bored, he will find a way to become interesting." Everyone filed this information away carefully.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks sat at the table in a tiny red waistcoat that Uncle Eddie had stitched for him. He watched everyone use their fork with great attention. Then he picked up his own fork and used it correctly. Then he threw the fork across the room. "He does that every evening," said Uncle Eddie. "We've never understood why."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: That night, Dad built Socks a cosy sleeping box — a wooden crate lined with a soft fleece blanket — and settled it in the warm corner of the kitchen. In the morning, Socks was not in it. He was curled up fast asleep at the foot of Aiden's bed, his small black hand curled around Aiden's pencil torch.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Over the following weeks, Socks wove himself into the house. He had his own peg for his waistcoat. He met them at the door when they came home from school. He sat on Dad's shoulder while Dad read the newspaper and turned the pages for him, very seriously.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "He couldn't have got out," said Dad. "All the windows were shut last night." Then Mum remembered the bathroom window — the small one above the bath, left open just a crack for steam. She looked at Aiden and Aiden looked at Betty. A crack that was, they all realised at the same moment, almost exactly the width of a small monkey.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "He couldn't have got out," said Dad. "All the windows were shut last night." Then Mum remembered the bathroom window — the small one above the bath, left open just a crack for steam. She looked at Aiden and Aiden looked at Betty. A crack that was, they all realised at the same moment, almost exactly the width of a small monkey.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "He couldn't have got out," said Dad. "All the windows were shut last night." Then Mum remembered the bathroom window — the small one above the bath, left open just a crack for steam. She looked at Aiden and Aiden looked at Betty. A crack that was, they all realised at the same moment, almost exactly the width of a small monkey.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Aiden re-read his field notebook carefully, looking for anything useful. He had written: Drawn to shiny objects. Drawn to warm spots. Will follow interesting smells. Exceptionally good at getting into places he shouldn't. He stared at that last line for quite a long time. It did not narrow things down.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Aiden re-read his field notebook carefully, looking for anything useful. He had written: Drawn to shiny objects. Drawn to warm spots. Will follow interesting smells. Exceptionally good at getting into places he shouldn't. He stared at that last line for quite a long time. It did not narrow things down.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: The school hall was full of projects — a volcano that erupted three times, a model solar system, a survey about favourite foods with real graphs. Betty looked at all of them carefully and said nothing. Aiden chewed the inside of his cheek.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: The reserve was layered with sounds — insects, birds, the river — all at once and all different. Socks sat on Aiden's shoulder and went completely still, his head turning slowly to track each sound. Aiden had never seen him so quiet.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Socks had other interests. He had crossed a wide fallen tree over the river before anyone had finished the sentence. Aiden said they should follow. Uncle Eddie said absolutely not. Then Uncle Eddie looked at the tree. Then they crossed it.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: He led them to a shallow pool in a mossy clearing — fed by a spring, perfectly clear and still. Two dragonflies skimmed the surface, electric blue. Aiden crouched at the edge and looked in. Small things moved in the shallows. He forgot to breathe.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: "Do you think he misses the rainforest?" Aiden asked one evening. Betty thought for a long time. "I think he's decided this is his rainforest," she said. Aiden looked at Socks on his shoulder. "Yeah," he said. "I think so too."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: There was a boy in Year 2 called Marcus who thought it was funny to call people names. He had decided, for reasons that made no sense at all, that Aiden's name was Lazy-den. He said it on Wednesday. Two children laughed, which made him say it again on Thursday.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Aiden didn't say anything. He went home and sat on his bed and stared at the ceiling. He wasn't crying, but he wasn't fine either. He didn't really want to talk about it — which Betty noticed immediately.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "What happened?" said Betty. Aiden told her in pieces, looking at the floor. Betty listened to all of it without saying anything. Then she said: "He's wrong. And being wrong loudly is still just being wrong." Aiden thought about that.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: On Friday, Marcus said it again in the lunch queue. Betty was right there. She looked at Marcus with exactly one raised eyebrow and said, clearly: "His name is Aiden. Which you know." Marcus looked surprised. He didn't say anything else.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: On Monday, Marcus said it one more time, in front of a small group. Aiden turned around. He looked at Marcus directly for a moment. Then he said, clearly: "My name is Aiden." That was all. He turned back.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: A week later, Marcus bumped into Aiden's tray at lunch — accidentally this time, genuinely. He said sorry, just once, with his eyes down. Aiden nodded. He didn't make a big thing of it. Some things, he thought, didn't need to become a story.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Miss Okafor had noticed, in the way that good teachers always notice. She started a class discussion about what it means to be fair, and what you do when things aren't. Several children looked at the floor. Marcus looked at the window.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Miss Okafor had noticed, in the way that good teachers always notice. She started a class discussion about what it means to be fair, and what you do when things aren't. Several children looked at the floor. Marcus looked at the window.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Betty lost her first tooth the very next day, which nobody had seen coming. It came out at lunch, and she held it up and examined it with great interest before putting it in her pocket, as if this were a routine scientific procedure.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: "Does it hurt?" said Aiden. "Not really," said Betty. "It felt strange for a second. Then it was over." She looked at the gap in her mouth in a small mirror. "It's just a tooth," she said. "A very old, very small tooth."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Aiden's tooth came out on a Thursday. Not dramatically — he was reading his book and he touched it and then it was just there in his fingers, which was very quick and very strange and did not hurt at all.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Three weeks later, the new tooth began to come through. It was enormous relative to the gap — a proper square adult tooth in a mouth that had been full of small rounded baby ones. Aiden looked at himself in the mirror and felt extremely strange.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: "I think he'll be disappointed when we stop changing," said Aiden. "He already has all the teeth he'll get," said Betty. Socks demonstrated this by grinning at them both from very close range, showing every single tooth.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The entrance was a proper drawbridge — working, over a real water-filled moat. It was smaller than he'd imagined and more real than he'd imagined. Aiden crossed it one step at a time, listening to the echo of his footsteps on old wood, thinking about every person who had crossed it before him.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The great hall was vast and grey and cool. The stone floor was uneven and worn in paths where feet had walked for centuries. Aiden crouched and pressed his hand flat to the floor. Six hundred years of footsteps had passed here. He could not quite hold that thought all at once.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: Betty had the guide map. She navigated with precise efficiency — Great Hall, Armoury, North Tower, King's Chamber, Dungeon — the best order for minimum backtracking. Aiden followed behind her, reading every information board they passed, completely at home in a world of facts.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The North Tower had one hundred and twelve steps. They counted every one, out loud, all together. The staircase was so narrow they had to go single file. At the top: the whole landscape, the river, the town, a motorway miles away. The same view and entirely different.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: On the way down, Aiden stopped at a narrow slit window in the tower wall — an arrow loop. He looked through it. The angle was exact — a perfect line of sight across the approach. Everything in this building was designed for a specific purpose.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The drive home was quiet in the way that follows something large. "What are you thinking about?" said Mum. Aiden and Betty both answered at the same time, with completely different answers. "That," said Mum, "is exactly right."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: That evening, Aiden wrote in his field notebook for a long time — the drawbridge, the worn floor, the arrow loop, the view. At the bottom of the last page he wrote: Things were happening before we got here. They'll keep happening after. That's not sad. That's just how big it is. He underlined it.

uses.title: Chompy's Big Lunch
uses.pageText: That night, Chompy looked at the stars. I wonder what breakfast will be, said Chompy.

uses.title: Bouncy Bumps Into Everything
uses.pageText: All the Dino Pals looked at Bouncy. Sorry, said Bouncy, smiling.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down
uses.pageText: Sunny found Zippy. I was looking at a flower, said Zippy. I went past it twelve times first.

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Now Cheeky was muddy. The Dino Pals looked at Cheeky. Cheeky looked at the Dino Pals.

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Now Cheeky was muddy. The Dino Pals looked at Cheeky. Cheeky looked at the Dino Pals.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: Cheeky had a plan. Cheeky would stay up all night to watch. Cheeky fell asleep at midnight.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: I cannot leave the cave, said Fancy. Not like this. Fancy sat very still and stared at the cave wall.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Honky offered to shout at it until it moved. Everyone agreed this would make things much worse.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Fancy looked in the pool. Oh, said Fancy. Oh, that is much better. Fancy looked at Wiggly. Thank you. A real thank you.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: The next morning, Fancy left a beautifully woven bracelet outside Wiggly's cave. Wiggly's tail knocked it away at once. Sorry! said Wiggly. It is fine, said Fancy. And meant it.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: It could be anywhere, said Bossy, looking at the clipboard. Sunny Hollow is very big.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: I can see the mud puddle, said Clumsy. I can see the berry bushes. I can see Chompy at the berry bushes, which is not a surprise.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: How did it get there? said Grumpy. Everyone looked at Bouncy. I bounced past it, said Bouncy. SORRY.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy tried eating leaves. Fine. Flappy tried catching insects mid-air. Remarkably good at this. Flappy was more surprised.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy went back to the tree. Got three wing-flaps up. Landed neatly on a branch. Sat very high up and looked at all of Sunny Hollow below. Oh, said Flappy quietly. That is quite good actually.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: One morning, Rainbow Waterfall was not making rainbows. It was not making anything at all. The waterfall had stopped.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: We need to move those rocks, said Bossy. Everyone tried pushing. The rocks did not move at all.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: Grumpy has a strong tail, said Sunny. Grumpy swung the club tail at the rocks. CLONK. One small rock moved. There were fifty more.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: Grumpy looked at Chompy in the ditch. Grumpy looked at the perfect flat rock. Grumpy sighed. Hold on.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: Grumpy looked at Chompy in the ditch. Grumpy looked at the perfect flat rock. Grumpy sighed. Hold on.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: This is a good rock, said Chompy. Yes, said Grumpy. Is there anything to eat near it? said Chompy. Grumpy pointed at the berry patch. Chompy went happily.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: I have an announcement! called Bossy, megaphone raised. We are having the First Sunny Hollow Games. Tomorrow. Everyone looked at each other.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: At the top of Mount Rumble, all the Dino Pals were there. Sitting on the warm peak. Watching all of Sunny Hollow spread out below, tiny and green and perfect.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: It was exactly like this, said Dozy, looking at all of them, but cloudier. Dozy's eyes closed again. Wake me for supper.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: Zippy held the small winner's pebble and looked at it. Zippy, said Sunny, are you all right? I nearly lost, said Zippy.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Bouncy bounced up to reach the high branches and secure anything at risk. Only bumped into three things. A new record, said Bouncy.

uses.title: Noisy Tries to Be Quiet
uses.pageText: Noisy is not good at quiet.

uses.title: Giggly and Clucky Bake a Cake
uses.pageText: Clucky got the eggs. Giggly giggled at the eggs.

uses.title: Giggly and Clucky Bake a Cake
uses.pageText: Clucky got the flour. Giggly giggled at the flour.

uses.title: Giggly and Clucky Bake a Cake
uses.pageText: Giggly giggled at the cake.

uses.title: The Big Farm Party
uses.pageText: Grumpy sat at the back.

uses.title: The Big Farm Party
uses.pageText: Everyone is at the party.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: Pip looked at the stone. "But I don't feel brave," he said. "I feel the same as always."

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: That evening, Pip sat by the Crystal Stream. He looked at the stone. The gold glow had gone out.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: Pip looked at the stone for a long time. "I'll keep it," he said. "To remember."

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: Stone looked at the bridge. Stone looked at the water. Stone looked at Burrow on the other side.

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: Stone looked at the bridge. Stone looked at the water. Stone looked at Burrow on the other side.

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: Stone looked at the bridge. Stone looked at the water. Stone looked at Burrow on the other side.

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: They crossed back together. Stone did not look at the water. Stone looked at the far end of the bridge. One step, then another.

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: They crossed back together. Stone did not look at the water. Stone looked at the far end of the bridge. One step, then another.

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: "You crossed the bridge," said Pip. "Yes," said Stone. "But there might still be a troll under it." Stone looked at the bridge. "I should probably check."

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: On the first day: a small puff of smoke. Just smoke. No fire at all.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: Glimmer stared at their own mouth. "Oh," said Glimmer. The fire had been inside all along. "I just needed to really mean it."

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: Wren looked at her hands. Her hands were a very long way away. She was not taller. She was one inch tall.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: Wren found her spell book. It was enormous now. She climbed up onto it and looked at the spell. She had read it backwards.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: Luna flew in through the window. She looked at the desk. She looked more closely. "Wren?" said Luna.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: She looked at herself carefully. She was exactly the same height as before. The growing spell had not worked at all.

uses.title: Wren and the Backwards Spell
uses.pageText: She looked at herself carefully. She was exactly the same height as before. The growing spell had not worked at all.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: Flint had decided to map every single path in Moonwood. He had a new roll of parchment and a good quill. He started at the Hollow Oak and walked north.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: Flint sat down on a mossy rock. He looked at the map for a long time. It was very beautiful. It was also completely wrong.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: You are interesting, said Dewdrop. You are the only fish in this stream with a blue stripe. The fish looked at its own stripe. That is true, it said.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: I have found something, Burrow told everyone. They gathered at the Hollow Oak. A door, said Burrow, underground. Very old. I don't know what is inside.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: They gathered around the door. Luna looked at it for a long time. I know this door, she said slowly. I think. A very long time ago.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: He sneezed at breakfast. The porridge turned into a bird. The bird flew out of the window. Spark stared at his empty bowl.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: He sneezed at breakfast. The porridge turned into a bird. The bird flew out of the window. Spark stared at his empty bowl.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: He sneezed in the Whispering Meadow. Every flower changed colour at the same moment. The meadow turned entirely blue. It was very quiet.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Sorry, said Spark. The flowers looked at him. He looked at them. His nose twitched again.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Sorry, said Spark. The flowers looked at him. He looked at them. His nose twitched again.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Whatever you do, said Fern, looking at the Crystal Stream, do NOT sneeze near the water.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: Was it something to do with the Crystal Stream? asked Dewdrop. Luna stopped walking. She looked at the stream for a moment. Wait, said Luna.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: What would have happened if you hadn't remembered? asked Wren. I did remember, said Luna. With help. She looked at all of them. That is the point.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
At the edge of the marsh, the noise came again.
It was even louder.
Pip's hair stood on end.
Stone appeared behind him.
"I came anyway," said Stone.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
They stood at the edge together.
The fog was thick and grey-green.
The noise bounced off the twisted trees.
"Together," said Stone.
Pip nodded.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
Stone knelt down carefully.
"We will help," said Stone.
The toadling looked at Stone.
"You are very large," said the toadling.
"Yes," said Stone. "But I am gentle."

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
Back at the Hollow Oak, everyone asked:
"What was the loud thing?"
"Very small," said Pip.
"Very loud," said Stone.
They both smiled.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
"It flows," said Fern.
"But it does not sing," said Dewdrop.
"Something is wrong at the source."

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
"The song comes from the source," said Dewdrop.
"We must follow the stream up."
Fern looked at the deep forest ahead.
"Then we go," said Fern.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
At the source, they found it.
A great boulder had fallen.
It lay across the singing stones.
The stones could not sing.

uses.title: Fern and Dewdrop Save the Stream
uses.pageText:
At the Hollow Oak, everyone heard it.
"The stream is singing again!" said Pip.
"We just moved a stone," said Fern.
"And asked the water nicely," said Dewdrop.
"It did the rest."

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
On the third day, the diagrams had multiplied.
There were charts about heat.
Charts about breathing.
Charts about dragon anatomy.
Glimmer stared at them all.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
"Spark," said Glimmer.
"You are trying too hard."
"Fire is not thinking."
"It is feeling."
Spark looked at Glimmer for a long time.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
At the end of the day, they sat down.
Spark could not fly.
Glimmer had not breathed fire properly yet.
But something was different.
Neither of them could say exactly what.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
"We are here," said Flint.
He pointed at the map.
Wren looked around.
Grey fog was appearing between the trees.
"That is the Fog Marsh," said Wren.
"We are not near the meadow."

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
Wren tried her direction spell.
The arrow spun three times.
Then it pointed at Flint.
"That's you," said Wren.
"I know I'm here," said Flint.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
They sat down under a large mushroom.
They were tired.
They were lost.
The mushroom glowed cheerfully.
Wren looked at it.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
They arrived at the Whispering Meadow.
It was exactly where they had been going.
Flint wrote something on his map.
"Mushroom trail," he said.
"I should have had that already."

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
"Why didn't we try that first?" asked Flint.
"I don't know," said Wren.
She looked back at the mushroom trail.
"They seemed happy about it though."
The last mushroom blinked once and went out.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
"This is the Memory Room," said Luna.
"This is where Moonwood keeps its oldest stories."
Burrow looked at the carvings.
"All of them?" he asked.
"All of them," said Luna.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Luna settled on a ledge.
She folded her wings.
She looked at the carvings for a moment.
"The first story of Moonwood," she began,
"is this."

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
Then — a sound.
A shuffling.
A round shape moving through the clearing.
Pip and Glimmer looked at each other.
They crept closer.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Dewdrop was at the Crystal Stream.
She was looking at something in the water.
It was a large fish.
It was stuck.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Dewdrop was at the Crystal Stream.
She was looking at something in the water.
It was a large fish.
It was stuck.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Dewdrop found Stone at the Hollow Oak.
"I need your hands," she said.
"Just to reach in and move a rock."
Stone understood immediately.
Then Stone understood all of it.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Stone stood at the edge of the Crystal Stream.
The water sparkled.
Stone's feet stayed on the bank.
"I don't like getting wet," said Stone.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
"Just your arm," said Dewdrop.
"Just the one arm."
"Just for a moment."
Stone looked at the arm.
Stone looked at the water.
Stone sat down on the bank.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
"Just your arm," said Dewdrop.
"Just the one arm."
"Just for a moment."
Stone looked at the arm.
Stone looked at the water.
Stone sat down on the bank.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Stone sat and dripped.
Stone looked at the arm.
Stone looked at the rest of Stone.
"The fish is free," said Stone.
"Yes," said Dewdrop.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
Stone sat and dripped.
Stone looked at the arm.
Stone looked at the rest of Stone.
"The fish is free," said Stone.
"Yes," said Dewdrop.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
The magic seeds were gone.
The box that held them was open and empty.
Luna looked at the box for a long time.
"This is not good," she said.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
Luna called everyone together.
"The seeds keep Moonwood glowing," she said.
"Without them, the forest will grow dark."
Everyone looked at each other.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
Wren and Spark tried search spells.
The spells pointed at each other.
Stone looked under every log.
Gently.
There were no seeds under the logs.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
Pip caught one.
It was warm.
It had very large golden eyes.
It looked up at Pip and giggled.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
Luna pushed forward.
She looked at the star spirit over her glasses.
"I know what these are," said Luna.
"They lose their grip once a year."
"They need to go back before dawn."

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
"They need height," said Luna.
"The highest point in Moonwood."
Flint reached for his satchel.
Everyone looked at Flint.
"I know exactly where it is," said Flint.
Everyone kept looking at him.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
"They need height," said Luna.
"The highest point in Moonwood."
Flint reached for his satchel.
Everyone looked at Flint.
"I know exactly where it is," said Flint.
Everyone kept looking at him.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
The star spirits went up.
Slowly at first.
Then faster.
One by one they found their places.
The sky filled back up with stars.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
The last star spirit sat in Stone's hand.
It blinked its large gold eyes at everyone.
"See you next year," it said.
Then it bounced once.
Then it went up.
Then it was gone.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Fern looked around the room.
Then she looked at Twig.
The spectacles were on top of Twig's head.
They had been there all along.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Fern came back through the door.
"Her name is Twig," said Fern.
"She has lived here for many years."
Everyone looked at Luna.
"Of course," said Luna.
"Twig."

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
