uses.pageText: As Aiden folded up the last table, he found something wedged at the very back — his old stuffed elephant, Nelly, who he had completely forgotten was there. He held her for a long moment. Then he carried her inside and put her on the shelf above his desk. Some things, he decided, were not for selling.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: They were going to the coast for a whole week — a small blue cottage right on the clifftop, with a gate in the garden wall that opened straight onto the coastal path. Mum had booked it in January. They had been counting down ever since.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: The drive took three hours. Betty counted every red car they passed. Aiden read two chapters of his book, fell asleep on his own shoulder, woke up, read another chapter, and then asked "Are we nearly there?" for the fourth time. They were, finally, nearly there.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: The beach was a five-minute walk down a steep sandy path through tall marram grass. When they came over the last dune and the sea appeared — wide and green and going all the way to the horizon — Aiden stopped walking entirely and just looked for a long moment.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie explained that he was returning to the rainforest for six months and couldn't bring Socks along this time. He looked at Dad with a hopeful expression. Dad said yes before Mum could say anything at all, which was exactly what Mum had expected him to do.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks sat at the table in a tiny red waistcoat that Uncle Eddie had stitched for him. He watched everyone use their fork with great attention. Then he picked up his own fork and used it correctly. Then he threw the fork across the room. "He does that every evening," said Uncle Eddie. "We've never understood why."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Over the following weeks, Socks wove himself into the house. He had his own peg for his waistcoat. He met them at the door when they came home from school. He sat on Dad's shoulder while Dad read the newspaper and turned the pages for him, very seriously.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Over the following weeks, Socks wove himself into the house. He had his own peg for his waistcoat. He met them at the door when they came home from school. He sat on Dad's shoulder while Dad read the newspaper and turned the pages for him, very seriously.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "He couldn't have got out," said Dad. "All the windows were shut last night." Then Mum remembered the bathroom window — the small one above the bath, left open just a crack for steam. She looked at Aiden and Aiden looked at Betty. A crack that was, they all realised at the same moment, almost exactly the width of a small monkey.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Aiden re-read his field notebook carefully, looking for anything useful. He had written: Drawn to shiny objects. Drawn to warm spots. Will follow interesting smells. Exceptionally good at getting into places he shouldn't. He stared at that last line for quite a long time. It did not narrow things down.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Aiden re-read his field notebook carefully, looking for anything useful. He had written: Drawn to shiny objects. Drawn to warm spots. Will follow interesting smells. Exceptionally good at getting into places he shouldn't. He stared at that last line for quite a long time. It did not narrow things down.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: They decided to grow crystals. It was Betty's original idea and Aiden's second choice, which Betty said made it the obvious answer. They ordered the kit and spent four days watching for the post.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: Third place, with a commendation for experimental method, went to HOW DO CRYSTALS GROW? The commendation was on a proper certificate with a gold border. Betty read every word of it, twice.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie came back for a long weekend in June — browner from the sun, with a new bag of unusual gifts and more stories than they had time to hear. Socks heard the doorbell and ran in circles for forty-five seconds without stopping.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie came back for a long weekend in June — browner from the sun, with a new bag of unusual gifts and more stories than they had time to hear. Socks heard the doorbell and ran in circles for forty-five seconds without stopping.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie told them about the nature reserve two miles from town — woodland, a river, meadows, a hide for watching birds. "Socks would understand it completely," he said. Mum said she wasn't certain that made it a good idea. They went anyway.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Through the binoculars, Betty saw a kingfisher — a bright impossible dart of blue-orange above the water, there and then gone. She had to put the binoculars down and close her eyes for a moment. She had seen it. She wrote it in the log book.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: "Do you think he misses the rainforest?" Aiden asked one evening. Betty thought for a long time. "I think he's decided this is his rainforest," she said. Aiden looked at Socks on his shoulder. "Yeah," he said. "I think so too."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: There was a boy in Year 2 called Marcus who thought it was funny to call people names. He had decided, for reasons that made no sense at all, that Aiden's name was Lazy-den. He said it on Wednesday. Two children laughed, which made him say it again on Thursday.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Aiden felt two things: grateful for Betty, and also frustrated, because he wanted to have done it himself. Betty, who had been watching him think, said: "Next time you'll do it. I was just practising with you."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: On Monday, Marcus said it one more time, in front of a small group. Aiden turned around. He looked at Marcus directly for a moment. Then he said, clearly: "My name is Aiden." That was all. He turned back.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Betty read it over his shoulder. She didn't comment on it. She put her hand on his shoulder for a moment and went back to her own desk. That was enough.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: It started with a slight wobble. Aiden was eating an apple when he felt, for the first time in his life, that one of his front teeth was moving in a way that front teeth were definitely not supposed to move.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Mum said it was completely normal and that they had both lost teeth before when they were smaller — Aiden had even eaten one inside a peanut butter sandwich and not noticed for an hour. Aiden was not certain this was reassuring.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: "Does it hurt?" said Aiden. "Not really," said Betty. "It felt strange for a second. Then it was over." She looked at the gap in her mouth in a small mirror. "It's just a tooth," she said. "A very old, very small tooth."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: He held it up for a long time. It was tiny. It was the smallest thing that had ever felt significant. He put it in the small envelope Mum left for him, and when he placed it under his pillow it felt ceremonial.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: He held it up for a long time. It was tiny. It was the smallest thing that had ever felt significant. He put it in the small envelope Mum left for him, and when he placed it under his pillow it felt ceremonial.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: Dad had been talking about the castle trip since January. A proper medieval castle, forty minutes away — with a tower you could actually climb, a dungeon that was a real dungeon, and a great hall whose stone floor had been there for six hundred years. Betty had already read a book about it.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: They drove there on a bright Saturday in April. Aiden pressed his face to the car window when the castle appeared over the hill — grey stone towers above the treeline, impossibly old and very much still there. He felt something he didn't yet have a word for.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The great hall was vast and grey and cool. The stone floor was uneven and worn in paths where feet had walked for centuries. Aiden crouched and pressed his hand flat to the floor. Six hundred years of footsteps had passed here. He could not quite hold that thought all at once.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: Betty had the guide map. She navigated with precise efficiency — Great Hall, Armoury, North Tower, King's Chamber, Dungeon — the best order for minimum backtracking. Aiden followed behind her, reading every information board they passed, completely at home in a world of facts.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The dungeon was underground and smelled of cold stone and old air. Betty read every board by torchlight. Aiden stood still in the near-dark for a moment and thought about how this exact place had been here through everything — and felt briefly, appropriately small.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: "Imagine standing here," said Betty quietly, "and not knowing what was coming." Aiden thought about that for a long time, looking out. There was something important in it he couldn't quite hold yet. He wrote it in his notebook anyway, to think about later.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: On the way down, Aiden stopped at a narrow slit window in the tower wall — an arrow loop. He looked through it. The angle was exact — a perfect line of sight across the approach. Everything in this building was designed for a specific purpose.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: That evening, Aiden wrote in his field notebook for a long time — the drawbridge, the worn floor, the arrow loop, the view. At the bottom of the last page he wrote: Things were happening before we got here. They'll keep happening after. That's not sad. That's just how big it is. He underlined it.

uses.title: Dozy Won't Wake Up
uses.pageText: We have a problem, said Bossy. We need Dozy for the picnic!

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: One day it was a smooth pebble for Grumpy. Someone knows I like pebbles, said Grumpy, suspicious but pleased.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: One day it was a pile of extra berries for Chompy. Someone knows me very well, said Chompy, already eating them.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: One day it was a leafy fan for Dozy. This is perfect, said Dozy, already asleep with it.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: Has anyone seen my pillow? said Dozy. Dozy had been looking for it all morning. This was serious.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Grumpy, said Flappy. Am I a dinosaur or a bird? Grumpy thought for a very long time. You are Flappy, said Grumpy. That is enough.

uses.title: Sneezy and the Waterfall
uses.pageText: Sorry, said Sneezy, dabbing with the handkerchief. Every leaf had fallen off every tree. Do not apologise, said Grumpy. For once, Grumpy was actually smiling.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: There would be a running race, a jumping contest, a loudness competition, and a prize for the tidiest corner of the Hollow. More events to be decided, said Bossy. I have a clipboard.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Dozy slept through most of the events and woke up in time for the picnic. Did I win anything? said Dozy. Most restful competitor, said Bossy. Deserved, said Dozy, and fell asleep again.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: One afternoon, Dozy fell asleep in the Long Meadow. This was not unusual. But this time, Dozy did not wake up for a very, very long time.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: Dozy has been asleep for three hours, said Bossy. Should we be worried? said Bossy. Dozy looks very peaceful, said Sunny. They watched Dozy sleeping. Dozy was definitely very peaceful.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: It was exactly like this, said Dozy, looking at all of them, but cloudier. Dozy's eyes closed again. Wake me for supper.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: The second runner came over. Good race, they said. You too, said Zippy, breathing hard for the first time ever.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: We need to get ready, said Bossy. For once, nobody argued. They needed the plan.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: Pip looked at the stone for a long time. "I'll keep it," he said. "To remember."

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: Pip thought for a moment. "Stone," said Pip carefully. "You are a troll."

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: Stone thought about this for a long time. "Yes," said Stone. "But I still don't like the bridge."

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: On the second day: a tiny spark. It landed on a leaf. It glowed for one second. Then it went out.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: He walked for three days. He did not stop. His map grew longer and longer. It was full of detail.

uses.title: Flint Makes a Map
uses.pageText: Flint sat down on a mossy rock. He looked at the map for a long time. It was very beautiful. It was also completely wrong.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: The fish was quiet for a while. It swam a small, slow circle. Then it came back. Because I am new here, said the fish. And I wanted to sound interesting.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: They gathered around the door. Luna looked at it for a long time. I know this door, she said slowly. I think. A very long time ago.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: They stayed for a long time. No one wanted to leave. The room was very quiet and very warm.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Spark had a cold. Usually a cold was nothing much. But Spark's magic crackled around him all the time. A cold, for Spark, was a very big problem.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Every fish in the stream turned purple. The water sang in a different key. One fish turned into a frog for a moment, and then turned back.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: Was it something to do with the Crystal Stream? asked Dewdrop. Luna stopped walking. She looked at the stream for a moment. Wait, said Luna.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: Yes, said Luna. I remember now. She picked it up. I put it there to keep it safe. For today.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: Moonwood seeds, said Luna. From the first trees. For the day the old trees grow tired and need new ones beside them.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: Luna gave one to each creature. One for each of them. The seeds glowed gently in their hands. Plant them this afternoon, said Luna.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
"Why were you shouting?" asked Pip.
The toadling blinked.
"I am lost," it said.
"I was calling for my family."
Its voice was very small now.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
That afternoon, it was Glimmer's turn to teach.
Glimmer spread both wings.
Glimmer hovered for a moment.
Then landed.
"Like that," said Glimmer.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
"Spark," said Glimmer.
"You are trying too hard."
"Fire is not thinking."
"It is feeling."
Spark looked at Glimmer for a long time.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Luna was very large for a tunnel.
She came anyway.
She did not say anything about this.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
Luna settled on a ledge.
She folded her wings.
She looked at the carvings for a moment.
"The first story of Moonwood," she began,
"is this."

uses.title: Fern and Wren and the Wrong Potion
uses.pageText:
Then all the plants began to walk.
They were very polite about it.
They walked around Fern.
They walked around Wren.
They went for a stroll.

uses.title: Fern and Wren and the Wrong Potion
uses.pageText:
Wren found the problem.
She had used the wrong book.
"This is the motion recipe," she said.
"Not the growing recipe."
She showed Fern.
They were both quiet for a moment.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
"Just your arm," said Dewdrop.
"Just the one arm."
"Just for a moment."
Stone looked at the arm.
Stone looked at the water.
Stone sat down on the bank.

uses.title: Stone and Dewdrop and the Stuck Fish
uses.pageText:
They sat by the stream together.
Stone dripped for a long time.
The fish surfaced once.
It seemed happy.
"Good," said Stone.
And meant it.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
The magic seeds were gone.
The box that held them was open and empty.
Luna looked at the box for a long time.
"This is not good," she said.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
"They need height," said Luna.
"The highest point in Moonwood."
Flint reached for his satchel.
Everyone looked at Flint.
"I know exactly where it is," said Flint.
Everyone kept looking at him.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
"There is a room here," said Burrow.
He found a small door near the roots.
It was very small.
Too small for most of them.
"I can go," said Fern.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Fern went through the small door.
She was inside for a moment.
Then she called back:
"There is someone here."
Everyone pressed their ears to the door.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
"Hello," said Fern.
The tiny creature looked up.
"Have you seen my spectacles?" she said.
"I've been looking for three days."

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
Fern came back through the door.
"Her name is Twig," said Fern.
"She has lived here for many years."
Everyone looked at Luna.
"Of course," said Luna.
"Twig."

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
They made Twig a slightly larger door.
Twig came out for acorn biscuits.
She sat in the big room and looked around.
"I like it here," she said.
"But I like my room better."
"This is also very nice."

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Dewdrop won a gold leaf for finishing.
Burrow won a gold leaf for best route.
"I did not win," said Flint.
"You went to the Fog Marsh," said Pip.
"I saw many things," said Flint.
He was already drawing them.

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Dewdrop won a gold leaf for finishing.
Burrow won a gold leaf for best route.
"I did not win," said Flint.
"You went to the Fog Marsh," said Pip.
"I saw many things," said Flint.
He was already drawing them.

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
They marked the boundary at the Hollow Oak.
Everyone placed a stone.
"The marsh is the marsh," said Luna.
"Moonwood is Moonwood."
"And we leave space for both."

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
They all went together.
Luna led — her eyes could see in any dark.
Glimmer breathed a small flame for the path.
The creature walked between them.
Into the deep.

uses.title: Day and Night
uses.pageText: The Earth spins around. That is why we have day and night.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Deep underground, rock gets so hot that it melts. This melted rock is called magma. Magma is hotter than anything you can imagine.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Sometimes, magma pushes up through a crack in the Earth. When it bursts out at the surface, we call it a volcano! The melted rock that flows out is called lava.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Some spiders do not use webs at all. Jumping spiders leap onto their food. They have big eyes that face forward to judge distance. A jumping spider can leap 20 times its own body length!

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Most spiders are harmless to people. They eat insects that damage our plants. Without spiders, our gardens and crops would be full of pests. Spiders are very helpful friends.

uses.title: Caves
uses.pageText: Long ago, people lived in caves. They painted pictures on the cave walls. Cave paintings have been found that are more than 40,000 years old. The artists were humans just like us.

uses.title: Frogs
uses.pageText: A female frog lays hundreds of eggs in water. The eggs are called frogspawn. Each egg is surrounded by clear jelly that protects it and keeps it safe.

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: "The dentist is very kind," said Mum. "She just takes a little look inside your mouth. That is all."

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: James pressed his nose flat to the glass. "That one looks just like a tiny striped rocket!" he said.

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: That night, they brushed their teeth for a very long time. Chips sat at the bathroom door and watched. "Good night, Chips," said Anna. Chips blinked.

uses.title: James and Anna build a Tree House
uses.pageText: That night, they got their sleeping bags and climbed up to sleep. Stars shone above them. "Best. Night. Ever," said James. Anna smiled. She agreed.

uses.title: James and Anna visit Grandma's Farm
uses.pageText: That evening, Grandma made soup from the garden and fried the eggs James had found. It was the best meal they had ever tasted.

uses.title: James and Anna and the School Play
uses.pageText: On the day of try-outs, James roared so loud that Mrs. Green's glasses slid right down her nose. He got the part!

uses.title: James and Anna and the School Play
uses.pageText: The play went brilliantly after that. James roared and stomped and the little ones in the front row screamed and giggled.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: Mrs. Chen stood at the garden gate and laughed so hard that she had to sit down on the grass.

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: "How did you DO that?" said James. "I kept my eyes on where I wanted to go," said Anna. "Don't look at the ground."

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: That night their legs ached. But they were both smiling. "Same time tomorrow?" said James. Anna was already asleep.

uses.title: James, Anna and Chips go Camping
uses.pageText: They played cards in the tent by torchlight. Chips ate two cards before they noticed. The game got harder after that.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Betty was not worried at all. She had already packed her bag twice. "We're going to have proper lessons and proper homework," she said, bouncing on her toes. "Isn't that brilliant?" Aiden wasn't absolutely sure that it was.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Betty was not worried at all. She had already packed her bag twice. "We're going to have proper lessons and proper homework," she said, bouncing on her toes. "Isn't that brilliant?" Aiden wasn't absolutely sure that it was.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: Their new classroom was bright and busy, with bookshelves along every wall and a large window that looked out onto the playing field. Their teacher was called Miss Okafor. She had bright yellow glasses and smiled like she really meant it.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: "In Grade 1," said Miss Okafor, "we will read chapter books, solve number puzzles and begin to understand how the world around us works." Aiden thought that sounded like an awful lot — but he found he was leaning forward slightly without meaning to.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: After lunch came Maths. Miss Okafor wrote sums on the board, each one slightly harder than the last. Some of them made Aiden's brain feel stretched in an unfamiliar way. He was discovering that this was not entirely a bad feeling.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty Start Grade 1
uses.pageText: "Grade 1 is brilliant," announced Betty, just before bed. "It's actually not that bad," said Aiden, which from Aiden meant exactly the same thing. He turned his light off, closed his eyes, and was asleep before he could think of anything to worry about.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: It was the first warm Saturday of spring, and Aiden and Betty stood in the middle of the playroom staring at something that had got entirely out of control. Toys, books, games and puzzles were piled up to the shelves. There was even a foam sword that neither of them remembered buying.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty have a Yard Sale
uses.pageText: It was the first warm Saturday of spring, and Aiden and Betty stood in the middle of the playroom staring at something that had got entirely out of control. Toys, books, games and puzzles were piled up to the shelves. There was even a foam sword that neither of them remembered buying.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: They were going to the coast for a whole week — a small blue cottage right on the clifftop, with a gate in the garden wall that opened straight onto the coastal path. Mum had booked it in January. They had been counting down ever since.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: The cottage smelled of sea salt and old wood and something warm that Aiden couldn't name. They raced upstairs to choose rooms. There was a small room and a slightly bigger room. They flipped a coin — Aiden got the bigger room, but Betty got the one with the sea view, which meant it was perfectly even.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: Aiden spent the whole first morning at a rock pool near the headland. He found three kinds of crab, a sea anemone that closed when you touched it, and a tiny fish he thought might be a blenny. He wrote everything down in his field notebook in careful columns.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: On their last evening, they sat on the sea wall with fish and chips wrapped in paper. The chips were crispy and perfectly salty. Aiden told Mum they were the best chips he had ever eaten in his entire life, and Mum said that was the sea air doing it, and she was right.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Carefully, Uncle Eddie unzipped the carry-case. Inside, curled up like a small comma, was the most compact monkey Aiden had ever seen. He had cream-white fur on his face and chest, darker brown on his back, and small black hands and feet that looked, unmistakably, like he was wearing a pair of extremely neat little socks.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie explained that he was returning to the rainforest for six months and couldn't bring Socks along this time. He looked at Dad with a hopeful expression. Dad said yes before Mum could say anything at all, which was exactly what Mum had expected him to do.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks sat at the table in a tiny red waistcoat that Uncle Eddie had stitched for him. He watched everyone use their fork with great attention. Then he picked up his own fork and used it correctly. Then he threw the fork across the room. "He does that every evening," said Uncle Eddie. "We've never understood why."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Socks sat at the table in a tiny red waistcoat that Uncle Eddie had stitched for him. He watched everyone use their fork with great attention. Then he picked up his own fork and used it correctly. Then he threw the fork across the room. "He does that every evening," said Uncle Eddie. "We've never understood why."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: That night, Dad built Socks a cosy sleeping box — a wooden crate lined with a soft fleece blanket — and settled it in the warm corner of the kitchen. In the morning, Socks was not in it. He was curled up fast asleep at the foot of Aiden's bed, his small black hand curled around Aiden's pencil torch.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: He was also, as promised, occasionally naughty. He dropped a teaspoon into the toaster. He unravelled the entire roll of cling film in the kitchen drawer. He stole every single one of Betty's hair bobbles and lined them up on the windowsill in a precise order that nobody could explain.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: Aiden had been keeping a field notebook — just as Uncle Eddie had shown him. He had titled it: Socks: A Field Study. He had written things like: Prefers grapes to apple. Expresses disapproval by sitting with back turned. Unusually precise about the order of objects. He turned to a fresh page. It was going to take a very long time to fully understand Socks. He hoped, quietly, that he had the time.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: "He couldn't have got out," said Dad. "All the windows were shut last night." Then Mum remembered the bathroom window — the small one above the bath, left open just a crack for steam. She looked at Aiden and Aiden looked at Betty. A crack that was, they all realised at the same moment, almost exactly the width of a small monkey.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Aiden re-read his field notebook carefully, looking for anything useful. He had written: Drawn to shiny objects. Drawn to warm spots. Will follow interesting smells. Exceptionally good at getting into places he shouldn't. He stared at that last line for quite a long time. It did not narrow things down.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: By three o'clock, the sky had gone grey and the wind had picked up. Aiden was sitting on the front step, not saying much. He kept thinking about what Uncle Eddie had said once: that animals raised by hand always know where home is. He held onto that thought very carefully.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: By three o'clock, the sky had gone grey and the wind had picked up. Aiden was sitting on the front step, not saying much. He kept thinking about what Uncle Eddie had said once: that animals raised by hand always know where home is. He held onto that thought very carefully.

uses.title: Socks Goes Missing
uses.pageText: Then the phone rang. It was their neighbour Mrs Obi, from number thirty-seven, three houses down. Her voice was very precise. "I believe," she said carefully, "that there may be a small monkey in my kitchen. He appears to be eating my shortbread."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: The school hall was full of projects — a volcano that erupted three times, a model solar system, a survey about favourite foods with real graphs. Betty looked at all of them carefully and said nothing. Aiden chewed the inside of his cheek.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: That evening, Aiden added a new page to his field notebook: WHAT MAKES A GOOD EXPERIMENT. He had six points. Socks sat on the desk and watched him write, which Aiden had never seen him do before.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Science Fair
uses.pageText: "I think he might be learning," said Aiden carefully, watching Socks watch the pen. "Don't encourage him," said Betty, from the doorway. Socks blinked once, in a way that suggested he had already learned considerably more than anyone knew.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Uncle Eddie told them about the nature reserve two miles from town — woodland, a river, meadows, a hide for watching birds. "Socks would understand it completely," he said. Mum said she wasn't certain that made it a good idea. They went anyway.

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: Aiden had started a new notebook that evening — not the Socks field study, but a nature notebook. He had titled it with the date. Betty had started a matching one, without them discussing it. Both were already half a page in.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: There was a boy in Year 2 called Marcus who thought it was funny to call people names. He had decided, for reasons that made no sense at all, that Aiden's name was Lazy-den. He said it on Wednesday. Two children laughed, which made him say it again on Thursday.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: There was a boy in Year 2 called Marcus who thought it was funny to call people names. He had decided, for reasons that made no sense at all, that Aiden's name was Lazy-den. He said it on Wednesday. Two children laughed, which made him say it again on Thursday.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "What happened?" said Betty. Aiden told her in pieces, looking at the floor. Betty listened to all of it without saying anything. Then she said: "He's wrong. And being wrong loudly is still just being wrong." Aiden thought about that.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: That night, Aiden wrote in his notebook: When something is unfair, you have two choices — pretend it isn't happening, or decide what to do. He starred the second option. He didn't quite know yet what doing something looked like.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: On Monday, Marcus said it one more time, in front of a small group. Aiden turned around. He looked at Marcus directly for a moment. Then he said, clearly: "My name is Aiden." That was all. He turned back.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: He wrote in his notebook that evening: Saying a true thing clearly is harder than it looks and better than it sounds. He underlined it twice.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Betty read it over his shoulder. She didn't comment on it. She put her hand on his shoulder for a moment and went back to her own desk. That was enough.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Miss Okafor had noticed, in the way that good teachers always notice. She started a class discussion about what it means to be fair, and what you do when things aren't. Several children looked at the floor. Marcus looked at the window.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "The point," said Miss Okafor, "is not that everyone will always be kind. The point is that you always have a choice about how to respond — and that choice is completely yours." Aiden wrote it down. It felt like something worth keeping.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "The point," said Miss Okafor, "is not that everyone will always be kind. The point is that you always have a choice about how to respond — and that choice is completely yours." Aiden wrote it down. It felt like something worth keeping.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "The point," said Miss Okafor, "is not that everyone will always be kind. The point is that you always have a choice about how to respond — and that choice is completely yours." Aiden wrote it down. It felt like something worth keeping.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: It started with a slight wobble. Aiden was eating an apple when he felt, for the first time in his life, that one of his front teeth was moving in a way that front teeth were definitely not supposed to move.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: It started with a slight wobble. Aiden was eating an apple when he felt, for the first time in his life, that one of his front teeth was moving in a way that front teeth were definitely not supposed to move.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: He told Betty. Betty got the torch and studied it with great interest. "It's definitely loose," she said. "It'll fall out and a permanent one will grow. That's much better, actually." Aiden was not entirely sure that it was.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: That night, Aiden worried about the tooth. It felt wrong — like something was breaking. He wrote in his notebook: Things that are strange: losing a tooth. Also, why teeth? Socks sat on the desk and watched him with great curiosity.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: That night, Aiden worried about the tooth. It felt wrong — like something was breaking. He wrote in his notebook: Things that are strange: losing a tooth. Also, why teeth? Socks sat on the desk and watched him with great curiosity.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Mum said it was completely normal and that they had both lost teeth before when they were smaller — Aiden had even eaten one inside a peanut butter sandwich and not noticed for an hour. Aiden was not certain this was reassuring.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: He held it up for a long time. It was tiny. It was the smallest thing that had ever felt significant. He put it in the small envelope Mum left for him, and when he placed it under his pillow it felt ceremonial.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: In the morning, the tooth was gone and there was a coin in its place. Aiden knew, in the way children who read a lot know things, that it was Mum or Dad who had swapped it. He said nothing, because some things are better left as stories.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: Three weeks later, the new tooth began to come through. It was enormous relative to the gap — a proper square adult tooth in a mouth that had been full of small rounded baby ones. Aiden looked at himself in the mirror and felt extremely strange.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: Dad had been talking about the castle trip since January. A proper medieval castle, forty minutes away — with a tower you could actually climb, a dungeon that was a real dungeon, and a great hall whose stone floor had been there for six hundred years. Betty had already read a book about it.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The great hall was vast and grey and cool. The stone floor was uneven and worn in paths where feet had walked for centuries. Aiden crouched and pressed his hand flat to the floor. Six hundred years of footsteps had passed here. He could not quite hold that thought all at once.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: In the armoury, there was a full suit of plate armour. It was smaller than Aiden expected. The guide told them that real knights were roughly the same size as Dad, which was very hard to imagine. Aiden tried on a gauntlet under supervision. His hand barely fit inside.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: "Imagine standing here," said Betty quietly, "and not knowing what was coming." Aiden thought about that for a long time, looking out. There was something important in it he couldn't quite hold yet. He wrote it in his notebook anyway, to think about later.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: In the castle shop, Betty bought a small accurate model of the castle as it looked in 1350, before a section of wall fell. Aiden bought a book on medieval building techniques. Dad bought a novelty ceramic goblet that Mum said, quietly but firmly, would not be coming into the kitchen.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The drive home was quiet in the way that follows something large. "What are you thinking about?" said Mum. Aiden and Betty both answered at the same time, with completely different answers. "That," said Mum, "is exactly right."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The drive home was quiet in the way that follows something large. "What are you thinking about?" said Mum. Aiden and Betty both answered at the same time, with completely different answers. "That," said Mum, "is exactly right."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: That evening, Aiden wrote in his field notebook for a long time — the drawbridge, the worn floor, the arrow loop, the view. At the bottom of the last page he wrote: Things were happening before we got here. They'll keep happening after. That's not sad. That's just how big it is. He underlined it.

uses.title: Chompy's Big Lunch
uses.pageText: That night, Chompy looked at the stars. I wonder what breakfast will be, said Chompy.

uses.title: Dozy Won't Wake Up
uses.pageText: Dozy sniffed. Dozy opened one eye. Is that... lunch? said Dozy.

uses.title: Grumpy Needs Help
uses.pageText: Thank you, said Grumpy. Not that I needed it. But Grumpy was smiling. Just a little.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down
uses.pageText: Zippy ran so fast that Zippy ran right past the picnic. And the waterfall. And Sunny Hollow.

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Even Cheeky had to laugh. Okay, said Cheeky. That one was funny.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Bouncy offered to bounce on it gently. That is not what gently means, said Fancy.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Fancy looked in the pool. Oh, said Fancy. Oh, that is much better. Fancy looked at Wiggly. Thank you. A real thank you.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Bossy flies, said Flappy. Bossy is a Pterodactyl. You are an Archaeopteryx. That is different. How is it different? said Flappy. Grumpy did not actually know.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Grumpy, said Flappy. Am I a dinosaur or a bird? Grumpy thought for a very long time. You are Flappy, said Grumpy. That is enough.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy went back to the tree. Got three wing-flaps up. Landed neatly on a branch. Sat very high up and looked at all of Sunny Hollow below. Oh, said Flappy quietly. That is quite good actually.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Honky won the loudness competition. Every leaf fell off every tree. We all knew that would happen, said Grumpy.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Grumpy won the grumpiest face competition that Cheeky invented. Grumpy won immediately. I am not sure that is a compliment, said Grumpy. It absolutely is, said Cheeky.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Grumpy won the grumpiest face competition that Cheeky invented. Grumpy won immediately. I am not sure that is a compliment, said Grumpy. It absolutely is, said Cheeky.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Who won the Games overall? said Chompy, having eaten most of the prize berries. Everyone won something, said Bossy. That is the point. Even me? said Chompy. Chompy wins: Most Enthusiastic Participant. That is because I ate all the prizes, said Chompy. Yes, said Bossy.

uses.title: The Sunny Hollow Games
uses.pageText: Who won the Games overall? said Chompy, having eaten most of the prize berries. Everyone won something, said Bossy. That is the point. Even me? said Chompy. Chompy wins: Most Enthusiastic Participant. That is because I ate all the prizes, said Chompy. Yes, said Bossy.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: Dream Bouncy bounced so high that Bouncy went above the clouds and kept going. Everyone watched. Nobody was surprised.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Clumsy stood tall and looked out over the whole Hollow. The storm is coming from the east, said Clumsy. The tall ferns are already bending. That gives us time.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Wiggly's long tail swept the Big Flat Rock clear in seconds. Food, supplies, anything that could blow away. Sorry, said Wiggly, sweeping everything. This time everyone was grateful.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: When it passed, Sunny Hollow sparkled. We did that, said Sunny. All of us. Not bad, said Grumpy. From Grumpy, that meant wonderful.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: When it passed, Sunny Hollow sparkled. We did that, said Sunny. All of us. Not bad, said Grumpy. From Grumpy, that meant wonderful.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: Burrow appeared from a nearby tunnel. "That is a Bravery Stone," said Burrow. "Whoever holds it will feel brave."

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: "The stone did that!" said Pip. He tucked it safely into his pocket. Then he walked toward the Fog Marsh.

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: That evening, Pip sat by the Crystal Stream. He looked at the stone. The gold glow had gone out.

uses.title: Fern Grows Too Much
uses.pageText: Luna smiled. "That is quite nice, actually," said Luna. Fern smiled. She was very tired.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: "That is not fire," said Glimmer. "No," agreed Pip. "But it smells nice." Glimmer did not look convinced.

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: That evening, a Fog Marsh fox came creeping into Moonwood. It had found Fern's seed collection. The seeds were small and precious. Glimmer saw the fox.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: Dewdrop went back to the Crystal Stream. Why do you say things that are not true? she asked. She said it kindly. She just wanted to know.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: You are interesting, said Dewdrop. You are the only fish in this stream with a blue stripe. The fish looked at its own stripe. That is true, it said.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: After that, the fish told Dewdrop true things. Small things, mostly. Where the water was coldest. Where the most unusual pebbles were. These things were true.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: Inside was a small round room. The walls were covered in tiny glowing drawings. Trees and streams. Creatures and old paths. Every living thing that had ever been in Moonwood.

uses.title: Burrow Finds a Door
uses.pageText: The memory room, said Luna. That is what it was called. She touched the wall very gently. I remember now.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: What would have happened if you hadn't remembered? asked Wren. I did remember, said Luna. With help. She looked at all of them. That is the point.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
That afternoon, it was Glimmer's turn to teach.
Glimmer spread both wings.
Glimmer hovered for a moment.
Then landed.
"Like that," said Glimmer.

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
That afternoon, it was Glimmer's turn to teach.
Glimmer spread both wings.
Glimmer hovered for a moment.
Then landed.
"Like that," said Glimmer.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
"We are here," said Flint.
He pointed at the map.
Wren looked around.
Grey fog was appearing between the trees.
"That is the Fog Marsh," said Wren.
"We are not near the meadow."

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
They arrived at the Whispering Meadow.
It was exactly where they had been going.
Flint wrote something on his map.
"Mushroom trail," he said.
"I should have had that already."

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
"Why didn't we try that first?" asked Flint.
"I don't know," said Wren.
She looked back at the mushroom trail.
"They seemed happy about it though."
The last mushroom blinked once and went out.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
"It was you," said Pip gently. "You sleep-dig."
"I am very sorry," said Burrow.
He put his boot by the door.
"Will that stop you?" asked Glimmer.
"I don't know," said Burrow.
"I am asleep."

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
The magic seeds were gone.
The box that held them was open and empty.
Luna looked at the box for a long time.
"This is not good," she said.

uses.title: The Missing Magic Seeds
uses.pageText:
That night, Moonwood glowed more than ever.
The seedlings lit the ground.
Everyone sat outside the Hollow Oak.
"I'm sorry I forgot," said Fern.
"Don't be," said Luna.
"They like it better here."

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
That evening, the fog stayed at the line.
The mushrooms began to come back on.
One by one.
Pip watched them light up.
The marsh was where it should be.
The forest was where it should be.

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
They walked back through the Dark.
At the edge, Pip looked back.
One silver light blinked twice.
"That was brave," said Glimmer.
Pip touched the stone in his pocket.
"Yes," he said. "It ran home."
"That's the bravest kind."

uses.title: Bugs
uses.pageText:
A bug can hide.
Can you see it?

uses.title: Shapes
uses.pageText:
What shape is it?
Can you find it?

uses.title: Fast and Slow
uses.pageText:
Fast or slow?
Which do you like?

uses.title: Look at the Colours!
uses.pageText: Colours are all around us! What colour can you see?

uses.title: The Four Seasons
uses.pageText: Four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, winter. Which do you like best?

uses.title: Animals on the Farm
uses.pageText: Farms give us food. Thank you, farm animals!

uses.title: Shapes Everywhere
uses.pageText: Shapes are everywhere! Can you find shapes today?

uses.title: Hot and Cold
uses.pageText: What is hot? What is cold? Can you tell?

uses.title: Push and Pull
uses.pageText: You push a door open. You pull a door open too.

uses.title: Push and Pull
uses.pageText: You push a door open. You pull a door open too.

uses.title: Push and Pull
uses.pageText: You push a swing. The swing goes up high!

uses.title: Push and Pull
uses.pageText: You pull a zip. The zip opens up.

uses.title: Hello, Sun!
uses.pageText: The sun is our nearest star. Thank you, sun!

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: Look up at night. You can see the moon! The moon is big and round.

uses.title: My Five Senses
uses.pageText: Which sense do you like best?

uses.title: Staying Healthy
uses.pageText: Eat good food. Fruits and vegetables are good for you.

uses.title: Staying Healthy
uses.pageText: Sleep is important. Your body grows when you sleep.

uses.title: Bees
uses.pageText: One jar of honey needs thousands of bee trips to make. Bees visit two million flowers for just one jar! Next time you eat honey, think of all those busy bees.

uses.title: Volcanoes
uses.pageText: Deep underground, rock gets so hot that it melts. This melted rock is called magma. Magma is hotter than anything you can imagine.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: You can see the Moon most nights. On a clear night with a telescope, you can see the craters clearly. Look up tonight — the Moon is always there.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: You can see the Moon most nights. On a clear night with a telescope, you can see the craters clearly. Look up tonight — the Moon is always there.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: You can grow your own plant. Put a seed in some soil. Add water. Put it in a sunny spot. Then watch the cycle begin.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The deepest part of the ocean is called the Mariana Trench. It is nearly 11 kilometres deep. If you put the world's tallest mountain inside it, it would still be covered by water.

uses.title: Under the Ocean
uses.pageText: The ocean makes more than half the oxygen we breathe. Tiny plants called phytoplankton float near the surface. They use sunlight to make oxygen. Every other breath you take came from the ocean.

uses.title: James and Anna go to Space
uses.pageText: A small green alien ran to say hello. "My name is Zim!" it said. "Do you want to play?"

uses.title: James and Anna and Chips
uses.pageText: Chips had a blue bell on his collar. JINGLE! JINGLE! JINGLE! You could hear him coming from far away!

uses.title: James and Anna go Shopping
uses.pageText: It was a bright autumn day. Mum had a long list. "I need help at the shop," she said. "Can you both come?"

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: "Well done, both of you," said Mum. "You were so brave today." They each got a sticker — James got a rocket, Anna got a star.

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: "Well done, both of you," said Mum. "You were so brave today." They each got a sticker — James got a rocket, Anna got a star.

uses.title: James and Anna build a Tree House
uses.pageText: "I can help," said Dad, "but you two are in charge. You tell me the plan."

uses.title: James and Anna build a Tree House
uses.pageText: "I can help," said Dad, "but you two are in charge. You tell me the plan."

uses.title: James and Anna's New Bikes
uses.pageText: "How did you DO that?" said James. "I kept my eyes on where I wanted to go," said Anna. "Don't look at the ground."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty go on Holiday
uses.pageText: Aiden spent the whole first morning at a rock pool near the headland. He found three kinds of crab, a sea anemone that closed when you touched it, and a tiny fish he thought might be a blenny. He wrote everything down in his field notebook in careful columns.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and Socks
uses.pageText: "His name is Socks," said Uncle Eddie. "He was orphaned when he was very small, and I've raised him from a baby. He understands a lot of what you say, he copies behaviour, and he is completely tame." He paused just a moment. "He is also, just occasionally, a little bit naughty."

uses.title: Aiden, Betty and Socks's Big Adventure
uses.pageText: "Do you think he misses the rainforest?" Aiden asked one evening. Betty thought for a long time. "I think he's decided this is his rainforest," she said. Aiden looked at Socks on his shoulder. "Yeah," he said. "I think so too."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: That night, Aiden wrote in his notebook: When something is unfair, you have two choices — pretend it isn't happening, or decide what to do. He starred the second option. He didn't quite know yet what doing something looked like.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: On Friday, Marcus said it again in the lunch queue. Betty was right there. She looked at Marcus with exactly one raised eyebrow and said, clearly: "His name is Aiden. Which you know." Marcus looked surprised. He didn't say anything else.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Aiden felt two things: grateful for Betty, and also frustrated, because he wanted to have done it himself. Betty, who had been watching him think, said: "Next time you'll do it. I was just practising with you."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: Miss Okafor had noticed, in the way that good teachers always notice. She started a class discussion about what it means to be fair, and what you do when things aren't. Several children looked at the floor. Marcus looked at the window.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: "The point," said Miss Okafor, "is not that everyone will always be kind. The point is that you always have a choice about how to respond — and that choice is completely yours." Aiden wrote it down. It felt like something worth keeping.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: "You don't look strange," said Betty. "You look older." She said it the way she said true things — simply, as though it were just a fact. Aiden looked in the mirror again. It was going to take some getting used to.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty: New Teeth
uses.pageText: "You don't look strange," said Betty. "You look older." She said it the way she said true things — simply, as though it were just a fact. Aiden looked in the mirror again. It was going to take some getting used to.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: Dad had been talking about the castle trip since January. A proper medieval castle, forty minutes away — with a tower you could actually climb, a dungeon that was a real dungeon, and a great hall whose stone floor had been there for six hundred years. Betty had already read a book about it.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: The drive home was quiet in the way that follows something large. "What are you thinking about?" said Mum. Aiden and Betty both answered at the same time, with completely different answers. "That," said Mum, "is exactly right."

uses.title: Chompy's Big Lunch
uses.pageText: Sunny shared her lunch. Here you go, Chompy! said Sunny.

uses.title: Grumpy Needs Help
uses.pageText: Thank you, said Grumpy. Not that I needed it. But Grumpy was smiling. Just a little.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down
uses.pageText: Zippy! called Sunny. Where are you going? I DON'T KNOW! called Zippy, already gone.

uses.title: Honky's Inside Voice
uses.pageText: Honky, said Bossy, you need an inside voice. What is an inside voice? A quiet one. I do not have one of those.

uses.title: Honky's Inside Voice
uses.pageText: Maybe Honky's voice is very useful after all, said Bossy. THANK YOU! said Honky. Every leaf fell off again.

uses.title: Cheeky's Prank Goes Wrong
uses.pageText: Cheeky helped clean Fancy's rock. Will you do any more pranks? asked Fancy. Maybe just one more, said Cheeky. And winked.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: Shy! said Sunny, softly. The gifts are from you, aren't they? Shy nodded, going very pink.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: They were the best gifts we ever had, said Sunny. Will you come and sit with us? Shy came out. Just a little way. But it was something.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Clumsy looked in from a great height. It looks fine to me, said Clumsy. You cannot even see your own feet, said Fancy.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Fancy looked in the pool. Oh, said Fancy. Oh, that is much better. Fancy looked at Wiggly. Thank you. A real thank you.

uses.title: Fancy's Bad Day
uses.pageText: Fancy looked in the pool. Oh, said Fancy. Oh, that is much better. Fancy looked at Wiggly. Thank you. A real thank you.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: Can you see the pillow? said Dozy. There was a long pause. Oh, said Clumsy. Yes. It is in the waterfall.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: Dozy hugged the pillow. Thank you, said Dozy. Both of you. Then Dozy fell asleep, right there, on the spot.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: Dozy hugged the pillow. Thank you, said Dozy. Both of you. Then Dozy fell asleep, right there, on the spot.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: We make a good team, said Clumsy. You see the problem. I reach the problem. Exactly, said Clumsy, and accidentally knocked off Wiggly's hat. Sorry.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: I should be able to fly, said Flappy. I have wings. You are also a dinosaur, said Grumpy. Dinosaurs do not fly.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Bossy flies, said Flappy. Bossy is a Pterodactyl. You are an Archaeopteryx. That is different. How is it different? said Flappy. Grumpy did not actually know.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy asked Sunny. You are wonderful just as you are! said Sunny. But what AM I? said Flappy. Wonderful! said Sunny. Flappy went away still confused.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Flappy asked Sunny. You are wonderful just as you are! said Sunny. But what AM I? said Flappy. Wonderful! said Sunny. Flappy went away still confused.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: Grumpy, said Flappy. Am I a dinosaur or a bird? Grumpy thought for a very long time. You are Flappy, said Grumpy. That is enough.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: But dinosaurs do not nest in trees, said Flappy. You do, said Grumpy. And birds do not live in Sunny Hollow with everyone else. You do, said Grumpy.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: But dinosaurs do not nest in trees, said Flappy. You do, said Grumpy. And birds do not live in Sunny Hollow with everyone else. You do, said Grumpy.

uses.title: What is Flappy?
uses.pageText: So I am something new? said Flappy. You are something Flappy, said Grumpy. Which nobody else is.

uses.title: Chompy and Grumpy's Day Out
uses.pageText: Thank you, said Chompy. Hmph, said Grumpy. They sat on the rock together. Less peaceful with Chompy. But not actually terrible.

uses.title: Dozy's Wonderful Dream
uses.pageText: I can see everything from here, said Dream Dozy. We can always see everything, said Dream Sunny. You just need to be up high enough. Dozy thought about this.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: Are you practising? said Wiggly. I am thinking, said Zippy. You run to think? I always run. The thinking happens in between.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: Are you practising? said Wiggly. I am thinking, said Zippy. You run to think? I always run. The thinking happens in between.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: The second runner came over. Good race, they said. You too, said Zippy, breathing hard for the first time ever.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: Zippy held the small winner's pebble and looked at it. Zippy, said Sunny, are you all right? I nearly lost, said Zippy.

uses.title: Zippy's Race
uses.pageText: But you didn't, said Sunny. Zippy ran four more circuits of Sunny Hollow. I know, said Zippy, on the third lap. I just like to make sure.

uses.title: Muddy Has a Bath
uses.pageText: "You need a bath," said Clucky.

uses.title: Grumpy's Secret
uses.pageText: "You can look," said Grumpy. "But do not tell."

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: Burrow smiled. "The stone doesn't do anything," he said. "I wanted to see what you would do. And you were brave."

uses.title: Pip and the Bravery Stone
uses.pageText: Burrow smiled. "The stone doesn't do anything," he said. "I wanted to see what you would do. And you were brave."

uses.title: Fern Grows Too Much
uses.pageText: "How did you make it stop?" asked Pip. "I didn't make it do anything," said Fern. "I asked it nicely."

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: Pip thought for a moment. "Stone," said Pip carefully. "You are a troll."

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: Stone reached the other side. Stone reached down and picked up Burrow very carefully. "Oh, thank you," said Burrow. "I was going in circles."

uses.title: Stone Crosses the Bridge
uses.pageText: "You crossed the bridge," said Pip. "Yes," said Stone. "But there might still be a troll under it." Stone looked at the bridge. "I should probably check."

uses.title: Glimmer Tries and Tries
uses.pageText: "Maybe you need to try harder," said Spark. Spark's own magic crackled around his ears. Glimmer tried harder. More smoke came out. Still no fire.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: Dewdrop went back to the Crystal Stream. Why do you say things that are not true? she asked. She said it kindly. She just wanted to know.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: You are interesting, said Dewdrop. You are the only fish in this stream with a blue stripe. The fish looked at its own stripe. That is true, it said.

uses.title: Dewdrop and the Lying Fish
uses.pageText: You are interesting, said Dewdrop. You are the only fish in this stream with a blue stripe. The fish looked at its own stripe. That is true, it said.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Whatever you do, said Fern, looking at the Crystal Stream, do NOT sneeze near the water.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: I think, said Dewdrop slowly, we should find you a cold remedy before anything else changes.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: This was the problem with forgetting things. You couldn't always remember what you had forgotten. Luna knew it was important. She knew it was today.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: This was the problem with forgetting things. You couldn't always remember what you had forgotten. Luna knew it was important. She knew it was today.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: What do you remember about it? asked Pip. I remember it was today, said Luna. And it was important. And... she paused. I think it was outside.

uses.title: What Luna Forgot
uses.pageText: What would have happened if you hadn't remembered? asked Wren. I did remember, said Luna. With help. She looked at all of them. That is the point.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
"Why were you shouting?" asked Pip.
The toadling blinked.
"I am lost," it said.
"I was calling for my family."
Its voice was very small now.

uses.title: Pip and Stone and the Loud Thing
uses.pageText:
Stone knelt down carefully.
"We will help," said Stone.
The toadling looked at Stone.
"You are very large," said the toadling.
"Yes," said Stone. "But I am gentle."

uses.title: Glimmer and Spark Make a Deal
uses.pageText:
"Spark," said Glimmer.
"You are trying too hard."
"Fire is not thinking."
"It is feeling."
Spark looked at Glimmer for a long time.

uses.title: Wren and Flint Get Lost
uses.pageText:
Wren tried her direction spell.
The arrow spun three times.
Then it pointed at Flint.
"That's you," said Wren.
"I know I'm here," said Flint.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
"Have you been here before?" asked Burrow.
"Yes," said Luna.
She looked around the room.
"A very long time ago."
"What is it?" asked Burrow.

uses.title: Burrow and Luna and the Old Secret
uses.pageText:
It was very late when Burrow noticed.
"Will you tell me the rest?" he asked.
"Yes," said Luna.
"There is quite a lot."
They both settled in.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
The next night, it happened again.
More things had moved.
"Was it you?" asked Stone.
"No," said Pip.
"Was it you?" asked Pip.
"No," said everyone.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
The next night, it happened again.
More things had moved.
"Was it you?" asked Stone.
"No," said Pip.
"Was it you?" asked Pip.
"No," said everyone.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
"It was you," said Pip gently. "You sleep-dig."
"I am very sorry," said Burrow.
He put his boot by the door.
"Will that stop you?" asked Glimmer.
"I don't know," said Burrow.
"I am asleep."

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
"It was you," said Pip gently. "You sleep-dig."
"I am very sorry," said Burrow.
He put his boot by the door.
"Will that stop you?" asked Glimmer.
"I don't know," said Burrow.
"I am asleep."

uses.pageText:
"It was you," said Pip gently. "You sleep-dig."
"I am very sorry," said Burrow.
He put his boot by the door.
"Will that stop you?" asked Glimmer.
"I don't know," said Burrow.
"I am asleep."

uses.title: Fern and Wren and the Wrong Potion
uses.pageText:
"Are you sure?" said Fern.
"Completely," said Wren.
She had practised many times.
Mostly.

uses.title: Fern and Wren and the Wrong Potion
uses.pageText:
Everything was back.
"I'm sorry," said Wren.
"Did you learn something?" asked Fern.
"Yes," said Wren. "I need more books."
"Fewer," said Fern.
"Fewer books."

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
"What are you?" asked Pip.
The star spirit blinked its large gold eyes.
"Star," it said.
Its voice was very small.
"Fell," it added.

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
"This way," said Flint.
He was right.
The Tumblerock Cliffs rose ahead.
"You found it," said Pip.
"I always find things," said Flint.
"Eventually."

uses.title: The Night the Stars Fell
uses.pageText:
The last star spirit sat in Stone's hand.
It blinked its large gold eyes at everyone.
"See you next year," it said.
Then it bounced once.
Then it went up.
Then it was gone.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
"Hello," said Fern.
The tiny creature looked up.
"Have you seen my spectacles?" she said.
"I've been looking for three days."

uses.title: The Big Moonwood Race
uses.pageText:
Dewdrop won a gold leaf for finishing.
Burrow won a gold leaf for best route.
"I did not win," said Flint.
"You went to the Fog Marsh," said Pip.
"I saw many things," said Flint.
He was already drawing them.

uses.title: The Fog Marsh Mystery
uses.pageText:
When the edge was clear, the spirit stood.
Its shape was clearer now.
"Thank you," said the spirit.
It was not mist anymore.
It was something more solid.
Something more itself.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
The fire faded slowly.
Moonwood kept its glow.
Luna looked at Glimmer over her glasses.
"Quite controlled," said Luna.
"Thank you," said Glimmer.

uses.title: Glimmer Breathes Fire at Last
uses.pageText:
"I did it," said Glimmer.
"You did," said Pip.
"I'd like to do it again," said Glimmer.
Everyone who heard this took a small step back.
"We know," said everyone.

uses.title: One Night in the Deep Dark
uses.pageText:
"We'll take you home," said Pip.
"But the Deep Dark—" said Wren.
"We'll go together," said Pip.
Everyone looked at each other.
"Together," said Stone.

uses.pageText: A whale is big. A fish is small.

uses.title: Big and Small
uses.pageText: Big or small — all things are special! What is big? What is small?

uses.title: Big and Small
uses.pageText: Big or small — all things are special! What is big? What is small?

uses.title: Things That Float and Sink
uses.pageText: A big rock is heavy. Heavy things often sink.

uses.title: Hello, Sun!
uses.pageText: The sun is a big, hot star. It is very far away.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: Look up at night. You can see the moon! The moon is big and round.

uses.title: The Moon
uses.pageText: People have been to the moon! They wore big white suits.

uses.title: How I Grow
uses.pageText: I eat well to grow. Food helps my body get big and strong.

uses.title: Rocks and Pebbles
uses.pageText: Rocks are hard. Rocks can be big or small.

uses.title: Spiders
uses.pageText: Some spiders do not use webs at all. Jumping spiders leap onto their food. They have big eyes that face forward to judge distance. A jumping spider can leap 20 times its own body length!

uses.title: Bob and Nan go to the Park
uses.pageText: Bob got on the big swing.

uses.title: Bob and Nan go to the Park
uses.pageText: Nan got on the big swing.

uses.title: Bob and Nan go to the Park
uses.pageText: Bob and Nan ran up the big hill.

uses.title: Bob and Nan's First Day at School
uses.pageText: It is the big day.

uses.title: Nan and Bob go to the Zoo
uses.pageText: Bob sees a big cat.

uses.title: Nan and Bob go to the Zoo
uses.pageText: Nan and Bob see the big fish.

uses.title: Nan and Bob go to the Zoo
uses.pageText: Bob and Nan see the big ape.

uses.title: Nan and Bob go to the Zoo
uses.pageText: The big ape ate a fig.

uses.title: Nan and Bob: Bob's Birthday Party
uses.pageText: It is Bob's big day!

uses.title: Nan and Bob: Bob's Birthday Party
uses.pageText: Nan has a big gift for Bob.

uses.title: Nan and Bob: Bob's Birthday Party
uses.pageText: Mum lit the big cake.

uses.title: Nan and Bob: Bob's Birthday Party
uses.pageText: Bob can see six big candles.

uses.title: Nan and Bob: Bob's Birthday Party
uses.pageText: Nan and Bob ate the big cake!

uses.title: Nan and Bob Learn to Read
uses.pageText: Nan has a big red book.

uses.title: Fluff Visits the Vet
uses.pageText: Fluff sits on the big bed.

uses.title: James and Anna go to Space
uses.pageText: James and Anna were in the garden. They had lots of big, flat boxes.

uses.title: James and Anna go to Space
uses.pageText: Anna grabbed her pen and drew the plan. "It needs big wings," she said, "and a pointed nose cone at the top."

uses.title: James and Anna go to Space
uses.pageText: They flew past big round planets. Some had red spots. Some had wide, shining rings!

uses.title: James and Anna go to Space
uses.pageText: They landed on the moon with a big BUMP! It was pale and still and very, very quiet.

uses.title: James and Anna and Chips
uses.pageText: James and Anna had a pet goat. His name was Chips. He was small and white with big brown patches.

uses.title: James and Anna and Chips
uses.pageText: Then Chips saw a big rose bush. He ran at it. CRUNCH! MUNCH! SNAP! The rose bush was gone.

uses.title: James and Anna and Chips
uses.pageText: "Oh, Chips!" said Anna. But she gave him a big hug. Chips licked her right on the nose.

uses.title: James and Anna go Shopping
uses.pageText: The shop was big and bright. It smelled of fresh bread and ripe fruit.

uses.title: James and Anna go Shopping
uses.pageText: Anna ran to find the bread. She picked the big round loaf with seeds on top. It smelled amazing!

uses.title: James and Anna go Shopping
uses.pageText: Then Anna spotted the cake stand! Big cakes, small cakes, jam tarts and iced buns — all in a long, shining row.

uses.title: James and Anna go Shopping
uses.pageText: James chose a big slice of lemon cake with thick white icing. Anna chose a pink strawberry jam tart.

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: At the dentist, there was a big fish tank in the waiting room! Bright fish darted in and out of rocks and weeds.

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: "James!" called the dentist. He stood up. He walked in. The big chair went up and down like a ride!

uses.title: James and Anna go to the Dentist
uses.pageText: "Anna!" called the dentist. Anna walked in. She sat in the big chair. She had to admit — it was like a ride.

uses.title: James and Anna build a Tree House
uses.pageText: At the end of the garden stood a big old oak tree. James and Anna had been staring at it for days.

uses.title: James and Anna build a Tree House
uses.pageText: Dad did the tricky high bits — the tall planks and the big nails. James and Anna passed the tools and held the wood still.

uses.title: James and Anna visit Grandma's Farm
uses.pageText: Grandma's farm was big and sunny. There were hens in the yard, ducks by the pond and a very fat pig called Percy.

uses.title: James and Anna visit Grandma's Farm
uses.pageText: Grandma had a big brown horse called Bess. She was huge and gentle. Her nose was the softest thing James had ever felt.

uses.title: James and Anna visit Grandma's Farm
uses.pageText: Anna got to brush Bess's mane. James gave her a big red apple. Bess sniffed it — then snaffled the whole thing in one go!

uses.title: James and Anna and the School Play
uses.pageText: Anna did not want to be the dragon. She wanted to paint the big backdrop — the scenery behind the stage.

uses.title: Chips's Play Date
uses.pageText: Their neighbour Mrs. Chen had a big, bouncy dog called Bella. "Would Chips like a play date?" Mrs. Chen asked one morning.

uses.title: James, Anna and Chips go Camping
uses.pageText: Dad put up a big green tent in the back garden. "We are going camping!" he said. "Just for one night."

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Bully
uses.pageText: A week later, Marcus bumped into Aiden's tray at lunch — accidentally this time, genuinely. He said sorry, just once, with his eyes down. Aiden nodded. He didn't make a big thing of it. Some things, he thought, didn't need to become a story.

uses.title: Aiden and Betty and the Castle
uses.pageText: That evening, Aiden wrote in his field notebook for a long time — the drawbridge, the worn floor, the arrow loop, the view. At the bottom of the last page he wrote: Things were happening before we got here. They'll keep happening after. That's not sad. That's just how big it is. He underlined it.

uses.title: Chompy's Big Lunch
uses.pageText: Chompy's tummy was very big now. I am... still a little hungry, said Chompy.

uses.title: Sunny's Rainy Day
uses.pageText: It rained in Sunny Hollow. Big dark clouds rolled in.

uses.title: Grumpy Needs Help
uses.pageText: Grumpy was stuck. Grumpy's tail was caught under a big rock.

uses.title: Zippy Slows Down
uses.pageText: It was very quiet. Zippy looked around. There were flowers. There was a big blue sky.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: Every morning, the Dino Pals found a small gift on the Big Flat Rock. Nobody knew who left them.

uses.title: Shy's Secret Gift
uses.pageText: The next morning, eleven gifts were on the Big Flat Rock. One from each Dino Pal. A small pink paw reached out and took them, one by one.

uses.title: Clumsy to the Rescue
uses.pageText: It could be anywhere, said Bossy, looking at the clipboard. Sunny Hollow is very big.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Storm coming, said Grumpy. Big one. Grumpy was almost always right about weather. Everyone believed Grumpy.

uses.title: The Big Storm
uses.pageText: Wiggly's long tail swept the Big Flat Rock clear in seconds. Food, supplies, anything that could blow away. Sorry, said Wiggly, sweeping everything. This time everyone was grateful.

uses.title: Tiny is Very Small
uses.pageText: Tiny cannot open the big door.

uses.title: Brave Climbs the Hay Bale
uses.pageText: The hay bale is big.

uses.title: Brave Climbs the Hay Bale
uses.pageText: Very, very big.

uses.title: Hungry Eats Everything
uses.pageText:
Hungry ate the big cake.
"My cake!" said Grumpy.

uses.title: Splashy Finds a Puddle
uses.pageText:
The puddle gets big.
The puddle gets very big.

uses.title: Splashy Finds a Puddle
uses.pageText:
The puddle gets big.
The puddle gets very big.

uses.title: Speedy Slows Down
uses.pageText: Speedy runs to the big hill.

uses.title: Cuddly Wants a Hug
uses.pageText: Woolly gave Cuddly a big hug.

uses.title: Bouncy and Speedy Have a Race
uses.pageText: They ran past the big hill.

uses.title: Tiny and Brave Go on an Adventure
uses.pageText: They went to the big hill. No hat.

uses.title: Shy and Cuddly Find Each Other
uses.pageText: Cuddly went past the big tree.

uses.title: Shy and Cuddly Find Each Other
uses.pageText: Shy is in the big tree!

uses.title: Shy and Cuddly Find Each Other
uses.pageText: They sat in the big tree.

uses.title: Grumpy's Secret
uses.pageText: Big red flowers. Big yellow flowers.

uses.title: Grumpy's Secret
uses.pageText: Big red flowers. Big yellow flowers.

uses.title: The Big Farm Party
uses.pageText: Clucky made a big cake.

uses.title: Spark's Very Big Sneeze
uses.pageText: Spark had a cold. Usually a cold was nothing much. But Spark's magic crackled around him all the time. A cold, for Spark, was a very big problem.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
Night fell.
Moonwood glowed softly.
Pip and Glimmer hid behind the big mushroom.
They watched.
Nothing happened.

uses.title: Pip and Glimmer and the Night Watch
uses.pageText:
Then Burrow sat down.
Against the big mushroom.
Pip and Glimmer were still behind it.
Burrow began to snore.

uses.title: Something Lives in the Hollow Oak
uses.pageText:
They made Twig a slightly larger door.
Twig came out for acorn biscuits.
She sat in the big room and looked around.
"I like it here," she said.
"But I like my room better."
"This is also very nice."

uses.title: What is Weather?
uses.pageText: Rumble! Flash! A storm is here. Then the rain falls.

uses.title: Day and Night
uses.pageText: Day, then night, then day again. Every single day!

uses.title: Day and Night
uses.pageText: Day, then night, then day again. Every single day!

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: First, a tiny root pushes down into the soil. Roots drink up water from the ground. Then a small shoot pushes up toward the light above.

uses.title: How Seeds Grow
uses.pageText: You can grow your own plant. Put a seed in some soil. Add water. Put it in a sunny spot. Then watch the cycle begin.
